stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Data Imagine we are comparing test scores across three different teaching methods (Group A, B, and C). If you look at the raw data in the visual panel, you'll notice that not everyone in Group A scored exactly the same. There is a natural spread, or noise , within every group. This is everyday biological, psychological, or measurement variation.

stages.title: The Research Question
stages.text: Stage 02 The Research Question Our question isn't about individuals; it's about the group averages (the black lines). Are the gaps between these group means large enough to confidently say the teaching methods have different effects? Or are the means just slightly off from each other by pure chance, drowning in the natural noise of the students? Teaching Interaction: Shape the Data Within-Group Spread (Noise) Low High Group Differences (Signal) Distinct Equal

stages.title: The Rules of the Game
stages.text: Stage 03 The Rules of the Game Before we build an ANOVA model, we must check our assumptions. If the data breaks the rules, standard ANOVA might mislead us. Normality Technically, ANOVA assumes the residuals (the error or distance of each point from its group mean) are normally distributed. In practice, researchers often check if the data within each group resembles a bell curve. Homogeneity of Variance The spread (variance) of scores should be roughly equal across all groups. ANOVA is robust to minor violations, provided sample sizes are equal. Independence Data points must not influence each other. If the same student is tested multiple times, you must use a Repeated-Measures ANOVA instead.

stages.title: Variance Decomposition
stages.text: Stage 04 Variance Decomposition ANOVA answers our question by splitting the total variation in the data into two components. Look at the canvas to see these distances visualized. Between-Group Variance (Signal) The systematic variance associated with the independent variable. Measured by how far each group mean (black line) deviates from the Grand Mean (dashed line). Within-Group Variance (Noise) The unsystematic variance or error. Measured by how much individual dots deviate from their own group mean.

stages.title: The F-Statistic
stages.text: Stage 05 The F-Statistic ANOVA summarizes this decomposition into a single ratio, the F-statistic . It compares the size of the treatment effect to the size of the error. $$F = \frac{\text{Between-Group Variance}}{\text{Within-Group Variance}}$$

stages.title: Degrees of Freedom
stages.text: Stage 06 Degrees of Freedom Before we can calculate our variance estimates (Mean Squares) for the F-statistic, we need to divide our Sum of Squares by our Degrees of Freedom (df) . In statistics, df simply means how many values are still free to vary once a constraint has been imposed . Imagine picking 3 numbers that must average to 10. You can freely choose the first two (say, 8 and 15), but the third is locked (-13). You have 2 degrees of freedom. In our specific teaching example, we have N = 36 total students spread across k = 3 groups: df between = k - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2 Once the overall Grand Mean is set, only 2 of our 3 group means are free to vary. df within = N - k = 36 - 3 = 33 Within each group, the students' scores must average out to their respective group mean. We lose 1 degree of freedom per group constraint. df total = N - 1 = 36 - 1 = 35 If we only knew the Grand Mean, 35 out of the 36 students' scores would be free to vary.

stages.title: A Worked Example
stages.text: Stage 07 A Worked Example Let’s bring this together using the data currently on display. We divide our sums of squared deviations (Sum of Squares, SS) by our degrees of freedom to get the Mean Squares (MS), which are variance quantities used in F = MS_between / MS_within. Under the null hypothesis and standard ANOVA assumptions, both estimate the same error variance. From The Displayed Scores Group means: A = 80, B = 68, C = 56. Grand mean = 68. Each group has n = 12, so N = 36. Between-Group Signal SS between = 12[(80 - 68) 2 + (68 - 68) 2 + (56 - 68) 2 ] = 3456 Within-Group Noise SS within = 132 + 132 + 132 = 396 Applying Degrees of Freedom df between = 2; df within = 33. MS between = 3456 / 2 = 1728. MS within = 396 / 33 = 12. F = 1728 / 12 = 144. Scroll down to see these quantities organized into the universal language of statisticians: the ANOVA table.

stages.title: Reading the ANOVA Table
stages.text: Stage 08 Reading the ANOVA Table When you run ANOVA in software like R, SPSS, or Python, the output is standardized into this table format. Interact with the table in the visual panel: Tap or hover over the column headers (SS, df, MS, F, p) and the rows to understand exactly what each number represents and how they mathematically connect. The Conclusion: Because our p-value (< 0.001) is less than our threshold (0.05), we reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that at least one teaching method has a significantly different mean score.

stages.title: How Big Is The Effect?
stages.text: Stage 09 How Big Is The Effect? A small p-value indicates that the observed result would be unusual under the null hypothesis, assuming the model assumptions hold. It is not the probability that the null is true or a measure of practical importance, so report an effect size and confidence intervals too. Eta-Squared ($\eta^2$) Eta-squared shows the proportion of the total variation in scores that is associated with differences between teaching-method groups, without establishing causation. We calculate it using the Sum of Squares from the table: $\eta^2 = \frac{SS_{between}}{SS_{total}} = \frac{3456}{3852} = 0.90$ About 90% of the variation is associated with the group differences; this does not establish causation. Notice the new column added to the ANOVA table in the visual panel. Depending on your software, this might be reported as Eta Squared, Partial Eta Squared, or $R^2$.

stages.title: Post-Hoc Testing
stages.text: Stage 10 Post-Hoc Testing A significant ANOVA is an omnibus test—it tells you a difference exists, but not where . Is A different from B? Is B different from C? The Multiple Comparisons Problem If you run three separate t-tests, your 5% chance of a false positive (Type I error) compounds. The more tests you run, the higher the Family-Wise Error Rate . To follow up safely, we use Post-Hoc tests like Tukey's HSD . Under its assumptions, Tukey's controls the family-wise error rate at the chosen alpha level across the full set of pairwise comparisons. Look at the visual panel for the breakdown.

stages.title: Enter Two-Way ANOVA
stages.text: Stage 11 Enter Two-Way ANOVA So far, we've used a One-Way ANOVA to ask a single question: Does the teaching method matter? But reality is complex. Let's extend our example. We take our original three teaching methods (A, B, and C) and introduce a second factor: the student's Sleep Level (High vs. Low). Two-Way ANOVA now asks three questions at once: Does teaching method matter? Does sleep matter? And crucially, does the effect of one depend on the other? We are no longer comparing only 3 group means, but 6 distinct cells (3 methods × 2 sleep levels). This allows us to explore how both variables simultaneously influence test scores.

stages.title: Cells & Marginal Means
stages.text: Stage 12 Cells & Marginal Means To understand a two-way design, it helps to see how the data is organized. Look at this numeric structure for our extended teaching example: Two-Way Data Structure Sleep \ Method A B C Sleep Mean High Sleep 82 74 66 74 Low Sleep 62 66 70 66 Method Mean 72 70 68 Grand: 70 Cell Means (The middle grid) A cell mean is the average score for one exact combination—like the students who received Method A AND High Sleep (82) . Our design has 6 distinct cells. Marginal Means (The outer edges) A marginal mean averages across one factor while ignoring the other. The marginal mean for Method A (72) combines both sleep levels. "Main effects" look only at these outer marginal means.

stages.title: The Interaction Effect
stages.text: Stage 13 The Interaction Effect If the gap between methods stays consistent regardless of sleep, the lines in our plot will be roughly parallel. That suggests no interaction . But if the lines are not parallel , it suggests an interaction . Crossing lines are not technically required for an interaction, but this example uses a strong crossing pattern to make the concept visually obvious: the effect of Method completely flips depending on Sleep. How to Read the Interaction Plot Step 1: Check for parallel lines. If lines are roughly parallel, there is likely no interaction. If they cross or clearly change relative position, an interaction is present. Step 2: Look at overall height. If one line tends to sit higher on average, that suggests a main effect of Sleep. Step 3: Look at how the ranking changes. Notice which method is best under High Sleep, and then notice how that changes under Low Sleep. Here, the best method completely reverses! No Interaction (Parallel) Interaction (Crossover)

stages.title: Building the ANOVA Table
stages.text: Stage 14 Building the ANOVA Table How do we get from our six cells to the statistical output? We partition the total variation into four distinct buckets: 1 Method (Main Effect) Variation among the three Method marginal means ( 72 vs 70 vs 68 ). It asks if one teaching method is better on average. 2 Sleep (Main Effect) Variation between the two Sleep marginal means ( 74 vs 66 ). It asks if well-rested students do better on average. 3 Method × Sleep (Interaction) The leftover structured variance when the gaps between methods change across sleep levels. For High Sleep, A beats C by +16 points. But for Low Sleep, C beats A by +8 points. 4 Error (Within-Cell Noise) The natural random noise of individual students within each of the six specific cells. To turn these buckets into our final results, each source gets its own Sum of Squares (SS) . We divide each SS by its degrees of freedom (df) to get a Mean Square (MS) . Finally, we compare each effect's MS to the Error MS to produce an F-ratio . Why Averages Can Hide The Truth Notice that our Method marginal means are quite close (72, 70, 68). Because the crossover pattern partly cancels out when averaged across sleep levels, the main effect of Method looks modest. But the interaction is large because the best method changes completely depending on sleep! This is why we always read the interaction row first.

stages.title: Reading the Two-Way Table
stages.text: Stage 15 Reading the Two-Way Table Notice how the ANOVA table expands in the visual panel. Our single "Between Groups" signal is now cleanly split into three specific rows: Method , Sleep , and Method × Sleep . Correct Reading Order Read the interaction row first. If the interaction is significant, the effect of one factor depends on the other. Be careful with main effects. If the interaction is significant, interpreting the main effect of Method or Sleep on its own can be highly misleading. Then read the main effects. Look at Method and Sleep to see if they matter on average across all conditions. Our Example's Conclusion: The Interaction is highly significant ( p < 0.001 ). This confirms what we visually saw—the lines clearly cross between Method B and Method C. Method A provides a large advantage for well-rested students, but Method C becomes the best option for tired students. The main effects (Method and Sleep) are also significant, but the interaction tells us the true story of how they combine.

stages.title: Caveats & Recap
stages.text: Stage 16 Caveats & Recap ANOVA is a beautiful, mathematically elegant tool for partitioning variance. But it is only a model of reality. Assumptions are Key ANOVA is robust, but severe violations of normality or independence will produce a completely meaningless F-statistic. Always check your residuals. Look at the Data Never rely solely on the p-value, tables, or bar charts. Plot the raw data (like our dot plot), check the boxplots, and ensure extreme outliers aren't driving the omnibus result. Choose the ANOVA variant from the design: use standard one-way ANOVA for similar variances, Welch ANOVA for unequal variances, Kruskal–Wallis or a robust alternative for strong non-normality or ordinal outcomes, and repeated-measures or mixed models for repeated observations. After a significant omnibus test, use planned contrasts or multiplicity-corrected post-hoc comparisons. Report group intervals and a named effect size such as eta-squared or omega-squared. In one sentence: ANOVA asks whether the observed between-group variation would be unusual under an equal-means null model, assuming the chosen model and design conditions hold.

stages.title: The Prediction Problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The Prediction Problem Plain English Every dataset contains two things: the true signal we want to learn, and random static we should ignore. Technical Meaning A model's goal is to capture the underlying function f(x) while ignoring the irreducible error ε . For our concrete example, let's predict a person's Income based on their Years of Education . 👀 Notice on the right: The dots are our raw historical data. The horizontal axis is Years of Education, and the vertical axis is Income. We need to draw a reliable line through them.

stages.title: High Bias (Underfitting)
stages.text: Stage 02 High Bias (Underfitting) Plain English The model is too stubborn. It assumes the relationship is completely straight and simple, ignoring reality. Technical Meaning Bias is the error introduced by choosing a model that lacks the complexity to represent the true data distribution. Why It Matters A high bias model makes the exact same systematic mistake over and over again, regardless of how much data you feed it. Quick Check: Does a high-bias model memorize the noise? No. It does the opposite. It ignores the noise entirely, but unfortunately, it also ignores the genuine shape of the data. 👀 Notice on the right: The rigid red line forces a straight path through curved data. It is completely missing the underlying wave.

controls.text: Quick Check: Does a high-bias model memorize the noise? No. It does the opposite. It ignores the noise entirely, but unfortunately, it also ignores the genuine shape of the data.

stages.title: High Variance (Overfitting)
stages.text: Stage 03 High Variance (Overfitting) Plain English The model is too easily distracted. It memorizes every single typo and random bounce in our training data. Technical Meaning Variance is the amount by which our model's curve would change if we estimated it using a different set of training data. Why It Matters Like a student who memorizes a practice exam but fails the real test, an overfitted model cannot generalize to unseen future data. 👀 Notice on the right: The erratic blue line twists wildly to touch almost every single dot. It has learned the noise alongside the signal.

stages.title: The Error Decomposition
stages.text: Stage 04 The Error Decomposition We cannot minimize both perfectly. Mathematically, the expected prediction error on a new observation breaks down into exactly three components: Err(x) = [E[f̂(x)] - f(x)]² + E[(f̂(x) - E[f̂(x)])²] + σ² Bias² The Stubbornness Error: How much the model's rigid average assumption misses the true reality. Variance The Distraction Error: How wildly the model's curve jumps around when given slightly different training sets. Irreducible Error (σ²) The Baseline Noise: The inherent randomness in the real world that no model can ever predict. Conditions for this exact equation: the familiar decomposition applies most directly to squared-error prediction at a fixed input, across repeated training samples, with an irreducible-noise model. Bias and variance remain useful ideas in classification, but the same algebra does not automatically apply to classification loss. 👀 Notice on the right: The green dashed line is the sweet spot—a gentle curve that follows the main trend but ignores the random static.

stages.title: Interactive: The Trade-Off
stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive: The Trade-Off Let's look at how error changes step-by-step as we add complexity. As flexibility increases (moving right), Bias drops but Variance eventually spikes. Drag to change Model Complexity Too Simple Sweet Spot Too Complex Complexity: Med Bias Trend: 0.12 Var Trend: 0.05 Total Error: 0.17 👀 Notice on the right: The purple model dynamically fits the data above, updating your position on the U-Curve below. Hitting the absolute bottom of the black Total Error curve is the Golden Rule.

stages.title: The Testing Problem
stages.text: Stage 06 The Testing Problem Plain English A model that aces the practice quiz might still fail the final exam. Technical Meaning Training error often underestimates test error and is not a reliable estimate of future performance. Why It Matters If we use all our finite data to train the model, we are flying blind. We must safely evaluate models on data they haven't seen yet. The Solution: Resampling Methods. Resampling is how we practically estimate where the sweet spot lies using finite data. We strategically recycle our data by making repeated splits, rotating held-out folds, or redrawing samples.

stages.title: 1. The Validation Set
stages.text: Stage 07 1. The Validation Set Plain English Think of this as a practice exam used to choose a study strategy. A separate final exam remains hidden until that strategy is locked. Technical Meaning The dataset is randomly partitioned into two mutually exclusive sets: a "training set" to build the model, and a "validation set" to test it. Why It Matters It is simple but noisy. If the validation pile happens to contain unusually hard cases, the score changes substantially. The estimate depends on one random split. The Process: 1. Shuffle eligible independent observations. 2. Split development data into training and validation piles. 3. Fit candidate models on training data. 4. Choose among them using validation data. 5. Keep the separate final test set untouched. The Trade-off: We use a 50/50 development split below so it is easy to see. An 80/20 training/validation split is common, but the right choice depends on sample size and structure. A small validation set produces a noisy selection score; the final test set is separate. 50% Train / 50% Test 80% Train / 20% Test Redraw Split Computed Test MSE 0.000 👀 Notice on the right: Click the Redraw Split button. Watch how the blue (Train) and orange (Test) blocks shift. Because our MSE is genuinely recomputed each click, you can see how wildly the estimated error jumps based solely on a lucky or unlucky shuffle!

stages.title: 2. k-Fold Cross-Validation
stages.text: Stage 08 2. k-Fold Cross-Validation Plain English Instead of risking one lucky or unlucky test, we take turns. We divide the class into groups. Every single group gets exactly one chance to be the test group while everyone else studies. Technical Meaning The data is divided into k equal chunks (folds). We train k separate models, holding out a different chunk for validation each time, then average the k validation errors. Why It Matters By averaging multiple different tests together, we dilute the "luck of the draw" from any single random split. It gives us a much fairer, more stable picture of how the model will actually perform in the real world. The Process: 1. Chop the data into 5 equal chunks (folds). 2. Train a new model on 4 chunks. Test it on the 1 chunk left out. 3. Rotate. Pick a new chunk to be the test. 4. Repeat until every chunk has been the test exactly once. 5. Average all 5 test scores together. Train Model 1 (Test on Fold 1) Running Error Record Awaiting first fold... Average MSE: 0.000 ✓ Cycle Complete: Every data point has been used for testing exactly once. 👀 Notice on the right: Step through the folds. The orange test block slides down automatically. We build 5 entirely different models and log their scores. By averaging them all, we smooth out the jumps and find the truth.

stages.title: 3. Leave-One-Out (LOOCV)
stages.text: Stage 09 3. Leave-One-Out (LOOCV) Plain English Imagine a class of 100 students. We send exactly one student out of the room. We teach the other 99. Then we test that single missing student. We repeat this 100 times. Technical Meaning This is cross-validation taken to the absolute extreme. We leave out just one data point, train on the rest, and do this for every point in the dataset. Why It Matters It uses almost all the data to train, which gives the model the best chance to learn perfectly. But training 100 separate models takes a massive amount of computing power. The Hidden Flaw: Because we only leave out one point, the 100 models we build are almost perfectly identical. Their answers are incredibly similar to each other. When you average answers that are highly correlated, their mistakes don't cancel out well. The final error estimate can still be surprisingly jumpy. Compared to 5-fold CV: LOOCV uses more training data. But it takes vastly longer to compute and rarely gives a better, more stable answer. Hold Out Observation # 1 Single Point Error² 0.000 👀 Notice on the right: Slide the slider to move the orange test block. Look at the 99 blue training blocks—they barely change! This means all 100 tests are too mathematically similar to average out noise effectively.

stages.title: 4. The Bootstrap
stages.text: Stage 10 4. The Bootstrap Plain English Imagine tasting a giant pot of soup. You take a spoonful and score it a 7.0. Is that score reliable, or was that just a lucky scoop? To find out, you stir the soup and taste it multiple times, getting slightly different scores: 6.8, 7.2, 6.9, 7.1. Bootstrap checks how much these scores vary or "wiggle." Technical Meaning Bootstrap is about generating many possible answers from the exact same data to check for stability. We repeatedly sample our original data with replacement , and recalculate our target number on each new sample. Why It Matters If our taste scores stay tightly packed together (e.g., 6.8–7.2), our answer is highly stable. If they spread out wildly (e.g., 5.0–9.0), our result is unreliable. This gives us our margin of error . The Process: Start with your original dataset (say it’s got 100 points). To make one ‘bootstrap sample,’ randomly pick one data point from your original set. Write it down, but don’t remove it. Put it back, so all points stay equally available. Repeat this random picking (with putting back) until you have a new sample the same size as the original. So if you started with 100 points, you pick 100 times. Now, calculate the average (or whatever metric you’re checking) from that new sample. Repeat this entire process hundreds or thousands of times. Each time, you get a slightly different average. Finally, look at all those averages. Their spread tells you how stable (or not) your original estimate is. ▶ Run Bootstrap ↺ Reset Calculate Average Income Calculate Trend Slope Generating Answers ( 0 ) -- Avg Across All Tries (Mean): 0.000 How Much It Wiggles (Std Error): 0.000 Where 95% of Answers Fall (Confidence Interval): [- , -] 👀 One-Sentence Takeaway: Click Run. Each pretend dataset produces one new answer, dropping as a single dot below. Watch how the spread tells us exactly how trustworthy our answer is!

stages.title: Limitations in Practice
stages.text: Stage 11 Limitations in Practice Each method carries trade-offs. Here is what they mean for your daily work: Validation Set: Be cautious with this when data are small; your results will change randomly every time you run the script. LOOCV: Takes forever to run on large data. It tends to have very low bias, but averaging nearly identical models makes the final estimate jumpy. k-Fold CV: In practice, 5-fold or 10-fold CV is often a strong default because it balances stability and computation well. Bootstrap: Excellent for answering "how confident are we in this specific number?", but not the first choice for estimating pure test error. Micro-Check: If I want to publish the uncertainty of my new variable, which do I use? Bootstrap. Bootstrap is commonly used to estimate uncertainty, standard errors, and confidence intervals.

stages.title: Summary & Synthesis
stages.text: Stage 12 Summary & Synthesis A successful model must navigate the error puzzle. It requires enough complexity to avoid Bias, but enough restraint to avoid Variance. We rely on computational resampling to estimate how our model will generalize to the real world. Memory Checklist Bias: The model is too rigid (Underfitting). Variance: The model is too jumpy (Overfitting). Cross-Validation: Used to estimate future Test Error. Bootstrap: Used to estimate Uncertainty and Std Errors. title: Chi-Square Test of Independence | StatML Academy

stages.title: The Raw Counts
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Counts The Chi-Square test evaluates categorical data —data placed into distinct bins or groups without an inherent numeric value. Imagine we survey 50 students to see if there is a relationship between two categorical variables: Club Choice (Art vs. Sports) and Favorite Snack (Apples vs. Chips). Rule of thumb: Chi-Square works with frequencies (counts), not averages. Every individual belongs to exactly one cell in our table.

stages.title: Hypotheses & Marginals
stages.text: Stage 02 Hypotheses & Marginals Are club choice and favorite snack related, or are they completely independent? We formalize this question using hypotheses. H₀ Null Hypothesis: Club choice and favorite snack are independent . (No relationship). H₁ Alternative Hypothesis: Club choice and favorite snack are not independent . (There is a relationship). To test this, we must first look at the margins. The row totals and column totals tell us the overall preferences of the group, ignoring the split between the variables.

stages.title: Expected Counts
stages.text:
Stage 03 Expected Counts If the Null Hypothesis is perfectly true, the counts inside the table should be directly proportional to the totals on the margins. This gives us our Expected Counts —the baseline of what we would expect if there were no relationship at all between club choice and snack preference. To find the expected count for any cell in our table, we use this simple formula: Expected Count = (Row Total × Column Total) ÷ Grand Total In standard algebraic shorthand, it is written as: E = (Row Total × Column Total) / Grand Total Step-by-Step Calculation: Art & Apple Let's calculate the expected value for the first cell (Art students who prefer Apples): Row Total (Art) = 30 Column Total (Apple) = 25 Grand Total = 50 E = (30 × 25) / 50 = 750 / 50 = 15 Why does this work? Out of 50 total surveyed students, 25 like apples. That is exactly half (50%) of all students.
                        If snack preference and club choice are completely unrelated (independent), then apples should be spread proportionally across both clubs. Since 50% of the entire sample likes apples, we expect 50% of each club to like apples. Art has 30 students, and half of 30 is 15. "If everything were random, about half of the Art students should like apples." Interactive: Build an Expected Count Select a cell to see how expected frequencies are generated under the assumption of independence: -- Choose a cell to calculate -- Art & Apple Art & Chips Sports & Apple Sports & Chips Show me why Calculating the Remaining Cells We apply the exact same formula to the other three cells: Art & Chips: E = (30 × 25) / 50 = 15 Sports & Apple: E = (20 × 25) / 50 = 10 Sports & Chips: E = (20 × 25) / 50 = 10 What is really happening? The total number of apples is 25. If independent, we split these apples across the rows based on the size of each club: Art has 30 out of 50 students (60% of the sample). Therefore, Art gets 60% of the expected apples: 60% of 25 = 15. Sports has 20 out of 50 students (40% of the sample). Therefore, Sports gets 40% of the expected apples: 40% of 25 = 10. The same logic applies to the chips category, which also has a column total of 25. Expected count means: how much this row deserves × how much this column deserves. Warning: Expected counts are not guesses from our opinion. They are calculated from the table totals under the assumption that the variables are independent. Check Your Progress: Expected Counts Question: What is the expected count for Sports & Chips? A. 5 B. 10 C. 15 D. 25

stages.title: Residuals & Contributions
stages.text: Stage 04 Residuals & Contributions The core intuition of Chi-Square is to compare what we Observed (O) with what we Expected (E) . We square the residuals and divide by the expected count to scale the difference. χ² = Σ [ (O - E)² / E ] Worked Example: Art & Apple contribution Let's calculate the individual score contribution for Art students who prefer Apples: Observed (O) = 20 Expected (E) = 15 Residual (O - E) = 20 - 15 = 5 Square the residual: 5² = 25 Divide by expected: 25 ÷ 15 = 1.67 This cell contributes exactly 1.67 points to the overall Chi-Square statistic. Bigger contributions mean that cell is more responsible for the overall relationship. Interactive Matrix: Hover over any cell in the table to inspect its Observed, Expected, Residual, and individual χ² contribution. We do this for every cell and add them all together to get our final test statistic. (Note: visual contributions are shown rounded to two decimals, but the true sum is roughly 8.33). Check Your Progress: Residuals Question: If observed = 20 and expected = 15, what does residual = +5 mean? A. There were 5 fewer people than expected. B. There were 5 more people than expected. C. There were exactly 5 people in total. D. The p-value is 5.

controls.text: A. There were 5 fewer people than expected.
B. There were 5 more people than expected.
C. There were exactly 5 people in total.

stages.title: The Reference Distribution
stages.text: Stage 05 The Reference Distribution To evaluate our test statistic of 8.33 , we map it onto a Chi-Square distribution. The curve's exact shape is determined by the Degrees of Freedom (df) . df = (Rows - 1) × (Cols - 1) = 1 If our statistic lands past the critical boundary (here, 3.84 for α = 0.05), the deviation is too large to be attributed to random chance.

stages.title: Reading the Output
stages.text: Stage 06 Reading the Output Statistical software synthesizes these steps into a standard output summary. Here is how to read the final result: Analysis Output Pearson's Chi-squared test X-squared 8.33 df 1 p-value 0.0039 alpha (α) 0.05 Decision Reject H₀ Effect Size (Phi) 0.41 (Moderate) ✓ Expected counts check All expected counts ≥ 5 Understanding our p-value: The p-value is 0.0039 . This means: if club choice and snack preference were truly unrelated, getting a pattern this strong or stronger would be very unlikely. So, we have strong evidence against the null hypothesis. ⚠️ Important: The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is the probability of seeing a result this extreme or more extreme, assuming the null hypothesis were true. Because the p-value (0.0039) is much smaller than our alpha threshold (0.05), we officially reject the null hypothesis. The Phi value of 0.41 confirms this is a moderate relationship. What kind of relationship is it? The p-value tells us: “Something is going on.” (The variables are associated). The residuals tell us: “What exactly is going on.” (The direction and pattern of the association). Group Apple Chips Art +5 -5 Sports -5 +5 Let's break this down in human language: Art students: The Art & Apple residual is +5 (more Art students liked apples than expected) and the Art & Chips residual is -5 (fewer Art students liked chips than expected). Therefore, Art students lean toward apples. Sports students: The Sports & Apple residual is -5 (fewer Sports students liked apples than expected) and the Sports & Chips residual is +5 (more Sports students liked chips than expected). Therefore, Sports students lean toward chips. Final Relationship Statement: "There is a relationship between club choice and snack preference: Art students are more likely than expected to prefer apples, while Sports students are more likely than expected to prefer chips." Caution: This is an association, not causation. We cannot say that joining Art causes students to like apples, or that joining Sports causes students to like chips. Check Your Progress: Interpretation Question: What does the p-value mainly tell us? A. The exact cause of the relationship. B. Whether there is evidence against the null hypothesis. C. Which group caused the result. D. The number of students surveyed.

stages.title: Assumptions & Caveats
stages.text: Stage 07 Assumptions & Caveats Before closing the book on this relationship, we must acknowledge the strict assumptions required for a valid Chi-Square test. Required Conditions (Assumptions) Before trusting any Chi-Square test, you must ensure your study meets these three non-negotiable assumptions: 1 Count Data (Frequencies) Beginner meaning: You must use actual counts of people or items falling into categories, not averages or scores. ❌ Bad: using average happiness ratings or continuous test scores. ✓ Good: counting how many students chose apples or chips. 2 Independence of Observations Beginner meaning: Each person should only appear once in the table. They cannot belong to multiple cells. ❌ Bad: the same student is counted under both Art and Sports. ✓ Good: each student belongs to one club category and one snack category. 3 Expected Counts are Large Enough Beginner meaning: The expected numbers computed under independence should not be too tiny. ❌ Bad: many expected cells are 1 or 2 (which invalidates our p-value). ✓ Good: all expected counts in this example are at least 5 (our cells are 15, 15, 10, and 10). Tiny expected counts can make the Chi-Square approximation unreliable. Yates' continuity correction applies specifically to 2×2 tables and does not guarantee a reliable approximation for very sparse data. Fisher's Exact Test is mainly used for small or sparse 2×2 tables; larger sparse tables may need other exact or Monte Carlo alternatives. Interactive: Test Your Interpretation Complete the sentences below to craft the final conclusion in plain English: "There is evidence of a relationship between -- select -- Apple and Chips club choice and snack preference Art and Sports . Art students are more likely than expected to prefer -- select -- apples chips . Sports students are more likely than expected to prefer -- select -- apples chips ." Check Answers Show Answer 📖 The Whole Story in Plain English Let's connect all the dots we've covered on this page into one simple, logical narrative: We counted students by club and snack: We started by putting students into categories based on two characteristics: their club (Art/Sports) and snack preference (Apples/Chips). We assumed independence: We asked: "What would this table look like if club and snack preferences had absolutely nothing to do with each other?" That gave us expected counts: Answering that question mathematically gave us our expected baseline counts (15, 15, 10, 10). We compared observed counts to expected counts: We looked at how far our actual observed numbers (20, 10, 5, 15) fell from that independent baseline. The differences were large enough: We squared and scaled these discrepancies, giving us a final test statistic of χ² = 8.33 . The p-value was small, so we rejected independence: A discrepancy at least this large would be unusual under independence (p = 0.0039), assuming the test conditions hold. The data provide evidence against independence; Cramér’s V and residuals describe magnitude and contributing cells. The residuals showed the pattern: Looking closely at our cells, we saw the exact direction of this pattern—Art students lean apples, Sports students lean chips. Synthesis We have strong statistical evidence that club choice and snack preference are connected. However, Chi-Square demonstrates association, not causation . We cannot declare that joining the Art club causes students to eat apples.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Data Every problem starts with data. We have measurements for fruit — Weight (x-axis) and Color Intensity (y-axis). Each fruit is already labeled: an Apple or an Orange . The goal of our tree is to learn rules to sort them into cleaner groups. The Whole Idea of Classification Trees A Classification Tree is a supervised machine-learning model that learns a sequence of simple yes/no flowchart-like questions to sort data into categories. Raw Labeled Data → Root Node → Scan Best Question → Split Data → Repeat Recursively → Leaf Prediction → Evaluation Tiny Tree Dictionary • Feature: A measurable property or input variable used to make predictions (e.g., Weight, Color Intensity). • Label: The target outcome or true answer we want the model to predict (e.g., Apple, Orange). • Class: One of the specific categorical outcomes (e.g., Apples vs. Oranges). • Root Node: The very first top-level block containing 100% of the training data. • Split: A division of a parent node into two child nodes based on a feature question. • Child Node: The subgroups created after splitting a parent node. • Leaf Node: A final terminal node that does not split further. It makes the final prediction. • Impurity: A measure of how mixed or diverse the class labels are within a particular node. • Gini Impurity: A mathematical metric used to calculate impurity (0.0 means perfectly pure; 0.5 is the maximum for a balanced binary node). • Weighted Impurity: The combined impurity of child nodes, weighted by the proportion of samples that went into each child. • Impurity Decrease: The difference between parent Gini and weighted child Gini. The tree maximizes this "gain". • Decision Boundary: The geometric line(s) dividing different class zones on the coordinate map. • Tree Depth: The length of the longest path from the root node down to any leaf node. • Pruning: Cutting back branches to simplify the model and improve generalizability on unseen data. • Overfitting: Memorizing noise in the training set, causing failure on unseen test data. • Underfitting: Creating a model that is too simple (e.g. too shallow) to learn the real underlying patterns. Training Data Preview This is a classification task because we want to predict a specific category or discrete group, rather than a continuous number.

stages.title: The Train / Test Split
stages.text: Stage 02 The Train / Test Split To build a robust model, we never evaluate our tree on the exact same data it used for learning. Instead, we divide our original dataset into two parts: Data Partitioning Training Set Used to scan thresholds, calculate Gini, and build rules. Count: 28 fruits Test Set (Held out) Kept completely hidden from the tree during training. Count: 6 fruits Data Leakage Warning: Using test data to choose splits, tune tree depth, or pick stopping criteria is a cardinal sin of machine learning. The test set must ONLY be used for final generalizability assessment. Check Your Knowledge Why is a Train/Test split essential for decision trees? It helps the tree grow deeper and generate more rules. It allows us to detect overfitting by measuring performance on unseen samples. It guarantees that Gini impurity reaches exactly 0.0.

stages.title: The Root Node
stages.text: Stage 03 The Root Node At the very beginning, a Classification Tree puts all the training data into one big group on the fruit map. We call this the Root Node . This starting box is very "messy" because it contains a mix of both apples and oranges. The tree's job is to split this box into smaller, cleaner sub-groups. Root Node Content -- Apples -- Oranges

stages.title: Measuring Messiness
stages.text:
Stage 04 Measuring Messiness To split effectively, the tree needs a way to measure how mixed a box is. We use a math rule called Gini Impurity . A Gini score of 0.0 means the box is perfectly pure . For this binary example, 0.5 is the maximum at a 50/50 mix; multiclass maxima differ. Gini Impurity Formula Gini = 1 - Σ pᵢ²

For two classes (Apple & Orange):
Gini = 1 - [ P(Apple)² + P(Orange)² ] Live Root Node Calculation Gini Impurity vs. Entropy While Gini is highly popular in CART (Classification and Regression Trees), another metric called Entropy is also widely used: Entropy = - Σ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ) Both metrics measure the same core property: disorder. A node with equal proportions of classes has a Gini score of 0.50 and an Entropy score of 1.0. Both reach 0.0 when a node is perfectly pure. In practice, Gini and entropy often choose very similar splits, but not always. This guide uses Gini because it is simple, common, and easy to compute. Concept Quiz What does a Gini Impurity of 0.0 indicate about a subset of fruit? The subset contains exactly 50% Apples and 50% Oranges. The subset is 100% pure (contains only one type of fruit). The subset is empty.

stages.title: Testing Every Question
stages.text: Stage 05 Testing Every Question How does the tree find the best split? It tries testing candidate split points between observed values across the map. Because the tree asks one feature question at a time (e.g., "Is Weight < X?"), each possible split becomes a straight vertical or horizontal cut across the graph. Watch the sweeping line on the canvas analyze both features. The Candidate Search Strategy How does a decision tree find the best threshold? It doesn't guess random decimals. Instead, it uses a deterministic mathematical process: Sort values: For a given feature (like Weight), it sorts all observed training values in ascending order. Compute Midpoints: It calculates the halfway points (midpoints) between every adjacent pair of unique values. Evaluate Splits: It treats each midpoint as a candidate threshold (e.g., Weight < 5.40 ), splits the data, and evaluates the resulting weighted Gini impurity. Live Search (Scanning...) Testing Split: Weight < 5.0... Average Gini: ~0.45

stages.title: How the Tree Scores One Split
stages.text: Stage 06 How the Tree Scores One Split The tree found the single best question! By splitting the data at this specific threshold, it gets the lowest possible combined Gini impurity. This first split is often very influential because it shapes the rest of the tree. It divides the fruit map cleanly into two distinct regions. The Golden Question Is Weight < X? How the Tree Scores This Split Split Calculation Quiz What property makes a candidate split the absolute "winner" in a decision tree? It always splits the dataset exactly 50/50 by quantity. It yields the largest Gini impurity decrease (lowest weighted children impurity). It guarantees that both left and right child nodes become 100% pure instantly.

controls.text: It always splits the dataset exactly 50/50 by quantity.
It yields the largest Gini impurity decrease (lowest weighted children impurity).
It guarantees that both left and right child nodes become 100% pure instantly.

stages.title: Recursive Splitting
stages.text: Stage 07 Recursive Splitting The tree isn't done. It now treats each of the two new boxes as a separate problem, and asks again: "Can I perform another split to make these even cleaner?" It repeats this process recursively, carving the map into smaller and smaller axis-aligned rectangles until a box becomes pure, gets too small, or reaches the depth limit. Tree Stopping Rules To prevent the tree from growing infinitely, we define stopping constraints (hyperparameters in ML frameworks): Node Purity: Stop if all items in a node belong to a single class (Gini = 0). Max Depth (`max_depth`): Stop if the path length from the root matches our limit. Min Samples Split (`min_samples_split`): Stop if a node contains too few samples to allow another split. Min Samples Leaf (`min_samples_leaf`): Prevent splits that leave a child with too few samples. Min Impurity Decrease (`min_impurity_decrease`): Stop if Gini gain is below a small threshold. Stopping Rules Quiz What is the main danger of growing a classification tree completely unchecked without any stopping rules? The tree will underfit and fail to capture simple boundaries. The tree will overfit by creating hyper-specific rules to capture training noise. The root Gini impurity will increase beyond 0.50.

controls.text: The tree will underfit and fail to capture simple boundaries.
The tree will overfit by creating hyper-specific rules to capture training noise.
The root Gini impurity will increase beyond 0.50.

stages.title: The Decision Boundary
stages.text: Stage 08 The Decision Boundary Once the tree stops growing, we fill in the colors. Each rectangular box becomes a "Leaf Node". The model assigns a prediction to the entire box based on the fruit type that appears most often in that box. Leaf Nodes: How Predictions Are Made Every final sub-box is a terminal Leaf Node . It predicts the majority class contained within its boundary. We can also calculate a Class Probability Estimate simply as the proportion of that class in the leaf box: P(Apple) = Leaf_Apples / Total_Leaf_Samples Warning: These leaf-proportion probabilities can be overconfident, especially in deep trees with small sample sizes in leaf boxes (e.g. predicting 100% confidence because a leaf contains exactly 1 Apple). stages.title: Depth Limiting vs. Post-Pruning
stages.text: Stage 09 Depth Limiting vs. Post-Pruning Look closely at the tiny boxes the tree made just to capture one outlier fruit. The tree has started memorizing noise in the training dataset. This is called Overfitting . If we give the tree new fruit, these hyper-specific rules will likely fail. We fix this by limiting the maximum depth of the tree (Pre-Pruning), so it learns general rules instead of tracking every detail. Pre-Pruning vs. Post-Pruning Method How it works Pros / Cons Pre-Pruning Stop tree growth early using rules like max_depth or min_samples_split . Very fast to compute, but might stop too early before discovering complex interactions. Post-Pruning Grow the full complex tree first, then cut back nodes that do not add predictive value (e.g. cost-complexity pruning). Often more systematic, but computationally heavier because you build the full tree first. The model achieves 100% accuracy on both training and test data. The model fits training noise perfectly but fails on test data. The model is too simple to capture the true underlying pattern, performing poorly on both datasets.

stages.title: Limitations & Model Choice
stages.text: Stage 15 Limitations & Model Choice Classification Trees are incredibly intuitive, but they are not always the best tool for every job. Understanding their trade-offs is crucial for a data scientist. Strengths vs. Weaknesses When they shine: Explainability: Outputs simple rules that any non-expert can read and audit. No Scaling Required: Features are evaluated independently, so feature magnitude does not matter. Handles Mixed Types Conceptually: Trees can split numerical and categorical predictors, but raw categorical support depends on the software. Some libraries require encoded categories; others implement native categorical splits. When they struggle: High Variance: Extremely sensitive to tiny training set alterations, which can yield completely different splits. Axis-Aligned Boundaries: Since splits are purely horizontal or vertical, diagonal patterns require jagged, inefficient steps. Overfitting: Easily memorize noise if depth is unchecked. Class Imbalance: If one class is much more common, the tree may favor that class unless class weights, resampling, or better evaluation metrics are used. Model Comparison Roadmap Model Boundary Type Interpretability Best Used For... Decision Tree Axis-Aligned Boxes High (Flowchart) Rules-based audits, mixed categorical/numerical data. Logistic Regression Smooth Linear Medium (Weights) Linear associations with log-odds; estimated probabilities may need calibration. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Irregular / Local Low (Instance-based) Complex local shapes, feature manifolds. Random Forest Complex / Smooth Low (Ensemble) High-accuracy, non-linear tasks (reduces variance). The Upgrade Path: To overcome the instability and high variance of a single Classification Tree, we combine hundreds of trees into an ensemble. Models like Random Forests (voting trees) and Gradient Boosted Trees (sequential error correction) represent the state-of-the-art for tabular data!

stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem Inference connects a noisy sample to a population quantity. Confidence intervals show compatible effect sizes; tests quantify how surprising the data are under a specified null model.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective A p-value is computed assuming the null and asks about results at least as extreme. A confidence procedure is calibrated across repeated samples. Neither replaces effect size, assumptions, or practical meaning.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example An estimated mean difference is 4 points with a 95% CI from 1 to 7 and p=.01. The data are inconsistent with zero under the test assumptions, while plausible effects range from small to substantial. The p-value is not a 1% probability that the null is true.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method A p-value is a tail probability calculated under H₀ and every model assumption; the null is conditioned on, not assigned a probability. A compatible confidence interval often inverts a family of tests. Sample size affects precision, so tiny effects can be statistically clear and important effects can remain uncertain. Power is planned against a specific meaningful alternative and is not the probability that an observed finding is true. Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis; α controls its probability under the test assumptions. Type II error means failing to reject a false null; its probability β depends on the particular alternative. Power = 1 − β is the chance of detecting that alternative. All else equal, lowering α generally lowers power, while larger sample sizes or larger effect sizes generally raise it. Family-wise and false-discovery-rate procedures answer different multiplicity goals. Neither repairs optional stopping, outcome switching or selective reporting after results are known. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive laboratory Change sample size and effect size. See the standard error, confidence interval and approximate p-value change—without changing what a p-value means.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions The test, estimator, sampling design and dependence model must match. Pre-specified hypotheses protect the advertised error rate. When the method fails Optional stopping, many uncorrected tests, model misspecification, low power and selective reporting invalidate simple interpretations.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Define estimand, H₀ and H₁ Choose α and analysis before results Check design and assumptions Compute estimate, effect size, interval and p-value Adjust for multiplicity when required Interpret practical significance

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text: Stage 08 Interpretation and reporting What to report: Report estimate and compatible interval, exact p-value where useful, effect size, assumptions, multiplicity plan, sample size and practical consequences. Common misuse: Calling p>.05 “no effect” or p<.05 “proof.”

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.text: Stage 09 Knowledge checks A 95% confidence procedure means… Across repetitions, 95% of intervals capture the parameter under assumptions There is always a 95% posterior probability inside this interval 95% of observations fall inside Answer and explanation Across repetitions, 95% of intervals capture the parameter under assumptions. Frequentist coverage is a long-run property of the procedure. A p-value is not… The probability the null is true A tail probability under the null Affected by sample size Answer and explanation The probability the null is true. The null is conditioned on when calculating the p-value. Testing 20 outcomes requires attention to… Multiplicity Feature scaling only Class prevalence Answer and explanation Multiplicity. Multiple opportunities for small p-values inflate false positives. Failing to reject means… Evidence was insufficient at the chosen rule The null is proven The effect is exactly zero Answer and explanation Evidence was insufficient at the chosen rule. Absence of sufficient evidence is not evidence of exact absence. What completes an inferential result? Effect size, interval and practical interpretation Only stars denoting significance Only the sample mean Answer and explanation Effect size, interval and practical interpretation. Magnitude and uncertainty are required for useful interpretation.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Data Correlation is a statistical technique used to answer one big question: When one thing changes, does another thing also change? To find out, we need paired observations. For example, let's look at the relationship between hours studied and test scores for six students. Student Hours Studied (X) Test Score (Y) A 1 52 B 2 57 C 3 63 D 4 68 E 5 74 F 6 79 By plotting these paired values on a scatterplot, we translate raw numbers into a visual pattern.

stages.title: Direction and Form
stages.text: Stage 02 Direction and Form The first thing we look for in a scatterplot is the direction and form of the relationship. If the dots rise from left to right, we have a Positive Correlation . As study hours go up, test scores also go up. The "Walking Friends" metaphor: Think of two friends. If they both walk forward together, that's a positive correlation. If one walks forward while the other walks backward, that's negative. We also check the form . Pearson correlation specifically measures linear relationships—meaning the dots tend to cluster around a straight line.

stages.title: Measuring Strength: r
stages.text: Stage 03 Measuring Strength: r We quantify this relationship using Pearson's correlation coefficient , written as r . The value of r always falls between -1.00 and +1.00. r = +1.0 : Perfect positive correlation r = -1.0 : Perfect negative correlation r = 0.0 : No linear correlation Interactive: Adjust the noise to see how r changes when the dots spread further from the perfect line. Data Noise: -- Pearson's r

stages.title: Formal Hypotheses
stages.text: Stage 04 Formal Hypotheses In statistics, we use a sample to make guesses about an entire population. To test if a correlation is "real", we set up formal hypotheses. Null Hypothesis (H₀): ρ = 0 There is no linear correlation between the variables in the population. Any observed relationship is just random chance. Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): ρ ≠ 0 There is a significant linear relationship between the two variables. We use the Greek letter rho ( ρ ) for the population, and r for our sample.

stages.title: How it works: Covariability
stages.text: Stage 05 How it works: Covariability How does the math actually figure out if they move together? It looks at the means . r = Σ((X - X̄)(Y - Ȳ)) √[Σ(X - X̄)² × Σ(Y - Ȳ)²] Translation: The sum of how they vary together, divided by the total of how they vary individually. We draw a vertical line for the average of X, and a horizontal line for the average of Y. This creates four quadrants. If points mostly fall in the Top-Right (both above average) and Bottom-Left (both below average), they are moving together. The formula multiplies their distances from the mean. Positive × Positive = Positive. Negative × Negative = Positive!

stages.title: Assumptions: Paired & Linear
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions: Paired & Linear Pearson's correlation is powerful, but you must check two critical assumptions before trusting the math: Paired Numeric Data: Both variables must be numeric, and each X must belong to the exact same subject as Y . Linearity: The relationship must be relatively straight. Imagine a scenario where cramming too much causes sleep deprivation, hurting test performance. Scores rise initially, then fall. -- Calculated r The math yields an r near 0, suggesting "no relationship." But visually, there is a strong curvilinear relationship. Always inspect the scatterplot first.

stages.title: Robustness Check: Outliers
stages.text: Stage 07 Robustness Check: Outliers Extreme outliers are a robustness concern , not a formal assumption for calculating Pearson’s r. Pearson’s r uses covariance—products of deviations from the two means—scaled by the standard deviations. Extreme deviations can strongly change these quantities; a distant point can have high leverage, pulling the apparent linear relationship and the r value toward itself. Watch how a single anomalous student (who studied 12 hours but scored 30) pulls the trendline down, severely weakening our strong positive correlation.

stages.title: The Inferential Result
stages.text: Stage 08 The Inferential Result Let's return to our original, clean data. We have calculated the sample statistic and must now make a formal decision. -- Sample Size (n) -- Observed r -- p-value Statistical Decision: Awaiting statistical computation... A small p-value means a result at least this extreme would be unusual under H₀: ρ = 0, assuming independent pairs and the test model hold. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, the probability that chance caused the result, an effect size, or evidence of causality. Pair r with a confidence interval and practical interpretation.

stages.title: The Golden Rule: Causation
stages.text: Stage 09 The Golden Rule: Causation We found a statistically significant relationship. But how far can we stretch our interpretation? Interpretation: "There was a significant positive correlation between hours studied and test score, r = -- , -- . Students who studied more tended to score higher." However, we cannot say that studying caused the score to increase. Correlation does not equal causation. Two variables might move together because of a third, confounding variable (e.g., Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise together, but the sun causes both).

stages.title: Limitations & Summary
stages.text: Stage 10 Limitations & Summary To recap, correlation is an observational tool, not an experimental proof. r measures linear tightness (from -1 to +1). Check the plot: r is blind to curves and highly sensitive to outliers. Significance vs. Size: A small p-value means the observed result would be unusual under H₀: ρ = 0, assuming the test assumptions hold. Report r , its confidence interval, sample size, and practical relevance. Pearson versus Spearman: Pearson measures linear association; Spearman measures monotonic association through ranks. Spearman is not simply an outlier-proof Pearson, and neither fixes confounding, dependence, or a non-monotonic relationship. Pearson vs. Spearman: Use Pearson for continuous data. Switch to Spearman if your data is ranked/ordinal or has a monotonic non-linear relationship. No Causal Claims: It is only evidence of an association. When you encounter a correlation, always ask: What does the scatterplot look like, and could a hidden variable be driving the pattern?

stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem A model can appear excellent because information crossed the boundary between development and evaluation. Leakage estimates performance for a procedure that cannot exist in deployment.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective Treat the pipeline—not only the final algorithm—as the model. Anything that learns a mean, category frequency, component, selected feature, threshold, or synthetic observation must learn it inside each training fold.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example Suppose missing ages are filled with the mean of all 1,000 rows and then five-fold CV is run. Every validation fold has influenced its own imputed values. The honest workflow fits five separate imputers, each on that fold’s 800 training rows, and applies it to the 200 held-out rows.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method Leakage can enter through features, rows, groups, time or repeated comparison. A post-outcome billing code is feature leakage; duplicate images across folds are row leakage; tomorrow’s rolling average is time leakage; repeatedly checking the same test score creates selection leakage. Nested cross-validation separates inner model selection from outer evaluation. Target encoding, oversampling, outlier rules, feature selection, PCA and threshold selection are all estimators. Each must be re-learned within every training fold. The decisive audit question is whether a value, rule or analyst decision could have known anything about the held-out outcome. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive laboratory Classify each pipeline as safe or leaking. Feedback identifies exactly where information crosses the boundary.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions The split must match the unit of independence and deployment timing. Features must exist at the moment a prediction is made. When the method fails Random CV fails for time order, repeated patients, households, organisations, duplicated rows, and target-derived features. Oversampling before CV creates near-duplicates across folds.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Define prediction time and independent unit Reserve the final test set Choose stratified, grouped, time-series, or nested resampling Fit every learned transform inside training folds Lock and evaluate once

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text: Stage 08 Interpretation and reporting What to report: Document split units, dates or groups, pipeline order, cross-validation variant, test isolation and every target-aware transformation. Common misuse: Preprocessing the full dataset before splitting because “it is not the model.”

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.text: Stage 09 Knowledge checks Which workflow leaks? Scale all rows, then cross-validate Fit scaling inside each training fold Apply a training-fitted scaler to validation rows Answer and explanation Scale all rows, then cross-validate. Scaling all rows lets each validation fold influence its own transformation. Where should oversampling happen? stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem A model produces many kinds of errors. A metric turns those errors into a comparison, but only after the real decision defines what matters. A hospital triage model and a spam filter should not inherit the same priorities by convenience.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective MAE counts absolute regression misses in outcome units; RMSE gives large misses extra weight. Accuracy counts correct labels, precision asks how many predicted positives were right, and recall asks how many actual positives were found. F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: F1 = 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall), when the denominator is positive. It is useful when both matter, but ignores true negatives and is not automatically the best metric. Log loss and Brier score evaluate probabilities, while calibration compares predicted risks with observed frequencies.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example A screening model sees 1,000 people: 100 have disease. It finds 80 of them and falsely flags 90 healthy people. TP=80, FN=20, FP=90, TN=810. Accuracy is 89%, recall is 80%, and precision is 47%. The apparently healthy accuracy hides that more than half of alerts are false.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method MAE targets absolute error in outcome units, while squared-error optimisation gives large misses extra weight. Accuracy summarises a thresholded confusion matrix; precision, recall and specificity condition on different denominators. ROC-AUC measures ranking across thresholds, whereas PR-AUC emphasises positive retrieval and depends on prevalence. Log loss and Brier score evaluate probabilities, and calibration asks whether predicted risks match observed frequencies. Out-of-sample R² compares with a mean-prediction baseline and may be negative. With asymmetric consequences, write expected cost explicitly and choose the threshold that supports the actual decision and operational capacity. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive laboratory Move the decision threshold. Watch the confusion matrix, precision, recall and expected error cost change together.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions The evaluation sample must represent the deployment population, labels must be trustworthy, and each metric must be calculated on genuinely held-out predictions. When the method fails Accuracy fails under imbalance or unequal costs. MAPE behaves badly near zero. ROC-AUC can obscure performance at the operating region, and a strong ranking score does not guarantee calibrated probabilities.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Define the decision and error costs Choose primary and secondary metrics before model comparison Tune model and threshold on validation data Lock the full pipeline Report final test metrics with bootstrap or repeated-sample intervals

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text: Stage 08 Interpretation and reporting What to report: State the metric definition, threshold, prevalence or outcome scale, baseline, point estimate, uncertainty interval and real-world costs. Common misuse: Selecting whichever metric makes a preferred model look best after seeing the results.

Treating 600 rows as independent exaggerates precision; analysis and power must account for 20 randomisation units and intraclass correlation.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem Instead of averaging independent trees, boosting builds a sequence in which each new weak learner targets the current model’s loss gradient.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective Learning rate controls how much each tree contributes; tree count controls how many correction steps occur. Small learning rates often need more trees, so these settings must be tuned together.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example At learning rate .3, validation loss falls quickly then rises after 60 trees. At .05 it improves more slowly and reaches a better minimum near 300 trees. Early stopping chooses the round from validation data, not the test set.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method Boosting creates an additive predictor by fitting each learner to a negative loss gradient. For squared error this resembles residual fitting, but other losses create different pseudo-residuals. Learning rate scales contributions, tree depth limits interactions, and row or feature subsampling regularises. These settings interact, so learning rate and round count must be tuned together. Training loss normally keeps falling and cannot select stopping. Validation-based early stopping is a hyperparameter choice. Class weighting changes the objective and can damage calibration. Gain importance and attribution methods explain the fitted model, not a causal mechanism. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions The loss must match the target and decision; validation must reflect deployment; preprocessing and early stopping must stay inside development data. When the method fails Too many rounds chase noise, poor tuning overfits, probabilities may be miscalibrated, and importance is unstable under correlated predictors.

stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Choose loss and baseline Create a leakage-safe validation scheme Tune learning rate, complexity and subsampling jointly Use validation-based early stopping Assess calibration and subgroup error Evaluate the locked model once
