stages.title: The Uncharted Planet
stages.text: Stage 01 The Uncharted Planet Imagine landing on a distant planet with no map or guidebook. Your goal isn't to reach a destination; it's simply to see what is there. This is the essence of Unsupervised Learning . Unlike supervised learning, where we try to predict a specific answer, here we only have features. We are discovering the natural structure of the data. The Toy Box Analogy: Think of a child given a massive box of mixed toys and told to "find the patterns." Without instructions, they group them naturally by similarity. To the right, we have a raw dataset. Just points in space waiting to be understood. Takeaway: Unsupervised learning is about revealing structure that is already hiding in the data.

stages.title: Measuring "Close"
stages.text: Stage 02 Measuring "Close" Before we can group anything, we must define what "similar" means. The most common way is to measure the physical distance between data points. We use the Euclidean distance (the straight-line distance) to find out who is closest to whom. It is common, but not the only option; Manhattan, cosine, or domain-specific distances can make more sense for different data. d(A, B) = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ] By measuring the distance between every single pair of points, we build a "distance matrix"—a lookup table for similarity. Takeaway: Clustering depends on your distance choice, because "close" is a design decision.

stages.title: The First Merge
stages.text: Stage 03 The First Merge Hierarchical clustering (specifically the Agglomerative or "bottom-up" kind) starts with a simple rule: Every point starts as its own separate cluster. Find the two clusters that are closest together. Merge them. Watch as the algorithm scans all points, finds the single closest pair, and binds them into a new, single cluster. Takeaway: Agglomerative clustering grows structure from the bottom up, one merge at a time.

stages.title: Defining Group Distance (Linkage)
stages.text: Stage 04 Linkage and distance are not interchangeable. Ward linkage is tied to Euclidean geometry and increases in within-cluster variance. Single linkage can chain; complete linkage favours compact groups; average linkage is a compromise. Dendrogram heights do not represent the same quantity for every method. Defining Group Distance (Linkage) Merging two individual points is easy. But how do you measure the distance between a single point and a group ? Or between two groups? This is called Linkage . The linkage method you choose changes the shape of the clusters. Select a linkage method to re-calculate the merges: Average Single Complete Ward Average: Mean distance between all pairs. Balanced. Worked Example: How is this calculated? Average = mean(...) Step 1: Before Merge A B C A — 2 10 B — 12 C — → Step 3: After Merging [A,B] [A,B] C [A,B] — 11 C — Takeaway: Linkage is the rulebook for deciding which groups are "closest" once clusters start to grow.

stages.title: The Process in Motion
stages.text: Stage 05 The Process in Motion Now, the algorithm repeats the rule over and over. It constantly recalculates distances using the linkage method, finding the next closest pair of clusters, and merging them. Slowly, tiny groups fuse into medium groups, which fuse into large groups. It only stops when everything becomes one giant family. Use the merge scrubber in the visual to step through the history one merge at a time. 17 Current Clusters 0.000 Next Merge Distance Average Current Linkage Takeaway: The algorithm keeps rebuilding the distance picture after every merge, so the path matters.

stages.title: The Family Tree (Dendrogram)
stages.text: Stage 06 The Family Tree (Dendrogram) Instead of just looking at circles on a map, we can record the exact history of these merges in a tree structure called a Dendrogram . As the points align at the bottom, watch the tree grow upwards. The vertical height of each branch is critical: it tells us exactly how far apart the two groups were when they merged. Rule of thumb: A fusion low on the tree means the items were very similar. A fusion high up means they were quite different. Takeaway: A dendrogram preserves the full merge history, and branch height tells you how costly each merge was.

stages.title: Cutting the Tree
stages.text: Stage 07 Cutting the Tree What if you don't know how many clusters you need? That is the superpower of hierarchical clustering: you don't have to guess upfront. By drawing a horizontal line across the dendrogram, you "cut" the branches. The number of vertical lines you intersect is your number of clusters ( K ). How do you choose the cut? A good first strategy is to look for a big jump in merge height and cut just below it, because that often means the algorithm has started forcing together groups that were meaningfully different. If you want a more quantitative check, you can also compare several cuts with a metric such as silhouette score . Cut Height (merge distance) 0.000 Resulting Clusters: Takeaway: Choose cuts where the tree shows a natural separation, not just where a slider gives a convenient K.

stages.title: The Detective's Challenge
stages.text: Stage 08 The Detective's Challenge Clustering is subjective detective work. Because there is no "true" answer (no target variable Y), the results rely entirely on your choices. The "Socks and Computers" Problem If variables use different units or their raw scales should not control distance, scale them using training data only. When variables share meaningful units and variance differences matter, standardisation may be undesirable. Furthermore, an outlier can distort the tree, pulling a group away from its true members just to accommodate the stranger. Takeaway: Scaling and outliers can change the tree dramatically, so preprocessing matters.

stages.title: Synthesis & Recap
stages.text: Stage 09 Synthesis & Recap Hierarchical clustering gives us a rich, explorable structure rather than a single flat answer. Let's compare it to the other famous method, K-Means: Feature Hierarchical K-Means Setup Pick K after Pick K first Output Tree (Dendrogram) Flat groups Speed Usually slower because it builds the full merge tree and repeatedly compares clusters Faster Final Advice: Never take one clustering result as absolute truth. Try different linkages and cut heights. If the same patterns emerge every time, you've found something truly interesting. Takeaway: Hierarchical clustering is valuable when you want an explorable merge history, not just one fixed partition.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem When positives are rare, a model can be highly accurate while missing every important case. Evaluation must reflect prevalence, asymmetric costs, and operational capacity.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective The threshold converts probabilities to actions. Lower thresholds increase recall and false positives; higher thresholds usually increase precision while missing more positives. Prevalence changes predictive values even when sensitivity and specificity stay fixed.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example Fraud prevalence is 1%. A rule with 90% recall and 95% specificity flags 1,395 of 10,000 transactions: 90 true frauds and 1,305 false alarms. Precision is only 6.5%, so investigation capacity matters.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method Sensitivity and specificity condition on actual class, while precision conditions on predicted positives; therefore precision changes strongly with prevalence. A small false-positive rate can still create an overwhelming number of alerts when negatives dominate. ROC and precision–recall curves show different trade-offs and neither chooses an operational threshold automatically. Weighting changes the training objective; resampling changes the examples seen. Synthetic cases must remain inside training folds and may be implausible. Calibration may need correction after altered sampling or prior shift. Confusion counts reveal workload that rates alone can hide. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive laboratory Adjust prevalence, threshold and false-negative cost. Watch precision, recall and expected cost respond.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions Evaluation prevalence and case mix must match intended use. Labels and error costs must be credible; grouped or time structure must be preserved. When the method fails Accuracy and ROC-AUC can look healthy while positive predictions are unusable. Oversampling outside folds leaks, and resampling changes apparent prevalence and calibration.

stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Define positive class and action Estimate realistic prevalence and costs Use stratified plus group/time-aware validation Resample or weight inside training folds Calibrate probabilities when needed Choose threshold on validation data Evaluate once on test data

stages.title: The Unlabeled Data
stages.text: Stage 01 The Unlabeled Data Imagine we have a list of customers. We know two things about each one: their Age and their Spending . Let's draw them! Each customer becomes a dot on our map. Their age moves them left or right, and their spending moves them up or down. Right now, there are no predefined group labels like ‘Cluster 1’ or ‘Cluster 2.’ The algorithm is simply looking at a scattered cloud of dots and trying to discover if some dots naturally sit close together in teams. Customer Age Spending A 24 $ 420 B 48 $ 8,100 ... ... ... Plain-language takeaway: We turn our list of customers into dots on a map. Our goal is to figure out which dots naturally belong together in teams.

stages.title: The Blind Guess (Initialization)
stages.text: Stage 02 The Blind Guess (Initialization) Before we can group the dots, we have to decide how many teams we want. We call this number K . But there is a catch: the algorithm needs a starting guess before it can ask which centroid (center star) is closest. In this demo, we use Random Partition . Here is how it makes its first guess: First , every dot is secretly assigned to a random, temporary team. Next , it looks at all the dots in a team and finds their exact middle by averaging their x and y values. Then , that average middle spot becomes the first centroid (star) for the team! Because the first teams were completely random, these starting stars are usually in weird, unhelpful spots. That is okay, the algorithm will fix them soon! Practical safeguard: use k-means++ to spread initial centroids intelligently, run multiple random restarts, and keep the solution with the lowest WCSS. Convergence reaches a local solution, so different starts can produce different clusters; empty clusters also need an explicit software rule. Plain-language takeaway: The computer needs a starting guess. It puts dots into random teams, finds the exact middle of each random team, and places a star there to act as the first center.

stages.title: Nearest Neighbor Assignment
stages.text: Stage 03 Nearest Neighbor Assignment Now that we have our starting stars, every dot looks around and asks a simple question: Which star is closest to me right now? The dot measures the shortest straight-line distance to every star on the graph. The math formula below might look fancy, but it just calculates that simple, straight-line distance from one point to another. Dist = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ] Every dot joins the team of the star that is closest to it. Hover over the dots on the canvas with your mouse to see their current distance to the star they joined! Remember, this team choice is only temporary. When the stars move, the dots might change their minds. Plain-language takeaway: Every dot measures the straight-line distance to all the stars. It then joins the team of the star that is closest to it.

stages.title: Recentering
stages.text: Stage 04 Recentering After the dots pick their teams, each star is surrounded by its new points. But the star is probably not sitting in the true middle of its new team anymore. So, the algorithm has to move the star to the perfect center of its dots. It does this by finding the average position of all the points assigned to that cluster. Here is a simple worked example of how that works: • Imagine a team has two dots. • One dot is at (2, 4) and the other is at (4, 8) . • We average the x-values: (2 + 4) / 2 = 3 . • We average the y-values: (4 + 8) / 2 = 6 . • The star moves to the exact new middle at (3, 6) ! The star slides to this new spot. It does not need to sit on top of a real customer dot. It just moves to the mathematical center of its team. Plain-language takeaway: The star looks at all the dots on its new team and slides over to sit perfectly in the middle of them.

stages.title: The Convergence Loop
stages.text: Stage 05 The Convergence Loop When the stars move, the map changes! A dot that used to be closest to the Blue star might suddenly find that the Red star is closer. So, K-Means repeats the same two steps over and over again: First , dots join the nearest star. Then , the stars move to the exact middle of their new teams. This loop keeps going until the clustering becomes stable. In practice, the algorithm stops when almost nothing changes anymore. That stable stopping point is called convergence . Convergence means things have settled down—but it doesn't guarantee this is the globally best clustering possible. Click the Step button to watch the loop happen! Run Algorithm Plain-language takeaway: The computer loops the same two steps over and over until the dots stop switching teams and everything finally settles down.

stages.title: Measuring Tightness (WCSS)
stages.text: Stage 06 Measuring Tightness (WCSS) How do we judge whether our teams are tight or loose? We want the dots in a team to be packed closely around their star. To measure this, K-Means uses a score called Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) . It measures the distance from every dot to its assigned star, squares that number, and adds them all up. Why square the distances? Because squaring makes large distances count much more strongly than small ones. A point that sits very far away from its star hurts the score a lot. We want this WCSS score to be as tiny as possible. Look at the Status Strip above the canvas. As the clustering improves, you will see the WCSS number move downward. Plain-language takeaway: The computer scores the teams by measuring how far every dot is from its star. A lower score means the dots are tightly hugging their centers.

stages.title: The Elbow Heuristic
stages.text: Stage 07 The Elbow Heuristic How do we choose K (the number of teams)? One common idea is to test out 1 team, then 2 teams, then 3 teams, and so on, recording the WCSS score for each. As you add more teams, the dots naturally get closer to a star, so the score almost always drops. But we don't want a million teams! We are looking for the bend or elbow in the chart. The elbow is a heuristic: it marks a possible point of diminishing returns, but it may be ambiguous or absent. Combine this chart with stability, silhouette scores, domain usefulness, and alternative clustering methods. Important: the elbow method is just a helpful hint. Some datasets show a clear bend, while others do not. It helps guide us, but it is not a magical rule. Plain-language takeaway: To find the best number of teams, we test different numbers and look for the "elbow" bend on a chart. It tells us when to stop adding more teams.

stages.title: The Scaling Trap
stages.text: Stage 08 The Scaling Trap K-Means measures distance with a simple ruler, but our data has a trap! Age ranges roughly from 20 to 60, while Spending is huge and ranges from 100 to 10,000. If we use these numbers directly, the giant Spending numbers completely dominate the calculation. Look at the canvas: this is a demo visualization of scale imbalance . The dots look like a tall, squished line! The computer is essentially ignoring Age because the numbers are too small to fight against the giant Spending numbers. This makes the distance calculation very unfair. Standardization fixes this! It shrinks and stretches the numbers so Age and Spending are placed on a fair, equal playing field before we measure the distance. Plain-language takeaway: If one category has giant numbers and another has tiny numbers, the giant ones take over. We have to standardize them so everything is fair.

stages.title: Limitations & Outliers
stages.text: Stage 09 Limitations & Outliers K-Means is super fast and helpful, but it has a few blind spots. Because it uses a single star and a simple ruler, it assumes every team is shaped like a neat, even circle. If the real teams are shaped like bananas, stretched out, or very uneven, K-Means might force them into awkward slices. It is also very sensitive to outliers . An outlier is a weird dot that sits super far away from everyone else. Because the star always moves to the average middle, one weird outlier can drag the star completely away from the main group. In this demo, an outlier has been added. Watch how that one lonely dot pulls its centroid away from the main mass of points! Check cluster stability across starts and resampled datasets, and report a silhouette score alongside domain usefulness. Compare Gaussian mixtures for probabilistic elliptical groups and density-based methods for irregular shapes or noise. Plain-language takeaway: K-Means likes neat, round teams. A single weird dot that is very far away can easily trick the star and drag it in the wrong direction.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Data Every machine learning model starts with data. Here we have measurements of fruits — each one scored on Sweetness and Color Intensity . Each fruit is already labeled: it's either an Apple or an Orange . Because we have labels, this is supervised learning . 💡 Supervised learning means the model learns from examples where the answer is already known. Here, each fruit already has a known label: Apple or Orange. Later, KNN uses these known examples as its "memory" to classify any new, unknown fruit. The Whole Idea of KNN KNN stands for K-Nearest Neighbors . The concept is incredibly straightforward: To classify a new unknown item, look at the K closest known examples (neighbors) in your dataset. Then, simply copy the label that appears most often among those neighbors! Example: If we want to identify a mystery fruit, and its 3 closest neighbors are 🍎, 🍎, and 🍊, then Apple gets 2 votes and Orange gets 1 vote. KNN predicts Apple . New unknown fruit → Find closest old fruits → Count their labels → Predict majority label Tiny ML Dictionary Before moving forward, let's establish a few basic terms: • Feature: A measurement used to make a prediction (e.g., Sweetness or Color Intensity ). • Label: The correct answer already known for our examples (e.g., Apple or Orange ). • Class: The category we are trying to predict (e.g., Apple class vs. Orange class ). • Query Point: The new, unknown item we want to classify. In our visual plots, the query point is represented by a star ★ . "We know the query point's features, but we do not know its label yet. KNN tries to guess the label based on its neighbors." Training Dataset 💡 KNN needs labeled examples to learn from. It doesn't build a formula — it simply remembers all the data and compares new points to what it already knows.

stages.title: Choosing Good Features
stages.text: Stage 02 Choosing Good Features Not every measurement helps separate classes. We pick features where the groups actually differ — like Sweetness and Color Intensity. Bad features (random IDs, row numbers) add noise without signal. KNN is especially sensitive to irrelevant features because they pollute the distance calculation. Why Feature Selection Matters A good feature helps separate the classes clearly. A bad feature adds confusion and distorts the distance between points. Useful Examples: Sweetness helps because apples and oranges have different natural sweetness profiles. Color Intensity helps separate reddish apples from yellowish-orange citrus fruits. Not Useful Examples: Row number is just the order in the table; it contains zero predictive power. Day picked is unrelated to fruit sweetness or species and would only add noise. Feature Quality ✅ Sweetness — The two fruit groups show different sweetness patterns ✅ Color Intensity — Apples score higher on red ❌ Row number — meaningless for prediction ❌ Day picked — no predictive power 💡 Notice how the two classes form somewhat distinct clusters on the plot — a good sign. KNN relies entirely on spatial proximity.

stages.title: Train / Test Split
stages.text: Stage 03 Train / Test Split We hold out a small test set (2 apples + 2 oranges) that the model will not see during training. The remaining points are used as the "memory" KNN will search through. Testing on training data is one of the most common mistakes — it gives inflated confidence. A model that memorizes isn't smart; it's just a parrot. Training vs. Testing Sets • Training Set: The collection of examples KNN is allowed to remember and search through. This is the model's "memory". • Test Set: Hidden examples set aside from the beginning, used ONLY at the very end to check if the model can accurately classify new, unseen data. ⚠️ Critical Warning (Data Leakage): Do not use the test set to choose K or tune features. If the model is exposed to the test set during its construction, your evaluation results are no longer honest. This is called data leakage ! — Training — Testing (held-out)

stages.title: Feature Scaling
stages.text:
Stage 04 Feature Scaling This is the most common mistake with KNN. If Sweetness ranges 0–10 but Color ranges 0–100, the Color feature would completely dominate distance calculations. We use Min-Max Scaling to squish every feature into the 0–1 range, giving each feature equal voice. Scaling is usually necessary when features use different units or magnitudes. If features already share meaningful units and scale, automatic rescaling may not be desirable. The distance metric and scaling choice together define what “near” means. Scaled Value = (Value − Min) ÷ (Max − Min)

Example: Sweetness = 7, Min = 2, Max = 9
Scaled Value = (7 − 2) ÷ (9 − 2) = 5 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.71 Important: Scale Using Training Data Only To prevent data leakage, we calculate the Minimum and Maximum values using only the training set. We then use this exact same scale factor for training, test, and any future query points. Training Data finds Min/Max ➔ same Min/Max scales training, test, and new query points If we used the test set to calculate the scale range, information from the test set would leak into the training process, leading to over-optimistic performance estimates. 🧠 Concept Check Why do we scale features before using KNN? To make the dataset smaller and faster to process. Because KNN relies on distances, and features with larger numeric ranges could unfairly dominate the calculations. To make sure all values are converted into whole integers. 💡 Watch the points shift on the plot — they're being rescaled to [0, 1] on each axis. The order of points along each axis stays the same, but the scale changes. This makes distance fairer because Sweetness and Color now use comparable ranges.

controls.text: To make the dataset smaller and faster to process.
Because KNN relies on distances, and features with larger numeric ranges could unfairly dominate the calculations.
To make sure all values are converted into whole integers.

stages.title: Measuring Distance
stages.text:
Stage 05 Measuring Distance KNN's entire logic boils down to one question: "Who lives closest to me?" To answer that, we need a way to measure distance between points. The most common choice is Euclidean distance — the straight-line distance between two points. Euclidean distance assumes each scaled direction should contribute through straight-line geometry. Manhattan, mixed-data, or domain-specific distances may be more appropriate. Scaling cannot rescue irrelevant features or the curse of dimensionality. d(a, b) = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]

This is just the Pythagorean theorem —
the same formula you learned in geometry class. What Does Distance Mean Here? In machine learning, distance represents dissimilarity between items: Short distance means high similarity. The items have very similar features. Long distance means high difference. The items are very dissimilar. Step-by-Step Distance Calculation: Let's calculate the distance between our mystery fruit and a training fruit manually: Query point (Mystery Fruit ★): Sweetness = 0.45, Color = 0.55 Training point (Known Fruit): Sweetness = 0.50, Color = 0.65 Euclidean Distance Formula: d = √[(0.50 − 0.45)² + (0.65 − 0.55)²] d = √[(0.05)² + (0.10)²] d = √[0.0025 + 0.0100] d = √0.0125 d ≈ 0.1118 (the straight-line distance) Note: While Euclidean distance is the straight-line default, other metrics exist (e.g., Manhattan distance , which calculates distance along grid paths like city streets). This page uses Euclidean distance. Live Distance Calculation Lines on the plot show the distance from a query point (★) to every training point. The darker lines emphasize the current teaching K nearest neighbors.

stages.title: Choosing K
stages.text: Stage 06 Choosing K K is one of the most important hyperparameters in KNN — the number of neighbors to consult before making a prediction. Small K (e.g. K=1): Very sensitive to noise. One outlier can flip the prediction. Large K (e.g. K=15): Too smooth. Local patterns get drowned out by distant voters. We do not just guess K blindly. Later, in Stage 12, we compare several K values using cross-validation and look for a sensible choice. Who Chooses K? K is a hyperparameter . In machine learning, a hyperparameter is a setting selected using validation data or cross-validation, rather than a coefficient fitted directly during training. The Trade-Off: Too Small K (e.g., K=1): Extremely sensitive to outliers and noise. The model may overfit (memorize noise as pattern). Too Large K (e.g., K=15): Overly smooth and generic. Local patterns are drowned out by far-away votes. The model may underfit (miss the actual pattern). How a Machine Learning Task is Configured: Component Who Decides? Meaning Features Human / Designer Measurements selected to describe items (e.g., Sweetness) Scaling Method Human choice How feature ranges are made comparable (e.g., Min-Max) Distance Metric Human choice Mathematical formula to measure closeness (e.g., Euclidean) K value Human choice Number of neighboring votes allowed to participate Training labels Existing Data The ground-truth answers for old examples Prediction KNN vote rule Majority vote among the K closest neighbors 🧠 Concept Check Who decides the value of K in K-Nearest Neighbors? The KNN algorithm automatically discovers the best K during training. K is a hyperparameter chosen using validation or cross-validation. The query points themselves decide based on how far away they are. Adjust K K = 3 K=3 is a balanced starting point. Try different values! 💡 Best practice: use an odd number for K to avoid ties. Use cross-validation to find the optimal K for your specific dataset.

controls.text: The KNN algorithm automatically discovers the best K during training.
K is a hyperparameter chosen using validation or cross-validation.
The query points themselves decide based on how far away they are.

stages.title: Finding Neighbors
stages.text: Stage 07 Finding Neighbors For our query point (★), we calculate the distance to every single training point , then sort from closest to farthest. The top K points become the "neighborhood council" that will decide the prediction. Watch the circles expand outward from the query to find them. Nearest Neighbors

stages.title: The Majority Vote
stages.text: Stage 08 The Majority Vote Classification is now a democracy. Each of the K nearest neighbors gets one vote. The class with the most votes wins. Equal Vote Democracy In standard KNN, each neighbor inside the K-limit gets exactly one equal vote . The category with the highest vote count wins the prediction. ⚠️ Note: Vote share estimates probability. If K=3 and Apples win 2-1, the neighbor class proportion gives a local class-probability estimate of 66.7%. This estimate may be noisy or poorly calibrated, especially with small K; it is not a guaranteed probability for this fruit. Why odd numbers for K? In two-class (binary) classification, choosing an odd K guarantees there will be no ties. If we used an even number (like K=4) and got 2 Apple votes and 2 Orange votes, the model would require a complex, arbitrary tie-breaking rule. Using odd K values elegantly prevents this! Current Vote Tally Breakdown: 🧠 Concept Check If K=3 and the 3 nearest neighbors are Apple, Apple, Orange, what does KNN predict? Orange, because it is the unique outlier. Apple, because it wins the majority vote (2 votes to 1). Undecided, because votes are split. Vote Tally 💡 For regression tasks, instead of voting, KNN takes the average value of the K neighbors. But for classification like ours, it's pure democracy.

controls.text: Orange, because it is the unique outlier.
Apple, because it wins the majority vote (2 votes to 1).

stages.title: Decision Boundary
stages.text: Stage 09 Decision Boundary What if we classified every possible point on the plot? The result is a colorful map showing which regions belong to which class. Unlike linear models, KNN boundaries are non-linear — they bend and curve around the data naturally. The boundary is just wherever the majority vote flips from one class to the other. What is a Decision Boundary? A Decision Boundary is the invisible dividing line or contour across the feature space where the model switches from predicting one class to another. Any point that falls on one side is predicted as Apple; any point on the other is Orange. • Non-parametric: KNN has no underlying assumptions or mathematical weights to fit (unlike linear equations). The boundary adapts organically to the data density. • Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Adjusting K alters this boundary: K = 1 (High Variance / Low Bias): Extremely flexible, wiggly, and complex boundary. It fits every outlier precisely, memorizing noise and likely overfitting. Medium K (Balanced Tradeoff): Smooth, reasonable boundary shapes that filter out minor noise while preserving genuine group clusters. Large K (Low Variance / High Bias): Highly smooth, almost straight boundaries. It ignores localized trends completely, risking underfitting. Boundary Properties The decision boundary emerges organically from the data — no formula is fitted. This is what makes KNN a non-parametric model. 💡 Small K = wiggly, complex boundaries. Large K = smoother boundaries. This is the classic bias-variance tradeoff .

stages.title: Classifying Test Points
stages.text: Stage 10 Classifying Test Points Now the moment of truth. We take the test points the model has never seen and classify each one using the same KNN procedure. Watch each test point light up with its prediction. Green rings = correct. Red rings = wrong. Test Predictions

stages.title: Evaluating the Model
stages.text: Stage 11 Evaluating the Model We don't just say "it works." We inspect how it works and where it fails using a confusion matrix and derived metrics. Confusion Matrix Click any quadrant below to see what it means in plain English: 💡 Click a grid cell above to display its evaluation description here. 🧠 Concept Check If Apple is the Positive Class, what does a False Positive mean in our fruit classification task? The model correctly predicted that the fruit was an Apple. The model predicted Apple, but the fruit was actually an Orange. The model predicted Orange, but the fruit was actually an Apple. Performance Metrics (Apple = positive class) These results come from a tiny 4-point held-out test set, so treat them as illustrative rather than stable performance estimates. 💡 With imbalanced data, accuracy alone can be misleading. Precision tells you "of all predicted apples, how many were actually apples?" Recall tells you "of all actual apples, how many did the model find?"

stages.title: The Effect of K
stages.text: Stage 12 The Effect of K K is one of the most important tuning knobs. Watch how the decision boundary changes as K increases. Start with Five-Fold Cross-Validation Five-fold cross-validation is the usual practical starting point. Ten-fold cross-validation is also common. In either case, the training data is divided into folds, and each candidate K is scored several times using different train/validation folds. ⚠️ This toy dataset is very small, so this lesson demonstrates leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) instead. That is a small-data teaching choice, not the usual default. With a larger dataset, five-fold or ten-fold CV would typically be more practical. Cross-Validation Compares K; It Does Not Choose K for You Cross-validation is a loop: try several candidate values of K, calculate an average validation score for each one, then choose the K with the strongest average score. The procedure produces the comparison; the modelling workflow makes the selection. Illustrative five-fold example: Candidate K Average CV accuracy What we do K = 1 75% Compare K = 3 88% Compare K = 5 92% Best average score K = 7 90% Compare In this example, we carry K = 5 forward because it has the highest average CV score. The live chart below uses LOOCV because this toy training set is tiny. Recommended Workflow Order Split once: Separate the full dataset into training and test sets. Keep the test set hidden. Cross-validate on training only: Run five-fold CV for several candidate Ks. In this demonstration, use LOOCV because the training set is very small. Choose K: Compare the average CV scores and select the best-performing candidate. Retrain: Fit KNN on all of the training data using the selected K. Test once: Evaluate that locked model once on the untouched test set. Elbow / Knee: A Secondary Heuristic An elbow or knee is where the CV curve begins to flatten as K increases. It can help you read the curve, but it is a heuristic, not a rule . In most cases, start with the K that has the best average cross-validation score. Use the elbow only as a secondary aid when nearby K values perform similarly, then document the tie-breaker you used. Example: If K = 5 has the highest average CV score and the curve also starts flattening after K = 5, the knee supports the choice. It does not replace the score comparison or select K automatically. ⚠️ Do not choose K from a single split, from the curve's shape alone, or by repeatedly checking the final test set. Compare K Values K = 1 K vs Cross-Validation Accuracy Each point shows the average cross-validation accuracy for one candidate K. Use the highest average score as the primary selection signal; the knee marker is only a secondary visual aid. Demo note: This chart uses leave-one-out cross-validation on the training set only because the toy training set is very small. In practice, start with five-fold or ten-fold CV. 💡 Try several Ks → compare average CV scores → pick the best. The elbow/knee can support the decision, but it is not an automatic rule. Big Picture Try several Ks → cross-validation on train only → pick the best average score → retrain on all train → test once.

stages.title: Strengths and Weaknesses
stages.text: Stage 13 Strengths and Weaknesses Before using K-Nearest Neighbors in practice, it is vital to know when it shines and where it struggles. 💪 Strengths Simple to understand: Intuitive to explain to stakeholders. No Parameter-Learning Phase: KNN does not fit weights or coefficients. It stores the training examples and uses them during prediction. Highly Flexible: Can easily construct complex, non-linear decision boundaries. Naturally Multi-class: Works seamlessly for predicting 3 or more classes. ⚠️ Weaknesses & Limitations Sensitive to Scale: Scaling is usually necessary when features use different units or magnitudes; otherwise larger-scale features dominate distance. The Curse of Dimensionality: When there are too many features, distance often becomes less useful because many points start to seem similarly far apart. This makes it harder for KNN to find truly meaningful neighbors. Slow at Scale: Must calculate distance to every single stored point for every new query. High memory and computing costs. Class Imbalance: If you have 95% Apples and 5% Oranges, votes will naturally skew heavily to Apple. The Whole Story in Plain English Here is the complete machine learning workflow we walked through today: Labeled Examples: Start with known data (fruits with known categories). Feature Selection: Select high-quality, relevant properties (sweetness, color). Train/Test Split: Set aside a final held-out test set to keep final evaluation fair. Feature Scaling: Fit an appropriate scaling transformation using the training data when feature units or magnitudes would otherwise dominate the distance calculation. Standardisation, min-max scaling, robust scaling and domain-specific transformations are all possible choices; apply the fitted transformation unchanged to validation and test data. Mystery Input: Introduce an unknown query point (★) on the plot. Distance Measuring: Run Euclidean distance against all stored training examples. Hyperparameter K: Choose K (the count of voting neighbors) using validation or cross-validation. Locate Neighbors: Gather the K nearest samples. Tally Votes: Perform a democratic, equal-weight majority vote. Predict: Assign the winning class to the unknown query point. Independent Testing: Run the held-out test points to check the model's accuracy. Evaluate Quality: Read the confusion matrix, recall, precision, and F1 metrics. Tune K: Use cross-validation inside the training memory to find the best K. Analyze Trade-offs: Know KNN's limits, such as scale sensitivity and the curse of dimensionality.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Data Every machine learning model starts with data. Here we have measurements of fruits — each one scored on Sweetness and Color . Each fruit is already labeled: it's either an Apple or an Orange . Because we have labels, this is supervised learning . The Whole Idea of LDA Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a supervised classification method. It uses labeled examples to learn a straight-line rule that separates classes. Simple Idea: LDA looks for a direction (projection axis) where: • Different class centers are as far apart as possible. • Points inside each class are as tightly bunched (low spread) as possible. LDA General Pipeline: Labeled Data → Class Centers → Class Spread → Optimal Direction → Boundary → Prediction "LDA is like looking at a messy 2D cloud of points from the best angle so the two groups look as separated as possible." Tiny LDA Dictionary Feature: A measurement used to make a prediction (e.g., Sweetness or Color). Label: The known category of an example (e.g., Apple or Orange). Class: The target group we want to predict (Apple class or Orange class). Mean (μ): The average position or center of a class point cloud. Variance: How much a single feature fluctuates. Covariance: How two features move in relation to each other. Scatter (S): A mathematical measure of data spread or messiness. Projection: Squashing 2D coordinates down onto a single 1D axis. Discriminant Score (δ): A numerical score LDA computes for each class; the highest score wins! Training Dataset LDA needs labeled examples to learn the pattern that separates classes. Without labels, it cannot learn.

stages.title: Choosing Good Features
stages.text: Stage 02 Choosing Good Features Not every measurement helps separate classes. We pick features where the groups actually show different patterns — like Sweetness and Color Score. Bad features (random IDs, row numbers) add noise without signal. LDA works best when features genuinely explain class differences. Feature Quality Evaluation • Sweetness: In this toy dataset, the two fruit groups show different sweetness patterns. • Color Score: In this toy dataset, apples and oranges have different color score patterns. • Row Number: Completely meaningless for classification. • Day of Entry: No predictive power. Warning: Bad or irrelevant features can seriously confuse LDA because they add noise to the calculated means, covariances, and final decision boundary.

stages.title: Train / Test Split
stages.text: Stage 03 Train / Test Split We hold out a small test set (2 apples + 2 oranges) that the model will not see during training. The remaining 20 points are used to learn the pattern. The test points are completely hidden until the evaluation stage. A model that only memorizes training data isn't actually smart — it's just a parrot with ambitions. — Training — Testing (hidden) How the sets are used: Training Set: Used to learn means, covariance, priors, and the decision rule. Test Set: Used exactly once at the very end to check whether the learned rule works on unseen, new data. Data Leakage Warning: The test set must stay absolutely hidden until final evaluation. Do not use the test set to choose features, tune settings, or adjust the model. If the test set influences training decisions, the final evaluation score becomes dishonest!

stages.title: Group by Class
stages.text: Stage 04 Group by Class LDA first separates the training data by label. All apples together, all oranges together. Now it can study each group independently. Why group by class? This step is critical because LDA calculates a separate center (mean) and spread (scatter) for each individual class. Understanding the hulls: A convex hull is just a visual outline drawn around the training points in a class. It is not the LDA model itself! It only helps us see where each class cloud lives in our feature space.

stages.title: Compute Class Means
stages.text: Stage 05 Compute Class Means The mean is the center of each class — its average position in feature space. LDA uses these to understand where each group lives. Mean = Class Center The class mean is the average location of all points in that class. It is like the center of gravity of the class cloud. Example: If most apples have high Sweetness and high Color Score, the apple mean center (μ_apple) will appear right in the middle of the apple cluster. μ_apple  = average position of all apple training points μ_orange = average position of all orange training points The markers on the plot show each class center. The gap between them is what LDA will try to exploit. Concept Check: Class Mean What does a class mean (μ) represent in LDA? A) The single most sweet fruit in the dataset. B) The average center of a class. C) The line that separates the two classes. D) The number of points in the dataset.

controls.text: A) The single most sweet fruit in the dataset.
B) The average center of a class.
C) The line that separates the two classes.
D) The number of points in the dataset.

stages.title: Within-Class Scatter
stages.text: Stage 06 Within-Class Scatter Not all apples are identical. S W measures how much the points in each class wiggle around their own mean. The covariance ellipses on the plot show the spread shape. Diagonal entries = how much each feature varies. Off-diagonal = how features vary together. What does within-class scatter mean? Within-class scatter tells us how messy or spread out each class is inside itself. • If all apples are clustered tightly together, apple scatter is small . • If apples are spread out all over the plot, apple scatter is large . What is covariance? Covariance tells us whether Sweetness and Color move together: • Positive covariance: Sweetness goes up, and Color Score also tends to go up. • Negative covariance: One goes up, while the other goes down. • Near Zero: They do not move together in any pattern. Understanding the Scatter Matrix: • Diagonal entries: How much each feature varies by itself (variance). • Off-diagonal entries: How much the two features move together (covariance). Concept Check: Within-Class Scatter What does within-class scatter measure? A) The distance between the Apple center and Orange center. B) How spread out or messy points are inside each class. C) The accuracy of the final predictions on unseen data. D) The total count of features we selected.

B) How spread out or messy points are inside each class.

stages.title: The Shared Covariance Assumption
stages.text: Stage 07 The Shared Covariance Assumption Here's LDA's key assumption : all classes share the same covariance shape. The groups can have different centers, but their spread is assumed to be roughly the same. So LDA pools the individual covariance matrices into one shared estimate. Watch the ellipses morph into a single shape. Why does LDA pool covariance? LDA assumes that the classes have similar spread shapes. Instead of keeping separate shapes for Apple and Orange, it combines them into one shared covariance estimate . Simple meaning: Different centers, same general spread shape. LDA vs. QDA Comparison: • LDA (Linear): Assumes shared covariance → Draws a straight decision line. • QDA (Quadratic): Allows different covariances per class → Can draw a curved decision line. Warning: If the class clouds actually have very different shapes, LDA's shared covariance assumption is violated. LDA may struggle, and QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis) might fit the data much better. Concept Check: Shared Covariance What is LDA’s shared covariance assumption? A) Every fruit in the dataset has the exact same sweetness value. B) The test set must have the same size as the training set. C) Classes can have different centers, but they are assumed to have similar spread shapes. D) The decision boundary must always be curved.

controls.text: A) Every fruit in the dataset has the exact same sweetness value.
B) The test set must have the same size as the training set.
C) Classes can have different centers, but they are assumed to have similar spread shapes.
D) The decision boundary must always be curved.

stages.title: Between-Class Scatter
stages.text:
Stage 08 Between-Class Scatter S B measures how far apart the class centers are. The further apart, the easier it is for LDA to separate them. LDA's goal is to maximize the ratio of between-class scatter to within-class scatter: Between-class scatter = gap between class centers Let's contrast the two scatter metrics: • Within-class scatter asks: "How messy and spread out is each class inside itself?" • Between-class scatter asks: "How far apart are the class centers (means)?" LDA's Ultimate Goal: We want the gap between classes to be BIG , and the messiness inside each class to be SMALL ! J(w) = wᵀ S_B w / wᵀ S_W w

In simple terms, J(w) is maximized when:
1. Projected class means are far apart.
2. Projected class spreads are small.

stages.title: The Optimal Direction
stages.text:
Stage 09 The Optimal Direction In this 2-class example, LDA gives one main discriminant direction w — the angle where classes appear most separated. What is projection and why do we do it? Projection means dropping every 2D point (Sweetness, Color) down onto a single 1D line or direction. This turns a 2D pair of numbers into a single 1D score : Fruit (Sweetness, Color) → [Project] → One LDA Score Why project? If the projected Apple scores sit neatly on one side of the line and the projected Orange scores sit on the other side, LDA has found an excellent direction for separation! w ∝ S_W⁻¹ (μ₁ − μ₂)

This isn't just the straight line between means.
It also tilts to avoid the direction of maximum within-class spread.

stages.title: The Decision Boundary
stages.text:
Stage 10 The Decision Boundary Because LDA is linear , the boundary between classes is a straight line (in 2D). Everything on one side is classified as Apple, the other as Orange. Discriminant Scores: Highest Score Wins LDA calculates a separate scoring function for each class, called the Discriminant Score (δ) : δ_apple(x)  = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Apple δ_orange(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Orange For any point, LDA compares the two scores: whichever score is higher is the predicted class! Example Fruit Prediction: (Simple illustrative example, not a live value from the current dataset) • Apple Score (δ_apple) = 2.31 • Orange Score (δ_orange) = -1.44 Since 2.31 is higher than -1.44, LDA predicts Apple ! What are priors (π_k)? The prior probability (π_k) represents the class probability before observing its features. Priors may be estimated from training prevalence or specified externally. • If apples and oranges are equally common, priors are equal (50% each). • If we estimate priors from 90% apples in training, the apple score gets a prior boost, shifting the boundary slightly to favor Apple predictions. δ_k(x) = xᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ_k − ½ μ_kᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ_k + log(π_k)

Predict class k with the highest δ_k(x) Concept Check: Decision Rule How does LDA decide the final predicted class of a point? A) It checks which class is physically closer using plain Euclidean distance. B) It calculates a discriminant score for each class and chooses the highest one. C) It always predicts the class that has more training samples. D) It uses random guessing when a point is near the boundary.

stages.title: Assumptions & Limitations
stages.text: Stage 14 Assumptions & Limitations To use LDA effectively, you need to understand when it thrives and when it falls short. LDA Works Best When: Linearity: A straight-line boundary is a reasonable way to separate classes. Normality: Each class looks like a symmetrical oval cloud (multivariate normal distribution). Equal Spread: All classes share roughly the same spread/covariance shape. Independence: Data samples are collected independently. Data Volume: There are many more rows than features. No Outliers: Extreme values are absent (outliers pull means away easily). LDA Struggles When: The true dividing boundary is highly curved. Classes have very different shapes or spreads (e.g., one is a tight circle, the other is a giant flat ellipse). There are severe outliers that skew centers. You have too many features and not enough rows (overfitting). Features are redundant or highly correlated (collinearity). Alternative Methods If LDA doesn't fit, consider these standard alternatives: QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis): Excellent if class spreads are highly unequal. Logistic Regression: Also estimates class probabilities, but avoids LDA’s Gaussian class-conditional and shared-covariance assumptions. KNN or Decision Trees: Great for highly complex, non-linear boundaries.

stages.title: It Starts with Data 🍦
stages.text: Stage 01 It Starts with Data 🍦 Imagine you run an ice-cream shop. Every day you note the temperature , whether it was sunny , and whether someone bought ice cream . The plot shows each day as a dot: temperature on the x-axis, outcome (bought or didn't) on the y-axis. Legend ● Bought (y = 1) ● Didn't buy (y = 0) What is probability? 🤔 Probability means "how likely something is to happen." It is always written as a number between 0 and 1: 0 means impossible (0% chance). 0.5 means 50-50 (50% chance). 1 means certain (100% chance). In this guide, probability means: "How likely is someone to buy ice cream?" Bought = 1 and Didn't buy = 0 are just category labels. They do not mean someone bought one ice cream or zero ice creams. They simply mark the two possible outcomes for the model. Notice how higher temperatures tend to cluster near y = 1? That's the signal our model will learn to capture. 📌 This is a small toy dataset with 20 rows designed for teaching. Real datasets have hundreds or thousands of rows.

stages.title: Why Lines Break 📏
stages.text:
Stage 02 Why Lines Break 📏 Your first instinct might be to draw a straight line through the data — that's linear regression . But watch what happens: the line predicts values above 1 and below 0 . Those aren't valid probabilities! ŷ = b₀ + b₁ · Temperature
Can give 1.5 or −0.3 … not a probability! Why Bounds Matter 🚧 A probability cannot be below 0 or above 1: Below 0 would mean “less than impossible.” Above 1 would mean “more than certain.” So a prediction like 1.5 means 150%, which makes no real-world sense. We need a curve that stays strictly between 0 and 1. We need a function that squishes any number into the 0–1 range. Enter the sigmoid .

stages.title: From a Raw Score to a Probability ✨
stages.text:
Stage 03 From a Raw Score to a Probability ✨ First, logistic regression starts the same way linear regression does. For each data point, one linear equation combines that point's features with the model's learned weights and produces one raw number, called z . z = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + ···

one data point → one raw score z z is not a z-score or a standard score. It is not learned separately for each point. It is simply the model's raw opinion before that opinion becomes a probability. z can be any number from negative infinity to positive infinity. If z = 0 , the model is exactly at 50/50. Only after that do we apply the sigmoid function to turn z into a probability between 0 and 1. p = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)

Large positive z → probability near 1
Large negative z → probability near 0
z = 0 → probability exactly 0.5 See the Sigmoid Respond Raw score z = 0.0 0.500 Probability Where Does z Come From? 🤔 For this interactive slider: yes , you are choosing the raw score z manually so you can see how the sigmoid responds. In a real machine learning model: no , you do not choose z manually. The model runs its linear equation on each data point's features and learned weights. Features + Weights → raw score z raw score z → Sigmoid → Probability “The z slider is only a teaching demo. In real logistic regression, the model calculates a separate raw score z for each row, then the sigmoid turns it into a probability.” 🧠 Concept Check Quiz 1 In real logistic regression, where does the raw score z come from? A. The model's linear equation combines each row's features with learned weights. B. The user chooses a new z for every row. C. The sigmoid chooses z after calculating the probability. D. z is the same as the decision threshold. 📐 The sigmoid on the canvas is a 2D slice — it plots probability vs. temperature while holding Sunny and Weekend fixed at a neutral 0.5. The real model uses all three features simultaneously.

stages.title: Weighted Clues 🧠
stages.text: Stage 04 Weighted Clues 🧠 How do we construct the score z ? Think of our features (Temperature, Sunny, Weekend) as clues. Each weight describes the change in log-odds for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding the other modeled predictors fixed: • A positive weight pushes the score toward "Buy" (y = 1). • A negative weight pushes the score toward "Don't Buy" (y = 0). • The final raw score z is the total combined push from all clues. The Sigmoid then turns this raw score into a clean final probability. These sliders are a sandbox. You are manually changing the weights only to see how the mathematical curve reacts. In real training, the model learns these weights automatically by reducing log loss. Stage 04 (Sandbox): You adjust weights manually to see the shapes of the decision curve. Stage 05 (Machine Learning): The model adjusts weights automatically using gradient descent. z = b₀ + b₁·standardized Temp + b₂·Sunny + b₃·Weekend b₀ = bias (baseline push) · b₁, b₂, b₃ = individual clue pushes Standardized temperature means we convert raw temperature values into a scaled version with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1. Scaling mainly helps optimisation run smoothly and makes regularisation penalties more comparable across features. Large raw values do not inherently overpower the final fitted model: coefficients account for feature units. stages.title: Learning from Mistakes ⚙️
stages.text:
Stage 05 Learning from Mistakes ⚙️ The model starts with initial weights , makes predictions, measures how wrong it was using log loss , then nudges the weights to improve. This is gradient descent . Training does not directly choose z. Training learns better weights. Once the weights improve, the model calculates better z values for each row of data automatically: Training updates weights → weights calculate z → sigmoid turns z into probability → threshold turns probability into Yes/No L = −[ y·log(p) + (1−y)·log(1−p) ]

The model is punished more when it's
very confident but very wrong. How Log Loss Thinks 🧠 Log loss measures the penalty of wrong answers. If the actual answer is 1 (Bought): Real Answer Predicted Prob Meaning Loss Penalty 1 (Bought) 0.95 Confident & correct Small Loss (0.05) 1 (Bought) 0.55 Unsure but leaning right Medium Loss (0.60) 1 (Bought) 0.05 Confident & wrong! Huge Loss (3.00) * Note: These loss values are examples for one single prediction. The training loss shown below is the average loss across all training rows. Gradient descent is like adjusting a recipe little by little. If the model is wrong, it changes the weights in the direction that reduces loss. The learning rate controls how big each adjustment step is.
      Gradient descent is one teaching-friendly optimiser, not the definition of logistic regression: Newton, quasi-Newton, coordinate-descent and other solvers are also common. Feature scaling often improves numerical optimisation and is especially relevant with regularisation; fit scaling inside training folds. ⚠️ Warning on Learning Rate: • Too small: Learning is very slow, requiring thousands of steps. • Too large: The model may jump right over the best values and fail to settle. 🧠 Concept Check Quiz 2 What does model training mainly learn/adjust? A. The final threshold only. B. Better weights that reduce log loss. C. The labels y = 0 and y = 1. D. The color of the dots. Train the Model ▶ Train ↺ Reset Learning rate 0.010 0 Epoch — Loss 💡 Temperature is standardized behind the scenes (mean=0, std=1) so all features are on comparable scales. This makes gradient descent more stable.

stages.title: Drawing the Line 🚦
stages.text: Stage 06 Drawing the Line 🚦 The sigmoid gives a probability . But we need a decision : Yes or No. We pick a threshold . If p ≥ threshold → predict Yes (1) If p < threshold → predict No (0) The model only gives probabilities. The threshold is a decision rule chosen by humans. We choose it based on what kind of mistake is worse or more costly for our specific situation: Threshold vs. Probability 🔍 The threshold does not change the probability itself . It only changes how we convert that probability into a final Yes/No decision. Example: If the model predicts a probability of 0.62 : • At threshold 0.50 → predict Yes (since 0.62 ≥ 0.50) • At threshold 0.70 → predict No (since 0.62 < 0.70) The probability stayed exactly 0.62. Only the decision rule changed. Lowering the Threshold (e.g., 0.30): Predicts "Yes" more easily. You catch more real buyers (high recall), but you also create more false alarms (false positives). Raising the Threshold (e.g., 0.70): Predicts "Yes" only when highly confident. You reduce false alarms (high precision), but you might miss many real buyers (false negatives). Set Threshold Threshold 0.50 Select this threshold on validation data, never the final test set. Use error costs, prevalence, capacity, and the real objective. Lock the threshold with all preprocessing and calibration choices, then report final test performance once. Probability calibration and classification accuracy answer different questions. 🧠 Concept Check Quiz 3 Who chooses the decision threshold? A. Usually the human/researcher, based on the problem. B. The sigmoid function. C. The raw temperature column. D. The y-axis. 💡 A medical test might use 0.3 (catch more sick people), while a spam filter might use 0.7 (avoid false alarms).

controls.text: A. Usually the human/researcher, based on the problem.

stages.title: Select the Decision Rule on Validation Data 📊
stages.text: Stage 07 Select the Decision Rule on Validation Data 📊 Use the validation set to explore threshold-dependent trade-offs. The final test set remains hidden while the threshold, metrics and model choices are still changing. Every validation prediction falls into one of four boxes: • TP (True Positive): Predicted Bought, and they really bought. Correct prediction! • TN (True Negative): Predicted Didn't buy, and they did not buy. Correct prediction! • FP (False Positive): Predicted Bought, but they did not buy. (False alarm!). • FN (False Negative): Predicted Didn't buy, but they actually bought. (Missed buyer!). Validation Confusion Matrix 👉 Click on any grid cell below to show its plain-English explanation. Use these development results to select and lock the rule; do not repeatedly inspect the test set. Validation Metrics Overall Accuracy -- Formula: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) Meaning: How often was the model correct overall? Best used when mistakes are equally costly. Precision (Reliability of Yes Predictions) -- Formula: TP / (TP + FP) Meaning: When the model predicts Bought, how often is it right? Critical when false alarms (FP) are expensive. Recall (Sensitivity / Detection Rate) -- Formula: TP / (TP + FN) Meaning: Out of all real positive buyers, how many did the model catch? Critical when missing a real positive (FN) is costly. F1-Score -- Formula: 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall) Meaning: F1 is a balance score between precision and recall. It is not a normal average; it gives a low score if either precision or recall is weak. Perfect when you want to look at general model balance. stages.title: The Validation ROC Curve 🔔
stages.text: Stage 08 The Validation ROC Curve 🔔 The validation ROC curve shows: at every possible threshold, how does recall trade off against false-alarm rate? It is a development visual and never reads the final test set. Think of a smoke alarm: too sensitive and it goes off when you cook toast; too lenient and it misses an actual fire. Accuracy vs. ROC / AUC: • Accuracy shows model performance at a single chosen threshold (like 0.50). • ROC shows performance trade-offs across all possible thresholds. • AUC (Area Under Curve) is not the same as accuracy. AUC summarizes how well the model separates/ranks positive cases from negative cases across all thresholds. Key ROC Metrics Explained An ROC curve plots two key metrics against each other at all possible thresholds from 0.0 to 1.0: True Positive Rate (TPR / Recall): TP / (TP + FN) Meaning: Out of all real buyers, what percentage did we catch? (Higher is better!) False Positive Rate (FPR / False Alarm Rate): FP / (FP + TN) Meaning: Out of all non-buyers, what percentage did we wrongly predict as buyers? (Lower is better!) The ROC curve checks many possible thresholds, not just 0.5. Each point on the curve comes from a specific threshold value. Moving the threshold changes TPR and FPR. — AUC (Area Under Curve) • AUC = 1.0: Perfect separation on this dataset. • AUC = 0.5: Random guessing. The model has no predictive strength. Note: AUC does not mean the model is perfect forever. It only summarizes separation performance on the data being evaluated. 📌 Note: Because this teaching example has a very small validation set, the ROC curve looks coarse and jumpy. With a larger validation sample, the curve would usually be smoother.

stages.title: What the Numbers Mean 📎
stages.text: Stage 09 What the Numbers Mean 📎 We often want to know how the model estimates each feature (temperature, sunny day, weekend status) is associated with higher or lower predicted odds, while holding other features constant. Logistic regression gives us weights that can be converted into Odds Ratios . Probability vs. Odds 🎲 Probability and Odds are related but express likelihood differently: • Probability (p) asks: "Out of all outcomes, how likely is Yes?" (Varies between 0 and 1). • Odds asks: "How much does the chance of Yes beat No?" (Varies from 0 to infinity). Formula: Odds = p / (1 - p) Probability (p) Odds Formula Odds Value Meaning 0.50 (50%) 0.50 / 0.50 1 to 1 (1.0) Yes and No are equally likely 0.75 (75%) 0.75 / 0.25 3 to 1 (3.0) Yes is three times as likely as No 0.80 (80%) 0.80 / 0.20 4 to 1 (4.0) Yes is four times as likely as No Taking the exponent of a weight ( e weight ) gives us the Odds Ratio (OR) . This ratio tells us how the odds of buying are multiplied for each unit increase in that feature. ⚠️ Beginner Warning: Odds are not the same as probability. An odds ratio of 2 does not mean the probability doubles! It means the odds ratio doubles (e.g. from 1:1 odds to 2:1 odds). ⚠️ Coefficient ≠ proof of cause: A positive coefficient means the feature is associated with higher predicted probability in this model. It does not prove that modifying the feature directly causes buying behavior. Our Weights & Odds Ratios Positive Weight (OR > 1): Feature is associated with pushing probability and odds up . Negative Weight (OR < 1): Feature is associated with pushing probability and odds down . Near Zero Weight (OR ≈ 1): Feature has little to no association with predicted odds.

stages.title: The Full Picture 🌟
stages.text: Stage 10 The Full Picture 🌟 You've walked through the entire logistic regression pipeline! Let's review the whole story in plain English: The Story of Logistic Regression 📖 We collect historical raw data : temperature, sunny weather, weekends, and whether someone bought ice cream. A straight linear regression line is not suitable because it predicts impossible values (below 0 and above 1) for probabilities. Instead, logistic regression builds an intermediate score called z by adding up weighted features (clues). The mathematical sigmoid function gracefully "squishes" this score z into a valid probability between 0% and 100%. A decision threshold translates probabilities into labels. Select it on validation data from error costs, prevalence and objectives; 0.50 is only a convention. During training , the model starts with baseline weights and iteratively adjusts them using gradient descent to minimize average log loss . A validation confusion matrix is used to compare threshold choices without touching the final test set. Performance is summarized using descriptive metrics: Accuracy (overall correctness), Precision (purity of Yes calls), Recall (capture rate of actual positives), and F1-score (their balanced harmony). The validation ROC curve and AUC summarize ranking trade-offs across thresholds during development. After the model and threshold are locked, the test set is revealed once for the final performance estimate. By analyzing coefficients and odds ratios , we can interpret how the model estimates each feature is associated with higher or lower odds of a purchase. stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem Missing values and categories carry structure. A convenient fill value or numeric code can change the estimand, introduce false order, or leak outcome information.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective Imputation predicts or substitutes missing values; encoding represents categories numerically. Both are learned transformations and belong inside the pipeline.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example Income is missing more often for high earners. Mean imputation pulls their values toward the centre and understates variation. A missingness indicator may help prediction, but it does not make the missing-at-random assumption true for inference.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method MCAR, MAR and MNAR are assumptions about the missingness process, not labels that a plot can prove. Complete-case analysis is valid for limited targets under restrictive conditions. Single imputation treats filled values as known and usually understates inferential uncertainty; multiple imputation combines within- and between-imputation variation. Encoding defines geometry: one-hot separates unordered levels, ordinal encoding asserts order, and target encoding borrows outcome information. Target and frequency encoders need fold-safe fitting and an unseen-level policy. Raw columns and a data dictionary should be retained so every transformation remains auditable. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive laboratory Change missingness rate and strategy. Compare remaining bias, predictive error and whether an encoding introduces artificial order.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions Missing-data methods rely on assumptions about why values are absent. Category encodings assume a structure—unordered, ordinal, or target-related—that must be defensible. When the method fails Single imputation understates inferential uncertainty; ordinal codes create fake distances; target encoding leaks without cross-fitting; unseen categories can break deployment.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Profile missingness and category levels Separate structural from accidental missingness Split data before fitting transforms Choose imputation for the analysis goal Encode with explicit reference and unknown-level policy Run sensitivity analyses

stages.text: Stage 08 Interpretation and reporting What to report: Report missingness rates, mechanism assumptions, imputation model, number of imputations, encoding, reference levels, unknown-category policy and sensitivity. Common misuse: Using zero as “missing” when zero has a real scientific meaning.

stages.title: The Overfitting Trap
stages.text: Stage 01 The Overfitting Trap Building a predictive model is tricky. It is tempting to include every available piece of data. We often assume that more clues guarantee better answers. However, adding too many variables introduces massive noise. This noise obscures the true relationship. The model ends up memorizing random accidents in the training data rather than learning the actual signal. The Illusion of Accuracy: A highly complex model performs flawlessly on its "homework" (the training data). But it collapses in the real world on unseen data. This failure is called overfitting .

stages.title: The n-p Puzzle
stages.text: Stage 02 The n-p Puzzle To build a reliable model, we must balance two things. First is the number of samples ($n$). Second is the number of variables or clues ($p$). Think of this in three simple steps: Step 1: You need enough examples to prove a real pattern exists. Step 2: Every new variable adds a whole new dimension for the model to search. Step 3: When $p>n$, ordinary least squares has no unique coefficient solution unless constraints are imposed. Ridge, Lasso, or other regularisation can still support useful prediction, although instability and overfitting are serious concerns. At this point, the design matrix is rank deficient . Without additional constraints, many coefficient vectors may fit the training data equally well. This makes coefficient interpretation unstable and creates a high risk of overfitting. Useful prediction may still be possible with appropriate regularisation, feature structure and honest validation. Keep the ideas separate: non-unique coefficients concern identifiability; interpolation means matching the observed training outcomes; overfitting is poor generalisation caused by learning sample-specific patterns; predictive performance must be measured on unseen data. Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net impose different constraints that can produce estimable predictors, but they are not automatic cures.

stages.title: Picking the Best Team
stages.text: Stage 03 Picking the Best Team One way to fix this is Subset Selection . This means literally picking a specific group of variables and throwing the rest out. Forward Start empty. Add the single best predictor. Then add the next one that helps the most. Keep going. Backward Start with all variables. Find the weakest predictor and bench them. Repeat until only the best are left. Hybrid Add the best predictors one by one. But constantly re-evaluate. If an old predictor becomes redundant, remove it. Mini-Check Why don't we just test every single combination of variables? It decreases accuracy. It is computationally impossible. Just 40 predictors creates over a billion models. Reset / Try Again ↻

controls.text: It is computationally impossible. Just 40 predictors creates over a billion models.

stages.title: The Scorecards
stages.text: Stage 04 The Scorecards As we add variables, the raw training error always goes down. The model looks better, even if it is just memorizing noise. To find the truly best model, we need scorecards. These scorecards punish us for adding unnecessary complexity. $C_p$, AIC, BIC Like a golf score: Lower is better. They measure Total Error + Complexity Penalty. Adj. $R^2$ Higher is better. Adjusts the traditional $R^2$ relative to total variation and complexity. $C_p = \frac{1}{n}(RSS + 2p\hat{\sigma}^2)$ $AIC = \frac{2p}{n} - \frac{2}{n}\ln(L)$ $BIC = -2\ln(L) + p\ln(n)$ $\text{Adj. } R^2 = 1 - \frac{RSS/(n-p-1)}{TSS/(n-1)}$ Plain English Breakdown Most scorecards use the same basic logic: Total Score = Error + Penalty . $C_p$, AIC, and BIC: These measure how much your model's guesses miss the actual marks ($RSS$ or $-2\ln(L)$) and add a mathematical tax for every variable ($p$) you use. You want these to be low . BIC's extra strictness: BIC multiplies the penalty by $\ln(n)$, meaning for most datasets, it applies a much harsher penalty than AIC, strongly forcing you to choose simpler models. Adjusted $R^2$: Unlike the others, higher is better here. It measures the percentage of variation your model explains, but mathematically penalizes you if you add useless variables to artificially inflate the score.
