You want these to be low . BIC's extra strictness: BIC multiplies the penalty by $\ln(n)$, meaning for most datasets, it applies a much harsher penalty than AIC, strongly forcing you to choose simpler models. Adjusted $R^2$: Unlike the others, higher is better here. It measures the percentage of variation your model explains, but mathematically penalizes you if you add useless variables to artificially inflate the score.

stages.title: The Shrinking Trick
stages.text: Stage 05 The Shrinking Trick Subset selection is an "all-or-nothing" approach. A variable is either in or out. But what if we just made a weak variable's influence smaller? This is called Regularization . Imagine a soundboard where each slider controls a variable. Regularization turns down the volume on loud, messy variables. It shrinks their coefficients ($\beta$) toward zero using a tuning dial called $\lambda$ (Lambda). Crucial Step: Variables should be centered first, and usually standardized when their scales differ, to create a level playing field. Otherwise, a variable measured in huge numbers (like dollars) would face unfair shrinkage compared to a variable measured in small numbers (like years). Mini-Check What is the main goal of Regularization? To delete all the variables and start over. To turn down the volume (shrink the coefficients) of noisy or less useful variables. Reset / Try Again ↻

controls.text: To delete all the variables and start over.
To turn down the volume (shrink the coefficients) of noisy or less useful variables.

stages.title: Ridge Regression (L2)
stages.text: Stage 06 Ridge Regression (L2) Ridge regression acts like a "Gentle Parent." It looks at the noisy variables and says, "Everybody calm down a little." Minimize: $RSS + \lambda \sum \beta_j^2$ Plain English Breakdown $RSS$: The raw error of your predictions. $\lambda$ (Lambda): The strength of the penalty. You control this dial. $\sum \beta_j^2$: The sum of all your squared coefficients. Ridge hates large coefficients. What to notice: Ridge adds a squared penalty. This mathematically forces all coefficients to shrink, but crucially, they never reach exactly zero . Watch this: Slide the $\lambda$ dial below. Notice how the colorful bars shrink together, but none of them vanish completely. Ridge Penalty ($\lambda$) 0 λ = 0: No penalty applied (Standard OLS).

controls.text: Plain English Breakdown $RSS$: The raw error of your predictions. $\lambda$ (Lambda): The strength of the penalty. You control this dial. $\sum \beta_j^2$: The sum of all your squared coefficients. Ridge hates large coefficients. What to notice: Ridge adds a squared penalty. This mathematically forces all coefficients to shrink, but crucially, they never reach exactly zero .

stages.title: Lasso Regression (L1)
stages.text: Stage 07 Lasso Regression (L1) Lasso regression is the "Strict Parent." It looks at the variables and says, "Some of you are helping. Some of you are just standing here. Leave." Minimize: $RSS + \lambda \sum |\beta_j|$ Plain English Breakdown $\sum |\beta_j|$: Instead of squaring the coefficients, Lasso takes their absolute value. What to notice: Because it uses absolute values, the geometry changes. Lasso can force coefficients to drop to exactly zero . Watch this: Slide the $\lambda$ dial and observe coefficients reach zero. In real samples we do not know which variables are truly useless. With highly correlated predictors, Lasso may select one, discard another, and swap that choice after a small sample change. Sparse does not mean causal or uniquely important. Lasso supports prediction and variable selection, but selection stability must be checked across resamples. Elastic Net combines L1 and L2 penalties and can behave more stably when predictors share signal. Lasso Penalty ($\lambda$) 0 λ = 0: No penalty applied (Standard OLS).

controls.text: Plain English Breakdown $\sum |\beta_j|$: Instead of squaring the coefficients, Lasso takes their absolute value. What to notice: Because it uses absolute values, the geometry changes. Lasso can force coefficients to drop to exactly zero .

stages.title: Finding the Sweet Spot
stages.text: Stage 08 Finding the Sweet Spot How do we know the right amount of shrinkage? We use K-Fold Cross-Validation to find the optimal $\lambda$ dial setting. Choose CV from the data structure. Use stratified folds for imbalanced classes, grouped folds for repeated subjects or organisations, time-series CV for ordered observations, repeated CV for stability, and nested CV when model selection and unbiased evaluation must both occur. Imputation, scaling, encoding, feature selection, PCA, outlier rules, oversampling and threshold tuning all belong inside the training folds. First, we divide our training data into chunks called "folds". Train Train Train Train Validate We train the model on four folds. We then validate it on the one held-out fold (highlighted above). We repeat this process, rotating which fold is held out, until every fold has been tested. Finally, we average the errors. Why average them? Averaging prevents a "lucky split." It stops us from accidentally choosing a model that just happened to get easy data during validation. Sweep $\lambda$ to find Minimum Error 0 Current λ: 0 | CV Error: ... | Too low! (Overfitting)

stages.title: The "Super-Variable" Secret
stages.text: Stage 09 The "Super-Variable" Secret If we have 100 highly correlated variables, they provide redundant information. Dimension Reduction allows us to "squish" them into a few super-variables called Principal Components. PCR Compress first, predict later. It squishes variables together without looking at what you are trying to predict. PLS Compress while paying attention. It squishes variables together by finding directions that best explain the target you want to predict. Think of PCR as combining 100 photos of a dog into a single "Super-Photo" of the whole dog. PLS knows you are trying to predict happiness, so it squishes the photos specifically to highlight the wagging tail.

stages.title: Decision Helper
stages.text: Stage 10 Decision Helper Select your goals to see which tool fits best (you can select multiple): I need to explain "Why" I want fewer variables I only care about pure accuracy I have highly correlated variables Best match: Lasso & Best Subset Selection You prioritize explaining 'why' and keeping models simple. Recommended Lasso & Best Subset Selection Best for Interpretability & Simplicity. These methods drop variables entirely, leaving a clean, short list of the most important drivers. Essential in healthcare or finance where explaining the "why" matters. Recommended Ridge & PCR Best for Pure Prediction & Correlated Data. When you have many overlapping clues and prediction accuracy matters more than a simple explanation, keeping all variables with smaller, stable weights helps minimize error on new data.

controls.text: I only care about pure accuracy

stages.title: Common Mistakes
stages.text: Stage 11 Common Mistakes Even advanced statistical methods are not magic. Here is how to avoid common traps. Mistake 1 Choosing a model based on training accuracy. Correct Practice Always compare and judge models based on cross-validation error. Training accuracy is always overly optimistic. Mistake 2 Testing on the final test set multiple times. Correct Practice Lock the final test set in a vault. Use it only once at the very end to check your final model. If you use it to tweak parameters, it is no longer an honest test.

stages.title: Final Synthesis
stages.text: Stage 12 Final Synthesis We do not want a model that is too simple (underfitting). We do not want a model that is too dramatic (overfitting). By using Cross-Validation , we compare and validate models fairly. By applying Regularization or Subset Selection , we penalize messiness and force the model to focus only on what matters. The ultimate goal is Generalization . We want to build a model that stays trustworthy and useful when reality shows up and starts ruining everyone's assumptions. Final Check What is the ultimate goal of model selection and regularization? To achieve 0% error on the training data. Generalization: performing well on unseen real-world data. Reset / Try Again ↻

Generalization: performing well on unseen real-world data.

stages.title: The Multi-Variable World
stages.text: Stage 01 The Multi-Variable World Life is messy. If we want to predict a student's Test Score , knowing how many hours they studied is helpful, but it's rarely the full story. What about how much sleep they got? What about the number of practice papers they completed? Multiple Linear Regression allows us to use several clues together to predict one number. Our Data Universe To the right, we plot a dataset of students in 3D space: X-Axis: Hours Studied Z-Axis: Hours Slept Y-Axis (Height): Test Score

stages.title: The Secret Recipe
stages.text: Stage 02 The Secret Recipe In simple regression, we draw a line. But with three predictors—Study, Sleep, and Practice—we technically need a 4D space! Since we can't see 4D, we'll draw a 3D plane as a visual stepping stone. We'll plot Study and Sleep on the axes, and hold Practice temporarily constant at its average to visualize one slice of the full model. Think of the full equation like a cake recipe with multiple ingredients: y = β 0 + β 1 x 1 + β 2 x 2 + β 3 x 3 + ε The Target (y) Test Score The Predictors (x) Study, Sleep, Practice The Boosters (β) Coefficients The Messiness (ε) Unexplained Error

stages.title: Finding the Fit
stages.text: Stage 03 Finding the Fit We want our model to pass as closely to the actual student scores as possible. The distance between our prediction and the actual score is called a Residual (the red dashed lines). Try adjusting the full set of coefficients manually. The indigo surface is the average-practice slice, while the hollow red markers show the full three-variable prediction used for the residuals and SSE. Base Score (β 0 ) 10.0 Study Boost (β 1 ) 1.0 Sleep Boost (β 2 ) 1.0 Practice Boost (β 3 ) 1.0 Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) ---

stages.title: The Least Squares Method
stages.text: Stage 04 The Least Squares Method Instead of guessing, the computer uses matrix algebra to instantly derive the absolute lowest possible Sum of Squared Errors directly from the dataset. By minimizing the squared residuals across all 3 dimensions simultaneously, it settles perfectly into the optimal fit. Snap to Optimal Fit Why Square the Errors? 1. It stops positive (+4) and negative (-4) misses from canceling out to zero. 2. It heavily punishes huge misses (a miss of 10 costs 100 points), forcing the model to compromise evenly across all variables.

stages.title: The Superpower: Holding Constant
stages.text: Stage 05 The Superpower: Holding Constant This is the most critical concept in multiple regression. What does a Study Boost (β 1 ) actually mean when we have an optimal fit? It means: If a student studies one extra hour, their score increases by exactly that boost amount— assuming their sleep and practice papers stay exactly the same. This logic applies to each predictor's coefficient: β 1 is the estimated association with Study while Sleep and Practice are held fixed, β 2 is the estimated association with Sleep while Study and Practice are held fixed, and β 3 is the estimated association with Practice while Study and Sleep are held fixed. These are not automatically causal effects. The model does not literally freeze variables in real life—rather, it does this mathematically to estimate each variable's conditional association holding other modeled predictors fixed . Notice the highlighted slice on the plane. We've locked "Sleep" at 6 hours (and Practice at its average). As we move purely along the Study axis, the score rises in a perfect straight line determined solely by β 1 . Score = β 0 + β 1 (Study) + Locked

stages.title: Building the Prediction
stages.text: Stage 06 Building the Prediction Now we transition away from the 3D plane. In multiple regression, the prediction is built from a base intercept plus separate contributions from each predictor. Each predictor adds or subtracts its own specific amount. The final score is simply the sum of all these individual parts. Because of how the model fits the data, each of these contributions is added while the other predictors are treated as fixed. Predicting a specific student Study 4.0 hrs Sleep 7.5 hrs Practice 2 pps How it stacks up: • Base Score = Starting point • Study Boost = β 1 × Study hours • Sleep Boost = β 2 × Sleep hours • Practice Boost = β 3 × Practice papers Final Score = Sum of all parts

stages.title: The Spurious Trap
stages.text: Stage 07 The Spurious Trap If multiple variables just stack, why not run a simple regression for each variable separately? Because of Spurious Correlations . Imagine we want to predict Shark Attacks . If we run a simple model using Ice Cream Sales , the correlation is huge! It looks like ice cream causes shark attacks. But the true driver is a lurking variable: High Temperature . Hot days cause both ice cream sales and beach visits (which lead to shark attacks). The Power of "Holding Constant" Multiple regression estimates a variable's conditional association holding other modeled predictors fixed , which can reveal when a variable only looked important because it moved together with another predictor. If we put both Ice Cream and Temperature into the model, the model essentially compares days with the same temperature . Holding temperature constant, ice cream sales have almost zero conditional association with shark attacks in this example. If a coefficient shrinks close to zero after the other predictors are included, that suggests it has little conditional association with the predicted outcome (y) after accounting for the others. This does not prove the variable has no real-world effect at all, only that its estimated conditional association is small within this specific model. Note: A larger coefficient doesn't always mean a "more important" predictor, as they depend on the unit of measurement.

stages.title: The Adjusted R² Penalty
stages.text:
Stage 08 The Adjusted R² Penalty How do we know if our team of variables is actually good? R² tells us what percentage of the variance we explained. For least-squares models with an intercept fitted to the same training observations, adding predictors makes training R² stay the same or increase . Even "Student's Shoe Size" may increase it, without improving predictions on new data. Adj R² = 1 - [ (1 - R²)(n - 1) / (n - p - 1) ] Adjusted R² corrects for this by penalizing model complexity.
                    In the formula, n is the number of observations and p is the number of predictors. Every new predictor ( p ) uses up flexibility and increases the penalty. Adjusted R² can rise or fall, even for an irrelevant variable in a particular sample. It is a descriptive aid, not an automatic feature-retention rule: consider validation performance, the modeling goal, and subject knowledge.

stages.title: Reading the Model Output
stages.text: Stage 09 Reading the Model Output When a data analyst fits a multiple linear regression, they don't look at a 3D plot—they look at a summary table to evaluate the results. Estimate: The coefficient (β). How much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in this predictor, holding all other predictors constant . Std. Error: The uncertainty around the estimate. A smaller standard error means we are more confident in the coefficient. t value: The estimate divided by its standard error. A larger absolute value (typically > 2) indicates strong statistical evidence that the true effect is not zero. Note: Each coefficient should be read as "the change in predicted y for a one-unit increase in this predictor, holding the others constant." Because predictors can be measured in entirely different units, coefficients cannot be compared as pure "importance scores" unless the predictors are on comparable scales. Diagnostics belong with the output. Inspect residual-versus-fitted, Q–Q, scale-location, leverage and influence plots. Use VIFs and coefficient intervals to diagnose multicollinearity; document categorical reference levels and interactions. Report confidence intervals for mean responses and wider prediction intervals for new observations. These coefficients are adjusted associations, not causal effects without a causal design. Multiple linear regression is a powerful detective. It models additive effects, isolates individual drivers, and finds the mathematically optimal fit by minimizing squared errors.

stages.title: Start with a pile of labeled emails.
stages.text: 02 Observe the case Start with a pile of labeled emails. Naive Bayes learns from examples where the answer is already known. In this miniature dataset, each row is an email, three clues are recorded, and the final column says whether the message was spam. The model does not understand the sentence the way a person does. It sees a structured record: free? winner? meeting? and a class label. A Start with the past. The model’s evidence comes from what happened in earlier examples.

stages.title: Separate the target from the clues.
stages.text: 03 Frame the question Separate the target from the clues. The thing we want to predict is the target variable , Y . Everything else becomes a feature , X —a measurable clue the model can use. For text, the original sentence is transformed into a vector of usable values. A word being present can become 1 ; absent can become 0 . X₁ = contains “free” → [1, 0, 1, 0]

stages.title: Keep the final exam hidden.
stages.text: 04 Protect the test Keep the final exam hidden. Before learning anything, divide the dataset. The training set teaches the model. The test set stays untouched until the end, so the final score tells us how the model handles examples it has not memorised. A common starting point is around 80% training and 20% test . Peeking at the test set early gives an overly optimistic picture. train = learn test = untouched

stages.title: Choose the version that fits the feature.
stages.text: 05 Match the evidence Choose the version that fits the feature. “Naive Bayes” is a family of models. The prediction logic stays recognisable, but the likelihood calculation changes with the kind of feature you have. Tap a model type to see what it expects. Bernoulli Multinomial Categorical Gaussian Selected Bernoulli yes / no features

stages.title: Count what each class tends to contain.
stages.text: 06 Learn the starting belief Count what each class tends to contain. Training is mostly about learning probabilities from the training data. First comes the prior : how common is each class before we inspect the new email? Scale note: the six-email ledger was a tiny pattern-finding example. The board below imagines a larger training set of 100 emails, so its 40/60 prior is a separate, clearly labelled example. Then come the likelihoods : inside each class, how often did each clue appear? In a count-based model, this is a probability table made from the data. P(Spam) = 40 / 100 = 0.40 P(Free | Spam) = 30 / 40 = 0.75

stages.title: Pretend the clues can speak separately.
stages.text: 07 Make the naive move Pretend the clues can speak separately. Real words can be related. “Free” and “winner” may travel together. Naive Bayes deliberately ignores that relationship once the class is known . This conditional-independence assumption is the shortcut: each feature contributes a separate piece of evidence, so the pieces can be multiplied together. When this assumption is strongly violated, posterior probabilities may be overconfident or poorly calibrated. Show what the shortcut ignores ↗

stages.title: Prior × evidence = a class score.
stages.text: 08 Score a new observation Prior × evidence = a class score. Our new email contains “free” and “winner”. The model asks the same question twice: how well would this evidence fit Spam ? How well would it fit Not Spam ? Tap the clues on the diagram to include or ignore them. The class scores and normalised posterior update immediately; ignoring a clue is different from observing that it is absent. Current prediction Spam 98.4% posterior Reset evidence

stages.title: Numbers need a different likelihood.
stages.text: 09 Change the kind of feature Numbers need a different likelihood. For a height, age, or temperature, counting exact matches is not useful. Nobody may be exactly 169 cm , but that height can still be typical of a class. Gaussian Naive Bayes learns a mean and a spread for each class, then asks how normal the new number looks under each bell-shaped distribution. Observation height: 169 cm Class A ≈ 168 cm Class B ≈ 181 cm

stages.title: Two small engineering fixes.
stages.text: 10 Keep the arithmetic stable Two small engineering fixes. If a feature was never seen in a class, its count can produce a likelihood of zero. One zero would erase the whole product. Laplace smoothing adds a small artificial count so “unseen” does not mean “impossible”. This applies to discrete/count variants, not Gaussian Naive Bayes. With hundreds of features, multiplying tiny numbers can underflow. Implementations use log probabilities : multiplication becomes addition, while the class ranking stays the same. Smoothing Log space

stages.title: Use folds while you build.
stages.text: 11 Develop honestly Use folds while you build. Do not keep checking the final test set while tuning the model. Instead, rotate through the training set with 5-fold cross-validation : four folds train, one fold validates, then the validating fold moves. After choosing the model, train once more on all training data . Only then do you test on the untouched 20%. Round 1 · Fold 1 validates 1 2 3 4 5

stages.title: A prediction is a decision with consequences.
stages.text: 12 Read the result A prediction is a decision with consequences. Accuracy is not the only question. Precision asks whether predicted spam really was spam. Recall asks how much of the real spam the model caught. F1 balances the two. In a spam filter, a false positive can bury an important email. The metric that matters most depends on the cost of being wrong. Protect inbox Catch more spam Precision focus · keep false positives visible.

stages.title: Prior → likelihoods → posterior.
stages.text: 13 Keep the mental model Prior → likelihoods → posterior. Naive Bayes is a detective with a disciplined shortcut: start with what was common, score how each clue fits each class, combine the evidence, then choose the most probable explanation. Remember four words: prior , likelihood , naive assumption , and posterior . What I believed before + what the evidence says = what I believe now. Return to the opening scene ↑

stages.title: The whole idea: learn patterns from examples
stages.text: Stage 01 The whole idea: learn patterns from examples A neural network is a model made of small calculation units called neurons. Each neuron receives numbers, gives some of them more importance than others, combines them, and passes a new number forward. Imagine teaching a child to recognize cats. You do not write every possible cat rule. You show many examples labeled cat or not cat . The child gradually notices patterns. A neural network does something similar with numbers. → Plain-English translation: examples go in, a prediction comes out, mistakes are measured, and the internal settings are adjusted so the next prediction is less wrong. Normal programming versus machine learning Normal programming: a human writes the rules, the computer applies them, and an answer comes out. Machine learning: a human supplies examples and correct outcomes, then the model learns useful rules from those examples. Neural networks are valuable when the rules are too numerous or complicated to write by hand. Before you continue You only need basic comfort with multiplication, averages, and percentages. Every specialist word is defined before it is used.

stages.title: Data becomes features and labels
stages.text: Stage 02 Data becomes features and labels Data is the collection of examples the model learns from. In our toy problem, each row describes one student. Study hours Sleep hours Attendance Passed? 8 7 90% Yes 2 4 40% No 5 6 70% Yes Features The clues the model receives: study hours, sleep hours, and attendance. Label The correct answer it must learn to predict: passed or failed. Supervised learning means the training examples already contain the correct answers. Features are the clues; the label is the answer key.

stages.title: Clean, encode, scale, then split
stages.text:
Stage 03 Clean, encode, scale, then split Real data is rarely ready to train on. Missing values, duplicates, impossible values, inconsistent labels, and suspicious outliers must be investigated before the model sees them. 1. Clean Fix or remove records that are missing, duplicated, impossible, or inconsistent. 2. Encode Turn words and categories into numbers because the network performs mathematics. 3. Scale Put numerical features on comparable ranges so a large unit does not look important merely because its number is bigger. 4. Split Keep separate training, validation, and test sets so memorization cannot impersonate learning. Training set   ≈ 70%  → teaches the model
Validation set ≈ 15%  → tunes choices during development
Test set       ≈ 15%  → final, untouched exam Keep the final exam separate: the test examples must not be used to teach or tune the model. Otherwise the final score no longer shows how well the model handles genuinely unseen data. Academic precision Why scaling is useful What it prevents A feature measured in thousands can dominate numerical updates even when it is not more meaningful. What it does not mean Scaling does not automatically decide which feature matters. The network still learns weights from the data.

stages.title: A network is layers of tiny calculators
stages.text:
Stage 04 A network is layers of tiny calculators The input layer receives study, sleep, and attendance. Each hidden neuron receives its own weighted mixture of those inputs. Across training, different mixtures become sensitive to different combinations—perhaps high study with low sleep, or strong attendance with moderate study. These are emergent feature detectors : useful sensitivities discovered from data, not roles assigned to neurons by a person. Student pass/fail architecture: 3 → 8 → 4 → 1
3 inputs → hidden patterns → 1 pass-score neuron What you choose Design decisions before training How many hidden layers How many neurons per layer Hidden and output activations Optimizer and learning rate What the model learns Parameters discovered from examples Every connection weight Every neuron bias Useful internal sensitivities Representations that reduce loss ? Why not something simpler? A linear model may be enough when one straight boundary captures the pattern. Hidden layers are justified only when interactions and reusable intermediate patterns improve performance on new data. The visual begins with the skeleton you designed, then animates the connection strengths that training learns. A larger network is not automatically better: more depth and width need more data, computation, and protection against overfitting.

stages.title: One feature has a different weight into every hidden neuron
stages.text: Stage 05 One feature has a different weight into every hidden neuron There is not one universal “sleep weight.” Sleep connects to every neuron in the next layer, and each connection learns a separate value. One neuron may respond strongly to sleep, another weakly, and another negatively because it combines sleep with different evidence. Connection explorer Choose an input to reveal its four independently learned connections. Study Sleep Attendance hidden neuron j score = study × wstudy,j + sleep × wsleep,j + attendance × wattendance,j + biasj w What: weights control sensitivity and biases shift activation. How: training changes all of them to reduce loss. Why: separate weights let neurons specialize in different combinations. Why not assign roles? Human labels would constrain the model before the data reveals which combinations are useful. Interpretability note: you can inspect every weight, but raw numbers rarely translate into one clean human rule. A neuron usually participates in a distributed pattern with many other neurons.

stages.title: Non-linearity lets stacked layers learn bends
stages.text: Stage 06 Non-linearity lets stacked layers learn bends First ask why an activation is needed. If every layer performs only a linear weighted sum, stacking ten layers still collapses into one linear transformation. The network gains more arithmetic, but not a more flexible decision boundary. inputs → weighted sum + bias → raw score → activation function → output signal Boundary experiment Linear only ReLU on Use the buttons to focus either path; both remain visible for a direct comparison. Hidden layers use ReLU by default here. The output activation changes with the task: Binary sigmoid Multiclass softmax Regression linear ↳ ReLU is a learned-pattern gate. A positive raw score passes as evidence that one learned pattern is present; zero means that neuron does not pass evidence for that pattern. It is misleading to say the network simply “throws away negative information”: other neurons—with different weights and biases—can represent opposing or complementary evidence. Hidden layers: ReLU ReLU(2.5) = 2.5 passes positive evidence; ReLU(-3) = 0 gates that detector off. Binary output: sigmoid One raw output becomes a score from 0 to 1, such as a pass score of 0.82 . Multiclass output: softmax Several class scores are converted together into probabilities that total 100%. Regression output: linear The output remains a direct number because a probability constraint would be inappropriate. Design decision: humans choose activations before training. Training learns the weights and biases that determine which patterns produce positive or non-positive raw scores.

stages.title: Forward propagation makes one pass-score prediction
stages.text:
Stage 07 Forward propagation makes one pass-score prediction Forward propagation means information moves from the three inputs, through every hidden layer, to the single output neuron used by this binary task. study + sleep + attendance
→ hidden-layer calculations and ReLU activations
→ one raw output score
→ sigmoid
→ pass score between 0 and 1 For one student, the output neuron might produce 0.82 . We read that as an 82% model score for “pass.” The corresponding fail score is 1 − 0.82 = 0.18 . The output neuron does not yet make the final Pass/Fail decision. Stage 14 will apply a separate decision threshold, such as 0.50, to turn this continuous score into a class label.

stages.title: Loss measures how wrong the prediction was
stages.text: Stage 08 Loss measures how wrong the prediction was A loss function converts prediction error into a number. Smaller loss is better. Larger loss tells the training process that the current weights need more correction. Regression When predicting a number, mean squared error is common. It squares mistakes, so large errors receive extra punishment. Classification When predicting a class, cross-entropy loss is common. It strongly penalizes a model that is confidently wrong. ! Loss is the teacher's marking pen. It does not merely say “wrong.” It gives the optimizer a numerical signal showing how much improvement is needed. Do not confuse these Loss versus metric Loss The quantity optimized during training. It guides weight updates. Metric A human-readable measure such as accuracy, precision, recall, MAE, or RMSE.

stages.title: Backpropagation computes gradients—only gradients
stages.text:
Stage 09 Backpropagation computes gradients—only gradients A gradient is a collection of slopes: for each weight, it answers “if this weight increased a tiny amount, how would the loss change?” The sign gives a direction and the magnitude describes local sensitivity. forward pass → prediction
prediction + truth → loss
backpropagation → gradient for every weight and bias
weights are still unchanged Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss backward through the network. It calculates how local changes connect to the final error. It does not choose a learning rate and it never updates a parameter. Plain distinction: backprop computes gradients only. The optimizer later uses those gradients to update weights.

stages.title: The optimizer takes iterative, local steps
stages.text: Stage 10 The optimizer takes iterative, local steps Gradient descent applies the update. It combines the local gradient with a learning rate : next weight = current weight − learning rate × gradient . Because the gradient describes only the slope near the current point, optimization must repeat rather than jump directly to the answer. Watch it walk downhill Tiny steps Medium steps Too large Pause Small steps need many updates. Medium steps descend efficiently. Large steps can overshoot and bounce away. Drag the current point on the curve to inspect a different local slope. ∇ What: a gradient is local slope. Why: it tells the optimizer which nearby direction lowers loss. How: multiply it by the learning rate and update. Why not one giant step? the landscape bends, and the local slope does not reveal the whole terrain. Why local does not guarantee global A low point reached from the current start may be a local minimum , while a lower global minimum exists elsewhere. Initialization, optimizer behavior, noise from batches, and the shape of the loss surface all affect the path.

controls.text: Why local does not guarantee global A low point reached from the current start may be a local minimum , while a lower global minimum exists elsewhere. Initialization, optimizer behavior, noise from batches, and the shape of the loss surface all affect the path.

stages.title: One update has a strict causal order
stages.text:
Stage 11 One update has a strict causal order The model usually learns from a small batch . Each update follows the same sequence; confusing these steps hides what actually causes learning. 1. take data
2. forward pass makes predictions
3. loss measures error
4. backpropagation computes gradients
5. optimizer applies parameter updates
6. updated weights change the next prediction
7. repeat Batch examples per update Iteration one update step Epoch one full pass through training data 1,000 examples ÷ batch size 100 = 10 iterations per epoch ↻ The forward pass supplies a prediction; loss supplies an objective; backprop supplies gradients; the optimizer supplies the update. Repetition turns many local corrections into learned behavior.

stages.title: Choose the model before validation gets worse
stages.text: Stage 12 Choose the model before validation gets worse Training loss can keep falling while validation loss eventually rises. That is the causal signature of overfitting: the model is improving on examples it trains on while becoming less useful on unseen data. Keep the checkpoint near the lowest validation loss, not the final training step. Local is not global: an optimizer follows nearby slopes and may settle in one valley even if a lower valley exists elsewhere. Validation asks a different question: whichever valley training reaches, does that model generalize? ! Why can dependence be bad? A neuron might learn a brittle shortcut such as “attendance decides everything.” If later neurons rely heavily on that one pathway, the network may fail when the shortcut does not hold for new students. Regularization control Dropout rate during training: 20% Decrease the rate and more hidden neurons stay active on the right. Increase it and more paths switch off, which can reduce shortcut dependence but may underfit; at 100%, this simplified visual switches off every hidden neuron. During training Different hidden neurons are temporarily switched off on different updates. Validation and real use Dropout is switched off, the full network is used, and the framework handles the required scaling. Decrease dropout More paths stay active, but the model may overfit by leaning on shortcuts. Increase dropout More paths switch off in the visual, spreading reliance until excessive dropout starts to underfit. Keep this model: save the checkpoint at the validation minimum. Dropout is one possible regularizer, not an automatic requirement; its value depends on the architecture, data, and observed overfitting.

stages.title: Humans choose the architecture and hyperparameters
stages.text: Stage 13 Humans choose the architecture and hyperparameters Parameters are learned by the model: every weight and bias. Hyperparameters are design decisions made before or around training. Design decisions Why each choice exists Depth and width Control representational capacity. Too little can underfit; too much can waste data and computation or overfit. Activations Add non-linearity and match output constraints. Hidden layers remain ReLU here. Optimizer Defines how gradients are converted into parameter updates. Learning rate Sets update scale: small is slow; large can overshoot. Output-layer explorer Binary class Multi-class Regression Binary classification Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: one neuron with sigmoid. Multi-class classification Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: one score per class with softmax. Regression Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: usually one linear numerical value. Feature engineering Structured problems may improve when raw fields are turned into more useful clues, such as date of birth → age. There is no universal “best” architecture. A design must match the task, data quantity, noise, complexity, and cost of mistakes.

stages.title: The test set evaluates both scores and decisions
stages.text:
Stage 14 The test set evaluates both scores and decisions After training and tuning are finished, the model is evaluated once on the untouched test set . For our binary task, sigmoid first produces a pass score. A separate classification decision threshold then converts that score into Pass or Fail. model pass score = 0.72
decision threshold = 0.50
0.72 ≥ 0.50
prediction = Pass This threshold is not the school’s exam passing mark . It is the model’s cutoff for turning a score between 0 and 1 into a predicted class. Decision control Classification decision threshold: 0.50 Lowering the threshold predicts Pass more easily: recall usually rises, but false positives may increase. Raising it is stricter: false positives may fall, but more actual passes can be missed. 0.75 Precision 0.75 Recall 0.75 F1-score Actually passed Actually failed Predicted pass True positive: 3 False positive: 1 Predicted fail False negative: 1 True negative: 3 Accuracy alone can mislead. Precision asks whether predicted passes were usually correct. Recall asks how many actual passes the model successfully found.

stages.title: Error analysis starts with individual students
stages.text: Stage 15 Error analysis starts with individual students Overall scores hide which people are affected. Move the threshold, inspect the highlighted false positives and false negatives, and connect each case to the metric that represents its cost. Case-level threshold explorer Classification threshold: 0.50 Sort by score Sort by distance to threshold Noor, score 0.68, actually failed: at the starting 0.50 threshold this is a false positive . If wrongly predicting success is costly, prioritize precision . Sam, score 0.43, actually passed: at the starting 0.50 threshold this is a false negative . If missing a student who would pass is costly, prioritize recall . Ana, score 0.57, actually passed: at the starting threshold this is a borderline true positive that flips when the threshold rises past 0.57. F1 is useful when both false positives and false negatives matter and one balanced summary is needed. From case to action Threshold changes only the decision rule; it does not repair weak features, biased labels, or poor calibration. Inspect concrete errors, diagnose the cause, change the appropriate part, then evaluate again by relevant groups.

stages.title: Saving, deployment, and monitoring finish the lifecycle
stages.text:
Stage 16 Saving, deployment, and monitoring finish the lifecycle Once performance is acceptable, the final model is saved. The saved package includes the architecture, learned weights and biases, and often the preprocessing rules needed to reproduce training-time inputs. new user input
→ same preprocessing used during training
→ saved model
→ prediction
→ application response Deployment puts the model into a website, mobile app, server API, edge device, or business system. A model sitting in a notebook is an experiment, not a working service. After launch Monitor accuracy, error types, input-data changes, speed, complaints, fairness, and security. When the world changes and performance falls, the model is experiencing drift .

stages.title: Different network families organize information differently
stages.text: Stage 17 Different network families organize information differently Feedforward network Information moves from input to hidden layers to output. This is the structure used throughout this lesson. Convolutional network (CNN) Common for images. Early layers notice edges; later layers combine them into shapes and object parts. Recurrent network (RNN) Designed for sequences and previous context, such as text, audio, and time series. Transformer Uses attention to connect relevant parts of data, allowing many relationships to be considered at once. This layered transformation is called representation learning . Raw inputs become increasingly useful internal patterns: pixels → edges → shapes → objects, or word pieces → phrases → context. Interpretability: weights are visible, but a representation is usually distributed across many parameters. Inspecting one large weight rarely yields a faithful human rule; use case-level explanations, sensitivity analyses, and validation evidence together. Neural networks are powerful because they can learn complex representations. They are used for images, speech, text, translation, recommendations, medical scans, fraud detection, forecasting, game playing, and large language models. They are not magic: they still depend on good data, sensible design, testing, monitoring, and human judgment.

stages.title: Try the tiny student-pass network
stages.text: Stage 18 Try the tiny student-pass network Move the inputs and watch the same network update. This is an illustrative toy, not a trained admissions or education model. Study hours: 6 Sleep hours: 7 Attendance: 75% 0.68 Toy pass score Pass At current threshold Moderate Distance from threshold A score is not a guarantee and does not explain causation. This toy only demonstrates how changed inputs can flow through a fixed set of weights.

stages.title: One full training cycle
stages.text:
Final synthesis One full training cycle The causal chain You choose the architecture, activations, optimizer, and learning rate. Data enters and a forward pass produces predictions. Loss converts prediction error into an objective. Backpropagation computes gradients only. The optimizer updates every weight and bias. Updated parameters change the next forward pass. Validation identifies the checkpoint that generalizes best. Testing, deployment, monitoring, and error analysis keep the model accountable after training. data → forward pass → loss → backprop gradients
→ optimizer step → updated weights → repeat ↻ What: a parameterized function. Why: to learn patterns too complex to specify cleanly. How: repeated local updates reduce loss. Why not something simpler? use a simpler model whenever it generalizes well enough and is easier to maintain or explain. Final check Which dataset should stay untouched until training and tuning are complete? Training set Validation set Test set The test set is the final untouched exam. Training teaches; validation tunes.

stages.title: What problem is One-R solving?
stages.text: Stage 01 · Observe What problem is One-R solving? Classification predicts a category, such as Yes or No . A feature is an input column. The target is the category we want to predict. Our teaching sample records 14 days. Each row contains outlook, humidity, wind, temperature, and whether someone carried an umbrella. The central question “If I may inspect only one column, which column should I choose, and what should I predict for each of its values?” 14 rows 4 candidate features Yes target No target

stages.title: First, make the lazy prediction.
stages.text: Stage 02 · Baseline First, make the lazy prediction. Before building a model, count the target classes. There are 8 Yes rows and 6 No rows, so the majority classifier predicts Yes for every case. majority accuracy = largest class count ÷ all rows 8 ÷ 14 = 57.1% This baseline is intentionally dull. That is its job. A new classifier that cannot beat it has not earned its electricity. Class imbalance warning. If 95% of rows are No, always predicting No scores 95% accuracy while learning nothing about Yes. Accuracy needs company. If a dataset has 70 Yes rows and 30 No rows, what does the majority classifier predict? Yes for every row, producing 70% training accuracy.

stages.title: Make a rule from one categorical feature.
stages.text: Stage 03 · Build Make a rule from one categorical feature. Choose a candidate feature, such as Outlook . Handle each distinct value separately and predict its local majority class. 1 Collect all rows where Outlook is Sunny. 2 Count Yes and No among those rows. 3 Use the local majority as the prediction for Sunny. 4 Repeat for Cloudy and Rainy. Example rulebook IF Outlook = Sunny THEN Umbrella = No IF Outlook = Cloudy THEN Umbrella = Yes IF Outlook = Rainy THEN Umbrella = Yes error for a feature value = rows that disagree with that value’s majority class

stages.title: Test every feature. Keep the lowest-error rule.
stages.text: Stage 04 · Compare Test every feature. Keep the lowest-error rule. One-R repeats the same construction for every candidate feature. Each feature gets a rulebook and a total error count. Feature Training errors Error rate Result Outlook 3 / 14 21.4% Selected Humidity 4 / 14 28.6% Runner-up Wind 5 / 14 35.7% Rejected Temperature* 5 / 14 35.7% After buckets selected feature = arg min(feature training errors) Inspect a rulebook Outlook Humidity Wind Ties are allowed. Declare a policy in advance: prefer fewer values, use a fixed feature order, or choose the winner under cross-validation. Do not improvise after seeing the result. *Temperature uses the fixed teaching intervals introduced next. Exact bucketing procedures vary by implementation.

stages.title: Turn numeric values into intervals.
stages.text: Stage 05 · Prepare Turn numeric values into intervals. A rule for every exact temperature would memorise the training sample and fail on a new value such as 23.6°C. One-R therefore discretises numeric values into intervals. 1 Sort rows by the numeric feature. 2 Group neighbouring values into sufficiently reliable buckets. 3 Assign each bucket its majority class. 4 Merge or adjust unstable neighbours according to the chosen implementation. One possible training-only discretisation Temperature ≤ 22.5 → Yes 22.5 < Temperature ≤ 27.5 → Yes Temperature > 27.5 → No Exact values Stable intervals Leakage alert. Fit cut-points using training data only. Choosing intervals after inspecting test labels is answer-shopping in a lab coat.

stages.title: Missing values and unseen categories are part of the model.
stages.text: Stage 06 · Safeguard Missing values and unseen categories are part of the model. Real inputs are rarely as cooperative as textbook tables. Decide what happens when the selected feature is missing, a category never appeared during training, classes tie, or a number falls outside the observed range. ? Missing input New Unseen category 4–4 Local tie Reasonable fallback Use the overall training-set majority class or estimated class prior. Another option is to learn “Missing” as its own category when enough training rows contain missing values. The fitted rule uses Outlook, but a future row has Outlook = “Hazy”. What happens? Use the declared fallback. Do not invent a rule from the test row.

stages.title: Prediction is deliberately cheap.
stages.text: Stage 07 · Predict Prediction is deliberately cheap. Read the selected feature, find its stored value or interval, return the class, and use the fallback if nothing matches. Outlook Sunny Cloudy Rainy Hazy Humidity Low High Wind Calm Breezy Strong Run the one-rule prediction Prediction: Outlook = Cloudy → Umbrella = Yes. Humidity and wind are ignored because Outlook won training selection. The model is saying Outlook is the strongest standalone predictor in this sample. It is not saying the other features have no relationship with umbrella use.

stages.title: One feature cannot express an interaction.
stages.text: Stage 08 · Understand One feature cannot express an interaction. Suppose people carry umbrellas only when it is both cloudy and very humid. Neither feature alone may be strongly predictive, but their combination is. useful pattern: Outlook = Cloudy AND Humidity = High 1 Feature used 0 Interactions Inspectability One-R sees One column and one lookup table. One-R misses Interactions, gradual multi-feature effects, and alternative routes to the same class. Interpretability is not innocence. A selected feature may be a proxy, unfair, operationally inappropriate, or merely associated rather than causal.

stages.title: Validate the whole learning process
stages.text: Stage 09 · Evaluate Validate the whole learning process Don’t judge the model only on the final prediction. Any choice the model makes—like selecting the best feature or building rules—must be done inside the training fold, then checked on data it has not seen. 1 Split the data into folds 2 Use the training fold to learn Build buckets, test candidate rules, and choose the best option here. 3 Freeze the rule Stop changing it. No more label peeking. 4 Test on the held-out fold Predict unseen rows and record the error. 5 Repeat and average Run this across all folds, then average the results. Grouped data: If several rows belong to the same person, device, or organisation, keep the whole group in one fold. Otherwise the model may recognise the group instead of learning a pattern that generalizes.

stages.title: Evaluate each fold. Decide what to do next.
stages.text:
Stage 10 · Measure Evaluate each fold. Decide what to do next. Cross-validation gives multiple views of performance. Use the right metric for your goal, check stability across folds, and decide whether to proceed, tune, or collect more data. 1 Choose the right metric Pick the metric that matches the problem and the cost of mistakes. Overall Precision Recall Overall accuracy Focus when classes are balanced and both types of errors matter similarly. Best for: General performance check, balanced datasets. Precision Focus when false positives are costly (predicting Yes when it’s actually No). Best for: Spam detection, fraud alerts, medical testing. Recall Focus when false negatives are costly (missing actual Yes cases). Best for: Disease screening, churn prevention, safety monitoring. 2 Measure stability across folds Compute the chosen metric for each fold. Then summarize the stability. Fold-score distribution Report individual fold scores and, when useful, repeat cross-validation with different splits. fold_scores = scores
mean = scores.mean()
sd = scores.std(ddof=1)
range_ = (scores.min(), scores.max()) Fold scores share overlapping training data; their spread is not a confidence interval for generalisation performance. Report all three (recommended) Always look at these together for the full picture. Mean (μ): average performance across folds Sample SD: spread of performance Score distribution: individual fold or repeated-CV scores Also check the min–max range across folds. 3 Interpret stability in context There are no universal percentage bands or automatic proceed/stop rules. Consider dataset size, class balance, the metric, domain, and the impact of errors. Report Interpretation What it means Fold scores Distribution Inspect the full spread, including unusually low scores. Mean Average Compare with a relevant baseline on the same splits. SD and range Spread Judge variation against the metric and consequences of errors. Repeated CV Split sensitivity Report scores across repeats; investigate changes across splits. Intervals Uncertainty State the method and account for dependence between CV scores. Read together: Mean, SD, range, and the score distribution describe these splits. Consistency alone does not establish useful performance or justify deployment.

stages.title: Use simple models as diagnostic instruments.
stages.text: Stage 11 · Compare & Reflect Use simple models as diagnostic instruments. Model Uses Typical purpose Majority No features Absolute minimum baseline One-R One feature, many value rules Transparent signal baseline Decision stump One tree split Single partition baseline Full tree Sequential splits Interactions and complexity One-R and a decision stump are related, but not identical. Categorical One-R can assign a separate class to every value of one feature; a stump is usually described as one split with leaf predictions. Suspiciously strong simplicity. If One-R nearly matches a complex model, one feature may dominate the task, or the evaluation may contain leakage. Investigate both before celebrating. Useful when interpretable benchmark small data cheap deployment strongest standalone feature Weak when interactions matter signals must combine feature drift unequal error costs

stages.title: Build the rule, then explain what it means.
stages.text: Stage 12 · Practice Build the rule, then explain what it means. Choose a candidate feature and a new case. The visual updates the value-level rulebook, training error, and prediction. The point is not merely to obtain a label, but to explain exactly how that label appeared. Candidate feature Outlook Humidity Wind New value Apply this rulebook 3 Training errors 3 Value rules No New prediction One-R selected Outlook. Humidity also relates strongly to the target. Is “humidity is useless” the correct conclusion? No. Outlook produced the best single-feature rule under this procedure. Humidity may still add useful information in a multi-feature model. Key takeaways One-R creates a majority-class rule for every value or interval of each candidate feature. It selects the lowest training error, but performance belongs on held-out data. Numeric buckets, fallbacks, ties, and missing values are fitted-model decisions. Its value is transparent baseline reasoning, not pretending one feature explains the universe.

stages.title: The Unsupervised Explorer
stages.text: Stage 01 The Unsupervised Explorer In traditional "supervised" machine learning, we act like students with an answer key. We know what we want to predict (e.g., house prices) and use features to find the answer. Principal Components Analysis (PCA) belongs to unsupervised learning . Here, we are explorers. There is no answer key. We are handed a messy box of variables and asked to find the hidden structure. Imagine measuring students on a full performance sheet instead of only two numbers: 60 rows x 6 columns The canvas will still use a 2D Speed-vs-Strength slice to build intuition, but the loadings, scores, and scree plot later on will come from the full generated dataset.

stages.title: The "Too Much Information" Problem
stages.text: Stage 02 The "Too Much Information" Problem Why can't we just look at the variables one by one? Because dimensionality explodes fast. With 6 variables you already have 15 pairwise plots, and with 10 variables you jump to 45. No single view tells the whole story. If we only look at Speed (squashing the data to the horizontal axis), we lose all information about strength. The points overlap and hide the true shape of our students. If we only look at Strength (vertical axis), we lose speed. Neither axis alone captures the main "soul" of the dataset, because athletic students tend to be both fast and strong. When variables are correlated (moving together), keeping them separate is redundant. We need a way to combine them.

stages.title: Finding the First Principal Component
stages.text: Stage 03 Finding the First Principal Component PCA looks for a brand new direction—a line sliced straight through the cloud of data. It rotates this line until the data points, when projected onto the line, spread out as much as possible . 0.0 Current Spread (Variance) The direction that creates the largest spread is called Principal Component 1 (PC1) . By maximizing the spread, this line stays closest to the entire data cloud, giving us the clearest single summary.

stages.title: The Secret Sauce: Loadings
stages.text: Stage 04 The Secret Sauce: Loadings How does PCA actually draw this line? It acts like a "dimmer knob", mixing the original variables together using weights. These weights are called Loadings . They tell us how much each original variable contributes to the new component. PC1 Score = Σ(wⱼ × standardized featureⱼ) For this generated dataset, the PC1 loadings are computed directly from the same PCA fit used for the scores and scree plot: PC1 blends the columns that move together into one broader summary axis.

stages.title: When Scaling Is Appropriate
stages.text: Stage 05 When Scaling Is Appropriate There is a massive trap in PCA. Because it hunts for maximum variance, it can be bullied by units. Even in this generated dataset, Strength naturally varies much more than Speed in raw units. Without scaling, PCA leans toward the higher-variance column; after Standardization , both columns get a fair vote. Step 1: Mean (μ) = Average of column Step 2: Center = X - μ Step 3: Variance (σ²) = Average of (X - μ)² Step 4: Std Dev (σ) = √Variance Step 5: Scaled (Z) = (X - μ) / σ Result: After scaling, every variable has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Units disappear, and no single variable dominates just because it has bigger raw numbers. Scaling is a modelling choice, not a universal rule. It is normally appropriate for variables in unlike units—such as height in centimetres and income in dollars—or when raw scale should not determine the components. If measurements share the same units and their variance differences are scientifically meaningful, scaling may be undesirable. Fit the scaler on training data only. 0.00 / 0.00 Raw Std Devs (Speed / Strength) 1.00 / 1.00 After Standardization

stages.title: Capturing the Leftovers: PC2
stages.text: Stage 06 Capturing the Leftovers: PC2 PC1 captured the main trend (overall athleticism). But there is still some "thickness" left over in the cloud. To capture this, PCA finds a Second Principal Component (PC2) . It follows the exact same logic, but with one non-negotiable rule: It must be exactly 90 degrees (perpendicular) to PC1. Because it is perpendicular, PC2 is completely uncorrelated with PC1. It captures the contrasts—for example, students who are stronger than expected for their speed.

stages.title: The Transformation (Scores)
stages.text: Stage 07 The Transformation (Scores) Here is where the magic happens. We don't just draw lines on the old graph. We rotate the entire coordinate system . PCA finds the directions that capture the greatest sample variance. These directions are not automatically the most scientifically important or most predictive. Original matrix: 60 x 6 PCA scores: 60 x 2 The same observations are represented in a new coordinate system. When all principal components are retained, the centred data can be reconstructed up to numerical precision. When components are discarded, some sample variance and potentially useful information are lost. A few rows from the original matrix become PC scores side by side: Student Speed Strength Endurance Agility Balance Jump PC1 PC2

stages.title: Proportion of Variance Explained
stages.text: Stage 08 Proportion of Variance Explained How do we know if our components are actually useful? We look at the Proportion of Variance Explained (PVE) using a Scree Plot . Think of the total sample variance as a pizza. PC1 takes the biggest slice and PC2 takes the next. The cumulative line approaches 100% of sample variance—not 100% of general information, scientific importance, or predictive signal. 0% PC1 Variance 0% Cumulative (PC1+PC2) Look for the "Elbow" in the plot. In datasets with 100 columns, you might find that just 2 or 3 components explain 95% of the variance. That's the "Magic Shrink Ray" at work. PCA is unsupervised and ignores the target. A low-variance component may still contain important predictive or scientific information. Discarding low-variance components reduces noise only when noise mainly occupies those directions; this is not guaranteed.

stages.title: Interactive Playground
stages.text: Stage 09 Interactive Playground Now you are the algorithm. Use the slider to rotate the projection line through the original data space. Watch how the spread (variance) changes based on the angle. Your goal is to find the angle that maximizes the variance. Projection Angle 0° 0.00 PC1 Variance 0.00 PC2 Leftover Variance PC2 is locked to stay 90° from PC1, so it always shows the next-biggest leftover spread instead of being chosen freely. The angle with the highest variance is exactly where the math places Principal Component 1.

stages.title: The Best Summary
stages.text: Synthesis The Best Summary PCA represents centred observations along directions of greatest sample variance. Those directions need not be the most scientifically meaningful or predictive. PCA may reduce noise when discarded directions mainly contain noise, but this is not guaranteed. Low-variance components can still contain meaningful structure or predictive signal. Remember: Decide whether scaling is appropriate based on the variables’ units and whether raw variance differences should influence the components. Loadings are the weights. Scores are the new coordinates. Stop when the "pizza slices" of variance get too small.

stages.title: Inspect the Raw Data
stages.text: Step 01 Inspect the Raw Data What we do Plot the raw input against the response. Why we do it To visually check the shape. A straight line will naturally fail to capture a curved dataset. What this means If the data forms a hill, a valley, or an S-curve, simple math won't be enough. Let's see what happens if we force a straight line anyway. ➔ Look at the black dots on the chart. Notice how they structurally form a curved shape rather than a straight path.

stages.title: Fit a Straight Line
stages.text: Step 02 Fit a Straight Line What we do Fit a basic, flat or sloped straight line. Why we do it To set a baseline and prove that standard linear regression fails on curves. What this means The line completely ignores the true shape of our data. This failure is called underfitting. We need to give the math the flexibility to bend. ➔ See the rigid blue line on the chart and the simple equation in the dashboard.

stages.title: Expand the Features
stages.text: Step 03 Expand the Features What we do Create new columns by squaring and cubing the input data. Why we do it Adding powers of the input gives the underlying formula the ability to curve. What this means First, we shrink the input numbers so squaring them doesn't create huge, unstable values. Then we build our Design Matrix. Now the model has more ingredients to build with. ➔ Check the Design Matrix overlay. The model now sees the squared input as just another normal feature to learn from.

stages.title: Fit the Weights
stages.text: Step 04 Fit the Weights What we do The algorithm calculates the best weights for each column in our matrix. Why we do it To find the exact mathematical combination that fits the dots. What this means The weights act like knobs that tell the curve how strongly to bend and in what direction. Let's check how close our curve actually gets to the data. ➔ Look at the Weights overlay and the new equation in the dashboard. The curve now gracefully follows the data points.

stages.title: Compute Errors
stages.text: Step 05 Compute Errors What we do Measure the vertical distance between the true dots and our curve. Why we do it To see exactly where the model is still wrong. What this means Small random misses are normal, but a clear pattern in the misses means the model is still failing. Let's see what happens if we add too many curves. ➔ See the dashed red lines and the Residual Plot. The Train MSE above scores how well the model fits the data it saw.

stages.title: Check for Overfitting
stages.text: Step 06 Check for Overfitting What we do Push the model to extreme complexity and test it on hidden data. Why we do it To catch overfitting before we use the model in the real world. What this means Training error can look amazing while validation error gets much worse, which is the warning sign of overfitting. We need to find the balance between too simple and too complex. ➔ Look at the validation curve. Training error drops, but validation error rises. The gold dots are validation observations used to choose degree; the final test set remains untouched.

stages.title: Find the Sweet Spot
stages.text: Step 07 Find the Sweet Spot What we do Compare candidate complexities using validation or cross-validation error. Why we do it The best shape changes depending on the data. What this means We want the simplest curve that generalizes well to new situations. Play with the controls until you find the perfect balance. ➔ Change the dataset shape, then use the slider to explore. Find the simplest near-best point on the validation curve before validation error rises. Candidate Degree 2 Show Point Residuals Regenerate Noise Split

stages.title: Lock in the Model
stages.text: Step 08 Lock in the Model What we do Select the final model and lock in the formula. Why we do it We only deploy a model after validation proves it works. What this means We choose the simplest model that performs almost as well as the absolute best one. This final equation is now ready for the real world. ➔ Review the Model Deployed card below the chart for your final, validated results. Final workflow: fit candidate degrees on training data, choose the degree by validation or cross-validation error, lock the basis and preprocessing, refit using the chosen setup, and evaluate once on the untouched test set. Inspect residual form, unequal variance and influential points. High-degree polynomials can oscillate near boundaries and are especially unsafe for extrapolation; centring and scaling polynomial features often improve numerical stability and make regularisation penalties more comparable, but are not mathematically required. Orthogonal bases can also improve numerical stability.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem Observed statistics vary from sample to sample. Probability provides a language for that uncertainty and sampling distributions describe how an estimator behaves under repeated study designs.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), for P(B) > 0, means the chance of A given B. Independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B): knowing one event occurred does not change the chance of the other. Expectation E[X] is the probability-weighted average of a random variable; variance Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²] measures its spread, when these quantities exist. A population distribution describes individual values. A sampling distribution describes a statistic—such as a mean—across repeated samples. Its standard deviation is the standard error.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example If individual scores have standard deviation 12, the mean of n=36 independent observations has standard error about 12/√36=2. Doubling n does not halve uncertainty; roughly quadrupling n does.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method Discrete probability masses add directly, whereas continuous density integrates to probability over an interval. Density height is not itself point probability and may exceed one. A statistic is a random variable before data are observed, and its sampling distribution depends on the population, statistic and design. The central limit theorem supports many normal approximations but does not make every small or heavy-tailed sample normal. Standard deviation describes individual variation; standard error describes estimator variation. Clustering, unequal weights and finite-population sampling change the familiar independent-sample formula and the effective amount of information. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive laboratory Choose sample size and draw repeated samples. The histogram of sample means narrows as independent information increases.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions Repeated-sampling claims presume the same population and design. The usual √n improvement requires independent or appropriately modelled observations. When the method fails Density height is not point probability; dependence reduces effective sample size; skew and heavy tails can slow normal approximations; convenience samples do not become representative by growing.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Define population and random variable Identify discrete or continuous support Specify the sampling design Choose a statistic Study or approximate its sampling distribution Quantify standard error

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text: Stage 08 Interpretation and reporting What to report: Name the population, sample mechanism, statistic, sample size, dependence structure, estimated standard error and approximation used. Common misuse: Confusing the spread of individual observations with the uncertainty of their mean.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.text: Stage 09 Knowledge checks A sampling distribution describes… A statistic across repeated samples Individuals in one sample Only the population density Answer and explanation A statistic across repeated samples. Its random object is the statistic produced by the sampling procedure. Why does standard error often shrink with n? Independent observations add information and averaging reduces noise The population variance disappears Large samples eliminate bias automatically Answer and explanation Independent observations add information and averaging reduces noise. For a mean under independence, SE scales approximately as 1/√n. Is a continuous density height a probability? No; probability is area over an interval Yes, always Only when above one Answer and explanation No; probability is area over an interval. A point has zero probability in a continuous model; interval area is probability. If observations are clustered, naive SE is often… Too small Always too large Unaffected Answer and explanation Too small. Within-cluster similarity means less independent information than the row count suggests. To halve a mean’s SE, n must be approximately… Four times as large Twice as large Half as large Answer and explanation Four times as large. Because SE is proportional to 1/√n, halving it requires quadrupling n.

stages.title: The Raw Data Cloud
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Data Cloud Imagine sorting fruit into Apples and Pears based on two measurements: Sweetness ($X_1$) and Roundness ($X_2$). In generative modeling, we look at where each class cluster sits and how the points are distributed across the features. The Whole Idea of QDA Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) is a supervised classification method. It models each class as its own independent multi-dimensional probability cloud. Simple intuition: QDA asks: "Which of these distinct class clouds does this new coordinate fit into best?" Unlike LDA (which forces every class to share the exact same shape), QDA allows each class to have its own unique spread, stretch, and tilt. This mathematical flexibility is what creates curved boundaries . QDA Pipeline: Labeled data → Split Train/Test → Fit class-specific shapes → Score new test coordinates → Make prediction → Evaluate performance Tiny QDA Dictionary Feature: An input variable/measurement (e.g., Sweetness, Roundness). Label / Class: The category we want to predict (e.g., Apple, Pear). Mean ($\mu$): The center coordinate of a class's data cloud. Covariance Matrix ($\Sigma$): The learned shape, spread, and tilt of a class cloud. Prior Probability ($\pi$): The baseline proportion of each class in the dataset. Mahalanobis Distance: A shape-aware distance metric scaled by a class cloud's variance. Posterior Probability: The calculated probability that a point belongs to a class after measuring its features. Discriminant Score ($\delta$): The classification value calculated by QDA; highest score wins. Regularization: Adding a small constant diagonal shift to stabilize covariance estimation. Prior Probability Controls Apples ($N_A$): 80 Pears ($N_B$): 80 Re-scatter Random Points Concept Check: What is the primary difference between LDA and QDA? LDA is a non-linear classifier while QDA can only handle straight-line separations. QDA allows each class to estimate and keep its own unique covariance shape, whereas LDA forces a shared pooled covariance shape. QDA requires the classes to have identical prior probabilities, whereas LDA does not.

stages.title: Train / Test Split
stages.text: Stage 02 Train / Test Split To perform proper Machine Learning, we cannot estimate our model and test its performance on the same data points. This is known as Data Leakage . The Rules of the Split: Training Set (80%): Used exclusively to calculate Class Priors, Means, and Covariance Matrices. Test Set (20%): Hidden away completely during the learning phase. Used only for final model evaluation. Warning: Including testing data in your mean or covariance calculations will falsely inflate performance metrics, making you think your model generalizes better than it actually does! stages.title: The Straight-Line Trap (LDA)
stages.text: Stage 03 The Straight-Line Trap (LDA) The simplest approach is Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) . It draws a straight boundary to separate the groups. To do this, LDA calculates the pooled average shape of all the data and forces both groups to share that exact same covariance matrix ($\hat{\Sigma}_{shared}$). The Limitation: Look at the dotted ellipses on the canvas. Because LDA forces them to be identical in shape and tilt, it misclassifies points near the edges. It completely ignores the unique diagonal stretch of the Pears. Concept Check: What happens when we force classes with different spreads to share a covariance matrix? The model becomes highly flexible and always overfits the dataset. We can no longer invert the matrix, resulting in computational errors. We average out their unique shape characteristics, resulting in an inappropriate straight decision boundary.

stages.title: Fitting QDA: What the Model Learns
stages.text: Stage 04 Fitting QDA: What the Model Learns To fit QDA, we estimate three key statistical parameters directly from our training set for each class $k$: Covariance Matrix Anatomy For our two features, the 2x2 Covariance Matrix is represented as: $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \text{Variance}(X_1) & \text{Covariance}(X_1, X_2) \\ \text{Covariance}(X_1, X_2) & \text{Variance}(X_2) \end{pmatrix}$ Diagonal entries: Represent the independent spread of Sweetness and Roundness. Off-diagonal entries: Represent the relationship. A positive value means sweeter fruit is generally rounder, creating a diagonal tilt! Determinants & Inverses The Determinant ($|\Sigma_k|$): Is a covariance-volume scaling factor. Its square root, $\sqrt{|\Sigma_k|}$, corresponds more closely to geometric area or volume. The Inverse ($\Sigma_k^{-1}$): Acts as a scaling standardizer. It mathematically divides distances by the variance in that specific direction so wide directions aren't artificially penalized. Concept Check: What do the diagonal values in a covariance matrix represent? The correlation between the two features. The individual variances of each feature. The coordinates of the class center.

controls.text: The correlation between the two features.
The individual variances of each feature.
The coordinates of the class center.

stages.title: Testing with Shape-Aware Distance
stages.text: Stage 05 Testing with Shape-Aware Distance Euclidean distance only measures straight-line distance. It assumes classes are perfect, un-tilted circles. QDA uses Mahalanobis Distance , which measures distance in units of class-specific standard deviations, aligning with the class's natural stretch and tilt. Try it: Tap and drag on the canvas to reposition the test probe. Look at the contour lines of equal distance wrapping around each class mean. A Note on Posterior Probabilities The posteriors are calculated assuming the features are strictly normally (Gaussian) distributed. If your real-world data is heavily skewed or multimodal, the model's confidence scores will be poorly calibrated! Concept Check: Why is Mahalanobis distance superior to Euclidean distance for elliptical clusters? It accounts for class-specific variance and correlation, standardizing distance along the cluster's actual tilt. It ignores the units of the features entirely to simplify calculations. It guarantees that all distances are transformed into positive integers.

It ignores the units of the features entirely to simplify calculations.
It guarantees that all distances are transformed into positive integers.

stages.title: The Curved Boundary
stages.text: Stage 06 The Curved Boundary The decision boundary is defined mathematically as the curve where the score for Apples exactly equals the score for Pears: $\delta_{\text{Apple}}(x) = \delta_{\text{Pear}}(x)$ Because the covariance matrices $\hat{\Sigma}_{\text{Apple}} \neq \hat{\Sigma}_{\text{Pear}}$, the quadratic terms in the equation do not cancel. The boundary naturally curves to encapsulate the unique shape characteristics of each class. LDA uses non-linear activation functions while QDA does not. Because the classes have different covariance matrices, the quadratic terms in the score equations do not cancel out. Because QDA uses more training data points than LDA.
