stages.title: Regularization & Shape Playground
stages.text: Stage 09 Regularization & Shape Playground When class distributions are close or contain few data points, the empirical covariance matrices can become unstable or singular (zero determinant), causing inverse division errors. To solve this, we add a regularization ridge ($\lambda$) directly to the diagonals of the covariance matrices: Regularisation depends on its target. A class covariance can shrink toward a diagonal matrix, an identity matrix, or a shared pooled covariance. Only shrinkage toward the shared covariance moves QDA directly toward LDA. Choose both target and amount through validation or cross-validation. $\Sigma_{\text{regularized}} = \Sigma + \lambda I$ Regularization Control Ridge Parameter ($\lambda$): 0.10 Low Ridge (0.0): Maximum flexibility, but highly sensitive to noise and singularity. High Ridge (1.5): Increases stability, squeezing matrices to be circular. The curved boundary smooths out, behaving more like LDA! QDA Shape Playground Modify the true underlying distributions below. The simulator will instantly re-draw points and recalculate QDA: Apple Base Parameters Mean X Mean Y Spread Stretch Tilt Pear Base Parameters Mean X Mean Y Spread Stretch Tilt Concept Check: What is the primary benefit of regularization in QDA? It eliminates the need for prior probability calculations. It prevents computational instability (singular matrix errors) and smooths out noisy decision boundaries. It forces the decision boundary to remain strictly linear.

stages.title: Assumptions, Complexity & Synthesis
stages.text: Stage 10 Assumptions, Complexity & Synthesis Every algorithm is a balance of flexibility and parameters. QDA estimates a separate covariance matrix for each class, which comes at a significant parameter cost. Parameter Complexity Calculator Adjust the class count ($K$) and feature count ($p$) to compare parameter counts: Classes ($K$): 2 Features ($p$): 2 LDA Parameters: 7 QDA Parameters: 10 When QDA Thrives: Classes have completely different shapes and orientations. The dataset is large enough to estimate parameters reliably. Boundaries are naturally curved. When QDA Struggles: Extremely small datasets (leads to overfitting and singular matrices). Datasets with many features (parameter explosion). Outliers present that distort covariance matrix estimation. Alternatives to QDA: LDA: If dataset is small or class spreads are similar. Logistic Regression: If you prefer to model class boundaries without making Gaussian distribution assumptions. KNN or SVM: If decision boundaries are highly complex or non-Gaussian.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem A single tree is interpretable but unstable. Random forests average many deliberately varied trees so individual split noise cancels while shared predictive structure remains.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective Each tree sees a bootstrap sample and a random subset of candidate features at each split. Averaging mainly reduces variance when trees make partly independent errors.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example One tree classifies 82% of validation cases, but across resamples it ranges from 74% to 87%. A 300-tree forest reaches 86% with a much narrower range. The gain comes from averaging; 300 trees are not 300 independent datasets.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method Bootstrap samples vary observations and random feature subsets vary candidate splits. Diversity matters because averaging highly correlated trees removes less variance. Out-of-bag predictions provide a development estimate, but extensive optimisation against that estimate still needs outer evaluation. More trees reduce Monte Carlo noise; they do not cure leakage, biased sampling or drift. Permutation importance measures predictive reliance under disruption, not causality. Correlated predictors can substitute for one another, and partial dependence can average over unrealistic combinations. Leaf size and weighting also affect the smoothness and calibration of predicted probabilities. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive laboratory Adjust tree count and features considered per split. Watch out-of-bag error stabilise and tree correlation change.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions Training data must represent deployment, observations must respect split structure, and features must be available at prediction time. When the method fails Forests extrapolate poorly in regression, probabilities may need calibration, correlated predictors distort importance, and large forests cost memory and latency.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Build a simple tree baseline Place preprocessing inside resampling Tune feature sampling and leaf constraints Grow enough trees for stable error Check calibration and subgroup performance Evaluate the locked forest once

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text: Stage 08 Interpretation and reporting What to report: Report tree count, feature sampling, depth/leaf constraints, seed, resampling, OOB use, final metrics with uncertainty, calibration and importance method. Common misuse: Treating impurity importance as a causal ranking of variables.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text: Stage 01 The problem A fitted equation always returns numbers; diagnostics ask whether the functional form, error behaviour, and individual observations make those numbers defensible.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text: Stage 02 Intuition and objective Residuals should fluctuate without systematic shape around zero. Curvature signals missing functional form, a funnel signals changing variance, a Q–Q departure challenges normal-error inference, and an isolated high-leverage point can rotate the fitted line.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text: Stage 03 Worked example A salary model has residual spread of ±5k for junior staff and ±40k for senior staff. The fan pattern violates constant variance. Coefficients may still describe a mean pattern, but ordinary standard errors and a single-width prediction band are unreliable; robust errors or a variance model may be needed.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text: Stage 04 Reasoning with the method Residual-versus-fitted plots examine mean form and variance structure. Q–Q plots compare ordered residuals with a reference distribution and matter for inference that relies on that reference; predictors and outcomes need not themselves be normal. Leverage describes unusual predictor combinations. Influence describes how fitted results change, so Cook’s distance is a screening tool rather than a deletion command. VIF shows how strongly a predictor overlaps the others and can explain wide coefficient intervals without proving bias. Diagnostics should prompt a scientific response: correct errors, represent nonlinearity, model variance or dependence, and report justified sensitivity analyses. A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.text: Stage 05 Interactive laboratory Switch between healthy, curved, funnel-shaped, and influential residual patterns. The plot and recommended response update together.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text: Stage 06 Assumptions and failure modes Assumptions Correct functional form, independent errors, stable conditional variance, and residual normality when classical small-sample inference needs it. When the method fails Outliers, high leverage, extrapolation, omitted nonlinearities, dependence and multicollinearity can destabilise estimates or uncertainty.

stages.text: Stage 07 Practical workflow Plot outcome and predictors Fit the pre-specified model Inspect residual–fitted and Q–Q plots Check leverage, Cook’s distance and VIF Run justified sensitivity analyses Validate predictions on unseen data

stages.title: The Raw Target
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Target A regression tree is a model that helps us predict a number . Not a category like "cat or dog", but a continuous value like an exam score, temperature, or a house price. Let's look at a small dataset of houses. We want to predict the Price (in thousands) based entirely on the Size of the house (in square meters). Look at the canvas. The horizontal axis is Size (m²), and the vertical axis is Price (in thousands of dollars, or $k). Hover over the canvas to see active tooltips.

stages.title: From Dataset to Model
stages.text: Stage 02 From Dataset to Model Before teaching an algorithm, we need a disciplined plan. A standard Machine Learning workflow protects us from creating models that look perfect on paper but fail in the real world. The ML Pipeline: Target y The number we want to predict (e.g., Price). Features X The inputs we use (e.g., Size). Data Split Divide points into Training and Validation sets. Tune & Predict Limit tree growth to generalize and make unseen predictions. Look at the canvas: The data has been split. We use the 16 training houses to grow our tree, keeping 6 validation houses hidden to test general performance.

stages.title: The Clumsy Guess
stages.text: Stage 03 The Clumsy Guess At the very start, the tree puts all houses in one big group (the Root Node ). Before asking any questions, it asks: "If I had to guess one price for all houses, what should I use?" The standard answer is the average . If we take all 16 training house prices and average them, we get exactly $483.1k. Root Prediction = Average(y) = 483.1 This is a clumsy guess. The red lines on the canvas show the Residuals —the mathematical distance (errors) between our flat guess and reality.

stages.title: The First Split
stages.text: Stage 04 The First Split Now the tree asks a question to divide the data: "Can I split the houses into 2 groups so the prices inside each group become more similar?" It checks a "cut point". Based on the math, the best first rule is: Is Size ≤ 100? If Yes , go Left. If No , go Right. Now, instead of one average for everything, we have two averages . A lower average ($363.3k) for smaller houses, and a higher average ($637.1k) for bigger houses.

stages.title: The Error Engine (RSS)
stages.text: Stage 05 The Error Engine (RSS) How did it know to split exactly at 100? The algorithm is "Greedy". It tests candidate split points between sorted training values and chooses the one that leaves the least amount of mess. It measures "mess" using the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) . It squares all the red error lines and adds them up. Lower RSS is always better. Before vs After Split ... Root RSS ... Split RSS ... Reduction Best first split found. This threshold gives the lowest RSS among the tested candidate splits. Test Threshold: Size ≤ 100 m² 61,744 Total RSS Snap to Minimum RSS Look at the mini-chart on the canvas. The true optimal split is the absolute bottom of that curve.

stages.title: Real Trees Check Many Questions
stages.text: Stage 06 Real Trees Check Many Questions In real machine learning, a regression tree is not limited to checking just one feature. It considers multiple input variables simultaneously, checking every possible partition point across size, age, rooms, and locations. The tree runs a "Greedy Search" : it picks the single feature and threshold that yields the largest drop in RSS. Interactive: Click any candidate split to visualize its partition boundary and resulting RSS on the right. Feature Candidate Rule Post RSS Reduction Size Size ≤ 100 m² 61,743 +295,201 Rooms Rooms ≤ 3 74,300 +282,644 MRT Dist Distance ≤ 2 km 82,000 +274,944 Age Age ≤ 15 years 90,500 +266,444 Note: For teaching clarity, the extra feature splits here are illustrative. In a real dataset, the tree would calculate these RSS values from actual feature columns. Winning Split: Size wins because partitioning by Size ≤ 100 m² leaves the least error (lowest post-split RSS) among all candidate features.

stages.title: Recursive Splitting
stages.text: Stage 07 Recursive Splitting After finding the best first split, the tree does the exact same thing inside each new group. It splits, then splits inside the split. Like cutting a cake into pieces, then cutting those pieces again. This is called Recursive Binary Splitting . With every split, the prediction line stops looking flat and starts looking like a set of stairs. Play: Grow Tree Sequentially Watch the regions split and slide to form deeper nodes.

stages.title: The Anatomy of a Tree
stages.text: Stage 08 The Anatomy of a Tree Even though we call it a tree, data scientists draw them upside down. Root Node: The top, where all data starts. Internal Node: A fork in the road where a decision is checked (e.g., Size ≤ 100). Terminal Node (Leaf): The final box that gives the prediction number. Interactive: Move your mouse over the canvas right now. The tree diagram will light up to trace the exact decision path for the region your cursor is in.

stages.title: The Overfitting Trap
stages.text: Stage 09 The Overfitting Trap What happens if we never tell the tree to stop? It will keep splitting until every single data point is alone in its own leaf, creating a zero-error fit on training data. This creates a massive risk of Overfitting —the model memorizes the random noise in our training set and fails to generalize to unseen houses. Bias-Variance Tradeoff Tree Depth Bias Variance Description Too Shallow High Low Underfits (Misses pattern) Balanced Medium Medium Best fit (Generalizes) Too Deep Low High Overfits (Memorizes noise) Overfit Comparison Depth 2 4 Leaves · Simplified Max Depth 10 Actual Leaves: 16 Note: After every training point is isolated, extra allowed depth no longer changes the tree.

stages.title: Stopping Rules
stages.text: Stage 10 Stopping Rules To prevent overfitting, we enforce Stopping Rules (also known as pre-pruning). We restrict depth and control minimum partition requirements before splits can occur. Validation Metric: RSS (Error Sum) MAE (Mean Error) RMSE (Typical Error) Metric Decoder Error Actual price − predicted price. RSS Σ(actual − predicted)² Add up all squared errors. Excellent for comparing model error, though numbers become quite large due to squaring. MAE average(|actual − predicted|) Average absolute mistake. Easiest to explain because it matches the original unit ($k). RMSE √average((actual − predicted)²) Square root of average squared error. Expressed in original units ($k), but heavily punishes larger individual mistakes. Example: If MAE = $30.0k, the model is off by about $30,000 on average. If RMSE = $33.0k, the typical error is about $33,000, with bigger mistakes punished more strongly. Why compare Train vs Validation? • Training Error tells us how well the tree fits the data it learned from. • Validation Error tells us how well it performs on unseen, hidden houses. • A deep tree can drive training error down to zero by memorizing noise, but will perform poorly on validation data. • Rule of thumb: Always choose settings that minimize validation error. If two trees perform similarly, choose the simpler one! Max Depth: 2 Min Samples per Leaf: 1 Total Leaf Nodes 4 ... Train RSS ... Validation RSS Current Decision Analysis Evaluating current parameters... The tuning curve changes max depth while holding leaf size fixed; the heatmap compares depth and leaf size together. How to Choose Stopping Rules Do not choose the model based solely on the lowest training error. Use validation error to estimate performance on unseen, real-world data. Prefer lower validation error. Minimize this value to find the sweet spot. If two settings perform similarly , always pick the simpler tree (Occam's razor). Use both rules together: max_depth limits levels, while min_samples_leaf prevents tiny leaves that isolate individual outliers. Notice that making the tree deeper eventually makes training error drop to 0, but the validation error starts increasing. That turning point is the sweet spot.

stages.title: Pruning: Let It Grow, Then Cut It Back
stages.text: Stage 11 Pruning: Let It Grow, Then Cut It Back Sometimes stopping early (pre-pruning) can be too short-sighted. It might stop before discovering splits that become useful in combination with other splits. The alternative is Post-Pruning : We allow the tree to grow deep first, and then collapse weak, low-utility sub-branches back into parent leaf nodes using a complexity penalty called ccp_alpha . Prune Weak Branches Success: Complexity penalized. The weak bottom splits did not support generalization on validation data. Post-pruning successfully reduced validation error by 7.7% (from 7,100 down to 6,550 )! Look at the canvas to see the overgrown staircase collapse into a cleaner, stable staircase when pruned.

stages.title: Trees vs. Lines
stages.text: Stage 12 Trees vs. Lines Linear regression fits a smooth, straight line. It assumes a constant rate of change. Regression trees carve the world into intervals and assign a flat average to each. Show Tree Model (Indigo) Show Linear Model (Green) Show Tree Errors Show Linear Errors If the data has sudden thresholds or "if/then" behaviors, trees capture it naturally. If it's a smooth trend, lines win.

The prediction is the average price of that leaf, not a guaranteed exact price. Metric Interpretation Training Train RSS: 1,750 Train MAE: $9.4k Train RMSE: $10.5k Validation Val RSS: 6,550 Val MAE: $30.0k Val RMSE: $33.0k • RSS: total squared error. Lower is better. • MAE: average absolute mistake. • RMSE: typical prediction mistake, with larger errors punished more heavily. Interpretation: Validation RMSE = $33.0k means that on unseen validation houses, the model is typically off by around $33,000. This is more realistic than the training error because the validation houses were not used to grow the tree. Common Mistake: “Do not say: The model is always correct.” Correct Interpretation: “Say: The model gives an estimate based on the average price of similar training houses in the same leaf.”

stages.title: Reality Check: Limitations
stages.text: Stage 15 Reality Check: Limitations While extremely powerful and explainable, single regression trees have key engineering limitations that you must look out for in practice. Poor Extrapolation Trend Fail Trees predict flat averages. If a house size is larger than any seen in training (e.g., 220 m²), the tree cannot continue a trend upward; it flatlines at the average of the largest leaf. Jagged Step Predictions Staircase Real-world factors often rise smoothly. Trees build staircases with sudden step jumps, struggling to cleanly represent smooth curves without huge depths. High Instability (Variance) High Variance A tiny shift in data (e.g., swapping one point's price) can completely re-arrange the root split boundary, producing a highly unstable prediction layout. Axis-Aligned Splits Orthogonal Basic trees split one feature at a time at right angles, making it difficult to capture diagonal correlations (like price dropping when size decreases and age increases simultaneously). Easy to Overfit High Complexity Without strict stopping rules or pruning, deep trees will easily grow until they isolate every single point, memorizing individual training points instead of discovering generalizable patterns. Interactive Demo: Click any card above to see a live visual simulation of that limitation on the right canvas.

stages.title: Synthesis
stages.text: Stage 16 Synthesis Let's review the final sequence to build and use a regression tree: 1. Put all training data in the Root Node . 2. Test possible splits (greedy thresholds) across all available features. 3. Pick the feature/split that results in the lowest RSS . 4. Repeat the process recursively inside each new branch. 5. Use validation error to choose stopping rules or pruning, instead of trusting training error alone. 6. Each final leaf predicts the average target value inside that leaf. While a single regression tree can be unstable on its own, this recursive logic is the fundamental building block for advanced modern algorithms like Random Forests and Gradient Boosting . Ensemble Learning: Ensembles improve single trees by combining hundreds of them, smoothing out jagged steps and yielding highly stable predictions.

stages.title: The Model Scorecard
stages.text: Stage 07 The Model Scorecard How much can we trust this line? We grade the model using your live data: R² (Proportion of Variation Accounted For): 0.00 R² tells us what proportion of the observed variation in test scores is accounted for by the fitted model using study hours; it does not establish causation. 1.0 means zero residual error on these data. We compare our line's errors (SSE) against the errors of just guessing the flat average (SST). R² = 1 - (SSE / SST) 🧠 What SST actually is SST = Total variation in your data It measures: "How spread out are the actual scores from the average score?" SST = Σ(y - ȳ)² Translate that into English y = actual value (like a student's score) ȳ = average of all scores y - ȳ = distance from the mean square it → so negatives don't cancel positives sum everything (Σ) → total spread 🔢 Step-by-step example Using your live data! The current average score (ȳ) is 0.0 . Score (y) Distance (y - ȳ) Squared (y - ȳ)² SST Total = 0.0 🔥 Why SST matters in R² SST is the "baseline total spread" (if we just guessed the average). SSE is how much error our fitted model still has. R² tells us what proportion of the original variation (SST) our fitted model accounts for. 1.0 means zero residual error on these data. RSE (Residual Standard Error): 0.00 This is the typical size of our miss. When we predict a score, we are typically off by this many points. Can we trust the line? Inspect residual-versus-fitted values for curvature and changing spread, a Q–Q plot when classical inference requires residual normality, and leverage/Cook’s distance for influential observations. Independence comes from the study design. Intervals answer different questions: a confidence interval describes uncertainty in the estimated mean response; a wider prediction interval describes uncertainty for one new observation. A high R² does not prove that the model is correct, causal, or useful on new data.

title: Support Vector Machines — Separate classes with breathing room

stages.title: Points, labels, and a decision boundary
stages.text: Stage 01 · Observe Points, labels, and a decision boundary Each point is one labelled training row with two features. Colour marks the class. A classifier needs a rule that places a future point on one side or the other. f(x) > 0  →  Class +1 f(x) < 0  →  Class −1 In two dimensions the boundary is a line. In three dimensions it is a plane. Beyond that, it becomes a hyperplane , a dramatic name for the same separating idea. The plot uses two features because humans remain tragically dependent on visible space. The model itself can work with many features.

stages.title: Why not choose any separating line?
stages.text: Stage 02 · Question Why not choose any separating line? When the classes are separable, several lines can classify every training point correctly. Training accuracy alone cannot tell us which line is safer. Narrow clearance Fits the training rows, but a small measurement change can flip a prediction. Wide clearance Leaves more room before the nearest point crosses the boundary. A linear SVM adds a preference: choose the separator with the greatest distance to the closest points from either class. Quick check: what extra criterion does SVM use? It chooses the separating line with the largest margin, subject to the model’s allowance for violations.

controls.text: Quick check: what extra criterion does SVM use? It chooses the separating line with the largest margin, subject to the model’s allowance for violations.

stages.title: The margin is protected space
stages.text: Stage 03 · Understand The margin is protected space The margin is the gap between two parallel support planes touching the closest training points on each side. Boundary: wᵀx + b = 0 Margin boundaries: wᵀx + b = +1 and −1 Geometric margin width = 2 / ‖w‖ Maximising the margin is equivalent to keeping the weight vector small while still satisfying the classification constraints. A wide margin can make the separator less sensitive. It cannot rescue biased data, leakage, poor labels, or a mismatched kernel. Geometry is useful, not divine intervention.

stages.title: Support vectors are the points that matter most
stages.text: Stage 04 · Focus Support vectors are the points that matter most Support vectors lie on or inside the margin. They directly constrain the fitted boundary. f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ yᵢ K(xᵢ, x) + b Only rows with αᵢ > 0 are support vectors. Move a distant, safely classified point a little and the boundary may not change. Move a support vector and the solution can shift immediately. Important distinction: “support vector” means the row constrains this fitted margin. It does not mean the row is causally or commercially important in every possible sense.

stages.title: Hard margins break when reality overlaps
stages.text: Stage 05 · Relax Hard margins break when reality overlaps A hard-margin SVM demands perfect separation with every row outside the margin. Real classes overlap, labels contain errors, and outliers appear because datasets enjoy sabotage. A soft-margin SVM introduces slack variables ξᵢ so violations are allowed but penalised. yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ,  with ξᵢ ≥ 0 Slack Meaning ξ = 0 Correct and on or beyond the margin 0 < ξ ≤ 1 Correct side, but inside the margin ξ > 1 Misclassified

stages.title: C decides how expensive violations are
stages.text: Stage 06 · Tune C decides how expensive violations are minimise  ½‖w‖² + C Σᵢ ξᵢ Small C Violations are cheaper. The model accepts more errors to preserve a wider, smoother margin. Large C Violations are expensive. The model fits training rows more aggressively, often with a narrower margin. C is an inverse regularisation parameter: larger C means less regularisation. A huge C does not mean “more accurate”. It means “punish training violations more”, which can also mean “memorise the noise with confidence”.

stages.title: Scale features before comparing distances
stages.text: Stage 07 · Prepare Scale features before comparing distances SVM geometry uses dot products and distances. A feature ranging from 0 to 100,000 can dominate another ranging from 0 to 1, even when the smaller-scale feature is genuinely informative. standardised value = (value − training mean) ÷ training standard deviation Fit the scaler inside each training fold, then apply that fitted transformation to validation, test, and production rows. Two distinct failures: scaling before the split leaks information; scaling the test set separately changes the coordinate system. Both are wrong in impressively different ways.

stages.title: Hinge loss ignores easy correct points
stages.text: Stage 08 · Formalise Hinge loss ignores easy correct points hinge loss = max(0, 1 − y × f(x)) Signed margin y f(x) Loss Interpretation ≥ 1 0 Correct and safely beyond the margin 0 to 1 positive Correct but inside the margin ≤ 0 ≥ 1 Misclassified Once a point is correctly beyond the margin, its hinge loss is zero. Distant easy points stop pulling the boundary. Quick check: y f(x) = 1.7. What is the loss? max(0, 1 − 1.7) = 0 .

controls.text: Quick check: y f(x) = 1.7. What is the loss? max(0, 1 − 1.7) = 0 .

stages.title: The decision score is not automatically a probability
stages.text: Stage 09 · Interpret The decision score is not automatically a probability The decision function reports which side of the boundary a row occupies and how strongly it lies in that direction. larger positive f(x) → stronger Class +1 decision larger negative f(x) → stronger Class −1 decision For a linear SVM, the score relates to signed distance after accounting for ‖w‖ . For a kernel SVM, treat it as a boundary score rather than literal distance in the original plot. f(x) = 2 does not mean 200%, nor twice the probability of f(x) = 1 . Probability estimates require a separate calibration model fitted with held-out predictions.

stages.title: A straight boundary cannot solve every pattern
stages.text: Stage 10 · Extend A straight boundary cannot solve every pattern Imagine one class forming an inner cluster and another forming an outer ring. No straight line can separate them in the original two-feature space. A transformed feature such as squared radius can reveal the structure: r² = x₁² + x₂² In transformed space, a simple threshold on r² can separate inner from outer points. A curved boundary in the original plot can still correspond to a linear rule elsewhere.

stages.title: The kernel trick avoids explicit feature explosion
stages.text: Stage 11 · Kernelise The kernel trick avoids explicit feature explosion A kernel computes similarities that behave like inner products in a richer feature space, without explicitly constructing every transformed coordinate. K(x, z) = φ(x)ᵀφ(z) RBF: K(x,z) = exp(−γ ‖x − z‖²) Small gamma Each point has broad influence. The decision surface changes slowly. Large gamma Influence becomes local. The boundary can wrap tightly around training points. Large gamma plus large C can create an intricate boundary that remembers noise instead of learning structure.

stages.title: Tune the whole pipeline inside cross-validation
stages.text: Stage 12 · Validate Tune the whole pipeline inside cross-validation Kernel, C , gamma , class weights, and preprocessing are hyperparameters. Choose them using validation folds inside the development data. Pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()) GridSearchCV(C, gamma, kernel, scoring) Create an untouched final test set when the dataset is large enough. Fit scaling and feature processing inside each training fold. Score candidate settings using a metric aligned with the task. Refit on all development data, then evaluate once on the test set. Search C and gamma on logarithmic scales. If the winner sits at the edge, extend the range rather than declaring the boundary divinely optimal.

stages.title: Measure the errors the problem actually cares about
stages.text: Stage 13 · Evaluate Measure the errors the problem actually cares about Accuracy alone can hide minority-class failures. Use confusion matrices, per-class recall, and precision–recall analysis when the positive class is rare. Class imbalance Consider class weights when minority-class mistakes deserve a larger penalty. Operational thresholds Tune the decision threshold on validation data when the default boundary is unsuitable. Calibration Map held-out SVM scores to probabilities using sigmoid, isotonic, or another calibration method. Multiclass Combine binary models using one-vs-rest or one-vs-one decisions. One-vs-one classifiers: K(K−1)/2 One-vs-rest classifiers: K A calibrated 0.8 has a frequency meaning: among cases assigned about 0.8, roughly 80% should belong to that class. Raw margin scores make no such promise.

stages.title: Change the knobs and watch the boundary answer back
stages.text: Stage 14 · Practice & Synthesis Change the knobs and watch the boundary answer back The playground fits a small SVM directly in your browser. Change the dataset, kernel, C , and gamma . Click the plot to add a labelled point. Support vectors are ringed. scale within a pipeline start linear when appropriate cross-validate C and kernel inspect support-vector count measure class-specific errors calibrate only when needed Strengths Effective in high dimensions, flexible kernels, margin regularisation, sparse dependence on support vectors. Limits Kernel training can scale poorly, tuning matters greatly, probabilities are not native, nonlinear models are hard to interpret globally. Final concept check: extremely large RBF gamma? Each point’s influence becomes very local, enabling an irregular boundary and increasing overfitting risk.

stages.title: The Raw Data & The Question
stages.text: Stage 01 The Raw Data & The Question Before any complex math, a time series begins as a sequence of observations. Imagine a company asking: "What will product demand look like over the next two years?" In standard data analysis, you can shuffle rows without losing meaning. In time series, order matters. Because today affects tomorrow, shuffling the dates destroys the story. Data Generation Parameters Trend Strength 1.0 Seasonality 15 Noise Level 10 Month (t) Observed Demand (Y) Displaying first 5 of 120 observations.

stages.title: The Time Plot
stages.text: Stage 02 The Time Plot The very first step in analysis is visual. A Time Plot connects our raw observations chronologically. By mapping time on the x-axis and our measured value on the y-axis, human intuition can instantly spot behaviors that spreadsheets hide. Does the sequence climb steadily? Does it repeat in a wave? Are there violent spikes? Hover over the canvas to inspect the exact values at any point in time.

stages.title: Decomposing the Pattern
stages.text: Stage 03 Decomposing the Pattern A time series is rarely a single, simple movement. We can typically decompose it into three underlying structural components: Trend Seasonality Noise / Residual Additive Decomposition Model Y t = T t + S t + R t Observed Data = Long-term Trend + Repeating Seasonality + Remainder (Noise) Note: The lines displayed on the canvas represent the exact, known components used to generate our simulation, rather than an estimated decomposition. In practice, models must infer these hidden components from the raw data.

stages.title: The Assumption of Stationarity
stages.text: Stage 04 The Assumption of Stationarity Many advanced statistical models require a series to be stationary before forecasting. For weak stationarity, the mean and finite variance are constant, and autocovariance depends only on lag, not calendar time. Stationarity Conditions Constant Mean: The average does not drift up or down. Constant Variance: The spread (volatility) stays consistent. Lag-dependent Autocovariance: Covariance between observations depends on how far apart they are, not when they occur. Watch the rolling moving average on the plot. If it climbs or falls significantly, the mean is not constant. This series violates the assumptions of basic autoregressive modeling and requires transformation.

stages.title: Fixing It: Differencing
stages.text: Stage 05 Fixing It: Differencing To stabilize the mean of a trending series, we apply differencing . Instead of looking at raw values, we analyze the change between consecutive months. Apply 1st-Order Differencing Y' t = Y t - Y t-1 Differencing can remove or reduce certain trends and help achieve stationarity. Check the transformed series: one difference does not guarantee stationarity. 0.00 Mean (Raw Series) 0.00 Mean (Differenced)

stages.title: Looking to the Past (Lags & ACF)
stages.text: Stage 06 Looking to the Past (Lags & ACF) A massive concept here is a lag —looking backward in time. Today's demand might be highly correlated with demand from exactly 12 months ago. The Autocorrelation Function (ACF) mathematically measures how strongly a series is related to its own past values across different lags. Max Lags to Compute 24 How to read this genuinely computed ACF: Bars outside the approximate confidence bounds suggest autocorrelation at those lags, but interpret the pattern collectively and in the context of the fitted model. Repeating spikes may suggest seasonality; confirm with residual ACF and model diagnostics. Use the PACF to examine the additional association at a lag after shorter lags are accounted for. After fitting, inspect the residual ACF and use a Ljung–Box test as an omnibus diagnostic. Seasonal or non-stationary series can make individual lag bars misleading.

stages.title: Forecasting the Future
stages.text: Stage 07 Forecasting the Future Validation must move forward in time. Never randomly shuffle observations. Use a chronological holdout, expanding-window evaluation, or rolling-window evaluation, and state whether forecasts are one-step or multi-step. Compare against naïve, seasonal-naïve, drift and moving-average baselines before treating a complex forecast as useful. Since this is an interactive environment, we project the future using a structural simulation forecast built from our known trend and seasonal generators, rather than estimating an ARIMA model from scratch. Forecast Horizon (Months) 24 Prediction Intervals A forecast is an estimate, not a prophecy. The shaded area represents the 95% prediction interval . Note: The expanding fan shown here is a simplified heuristic to illustrate how uncertainty accumulates over time, rather than a mathematically derived forecast variance.

stages.title: Diagnostics: Evaluating Residuals
stages.text: Stage 08 Diagnostics: Evaluating Residuals How do we know if a real-world forecasting model is adequate? We subtract the model's historical predictions from the actual raw data to check the residuals . Residual t = Actual Y t - Predicted Y t What Good Residuals Look Like Centered around zero: No overall drift up or down. Constant spread: Variance shouldn't wildly fan out. No waves or patterns: All seasonality and trend should be captured by the model. Occasional outliers: Random spikes are normal, but they shouldn't cluster. Simulate a "Bad" Model (Leftover Pattern) Toggle the switch to see what happens when a model fails to capture the underlying seasonality. A robust model leaves residuals that closely resemble pure random noise.

stages.title: Limitations & Caveats
stages.text: Stage 10 Limitations & Caveats Time series models fundamentally rely on the assumption that the future will structurally resemble the past . It is crucial not to overclaim the certainty of any forecast. What Models Can't Do Black Swan Events: Standard models cannot predict unprecedented external shocks (pandemics, sudden market crashes). Structural Breaks: If a company pivots its business model at month 100, data from month 1 is no longer highly relevant. Infinite Horizons: Prediction intervals eventually grow so wide that long-term forecasts become practically useless.
